items.title: Η μινιμαλίστρια μαμά χρησιμοποιεί 10 κόλπα από το «σύστημα καθαρισμού της Disney» για να κρατήσει το σπίτι της καθαρό το Magic Kingdom
items.titleOriginal: Minimalist mom uses 10 tricks from ‘Disney cleaning system’ to keep her home Magic Kingdom clean
items.description: Εκατομμύρια άνθρωποι επισκέπτονται τα πάρκα Walt Disney World κάθε χρόνο. Το 2024, 52 εκατομμύρια άνθρωποι έκαναν ένα ταξίδι στα έξι πάρκα της εταιρείας. Παρά τους τρελούς αριθμούς επισκεψιμότητας, τα πάρκα έχουν σταθερή φήμη για την καθαριότητα. Η Robyn Buchanan, μια YouTuber γνωστή ως Minimalist Home, εξήγησε σε ένα πρόσφατο βίντεο πώς διατηρεί το σπίτι της οργανωμένο και τακτοποιημένο με την Disney…
items.descriptionOriginal: Millions of people visit Walt Disney World parks every year. In 2024, 52 million people made a trip to the company’s six parks. Despite insane attendance numbers, the parks have a solid reputation for cleanliness. Robyn Buchanan , a YouTuber known as Minimalist Home , explained in a recent video how she keeps her home organized and tidy with Disney-inspired cleaning tips that its parks use to stay spotless despite “tens of thousands of people walking around every day with turkey legs, ice cream, sticky children, Dole Whips, and churros.” She adds that Disney has built “an entire system around keeping the parks clean.” Disney’s cleaning systems Disney employees, known as cast members, follow specific cleaning systems, procedures, and expectations that do not rely on motivation to get cleaning done, a major selling point Buchanan points out about home cleaners looking to Disney for inspiration. She notes a major downfall for home cleaning is the phrase: “I’ll clean when I feel like I should.” Instead of waiting for motivation to strike, she offers a few ways to get little jobs done each day, including: After dinner, wipe down the countertops. When the dishwasher finishes, empty it. Before bed, do a five-minute reset. On garbage day, empty all little bins in your home. “You don’t have to have a conversation with yourself every single time. The trigger is what makes the decision for you,” she added. View this post on Instagram 10 Disney cleaning tips Tip #1: Don’t save the mess for later Disney takes care of messes right away. Spills are cleaned up, and litter is immediately thrown into a bin. “Cleaning is happening continuously while the park is operating,” she said. “They’re not waiting until closing time going, ‘Right, well, let’s see what 50,000 people have done today.’” By utilizing small cleaning resets, which Buchanan refers to as the DASH Method, she explained, “You deal with little things as you move through your day” to avoid needing a full day of cleaning (along with a motivational speech to get you going). “You’re not constantly cleaning. You’re just preventing tomorrow’s cleaning job from becoming enormous,” she said. Tip #2: The 30-step trash can rule This rule was created by Walt Disney himself. Buchanan stated that Disney “wanted his guests to be roughly 30 steps from any garbage can.” The reason? “If throwing away something is easy, people are so much more likely to do it. If the garbage can is nowhere near you, suddenly that tiny wrapper becomes a logistical problem,” she explained. This translates into homes. “If garbage constantly collects beside your son’s computer, maybe you need a little garbage bin in a better spot,” Buchanan suggested. “If clothes always land on your bathroom floor, but your hamper is in your bedroom, maybe the hamper is in the wrong place.” She emphasized that putting in cleaning systems within your house where certain behaviors naturally happen is key for helping to keep your home clean. Tip #3: Put things at the point of performance Buchanan stated that Disney utilizes this tip by placing garbage cans near where garbage is likely to happen “near food, near exits, near places where somebody suddenly realizes they’re carrying what they don’t want anymore.” Buchanan explained that, in the home, this can look like keeping “cleaning cloths in the bathroom, a hamper where clothes come off, keep box cutters where you’re constantly opening up packages, putting a donation box near the closet where you usually decide you don’t want something.” She added, “Disney organizes according to what people actually do.” Tip #4: Design for prevention Disney specifically designs its parks for fewer messes to happen in the first place. Buchanan assured her viewers the same can be done at home. “If the front entrance is constantly exploding with shoes, bags, and jackets, the answer may not be: ‘I need to tidy this more often.’ Maybe you need hooks or fewer shoes there. Maybe every person needs one basket,” she said. This includes keeping cleaning tools and supplies close to where you use them in the home so they are easily accessible when needed. “I have toilet cleaner in every bathroom. I have cleaning cloths in every bathroom. I even have a few broom and dustpan sets a few places in my house—by the fireplace, down where the cat’s litter box is—where I feel like I need them!” said Buchanan. Tip #5: “Go Away Green” Buchanan explained that Disney uses muted colors, including one called “Go Away Green,” which doesn’t draw eyes or attention to things such as utility boxes, doors, and equipment. “The idea isn’t that the object disappears—it’s just that your brain really doesn’t pay much attention to it,” she noted. “I feel like Disney gave clutter a boring dress code, and I’m here for it.” At home, you can adopt the same method. She explained how “Bright cords, random containers, different colored baskets, a black charger hanging down a white wall” can all shout for attention. For boring functional items in the home, she suggested blending them into the room using “matching baskets, neutral storage, cord covers.” Tip #6: The utilidors Disney has a unique underground system of tunnels called utilidors that help keep behind-the-scenes operations of the parks, including moving cast members around, storing supplies, and other necessary logistics, out of sight. Buchanan compared it to managing a well-run home that needs discreet places to keep “cleaning supplies, tools, overflow pantry food, returns, recycling, half-finished projects, the vacuum—all the boring infrastructure required to operate a household. We need things neat, tidy, and organized.” In her home, Buchanan has a basket where she keeps returns, a linen closet, and a broom closet where she keeps things intentionally stored and out of sight to prevent clutter. Tip #7: Everybody picks up the trash This Disney rule is Buchanan’s favorite because parks are kept clean not just by custodial staff—but by all staff. When they see something that needs attention, they see to it. She added that it means “cleanliness has become part of the culture. It’s not just one person’s job.” She urged using the same philosophy in homes, with every family member contributing to help keep the house clean. “Everyone who lives in the house has some ownership of the space,” she added. View this post on Instagram Tip #8: Give people actual zones Custodial work at Disney is divided up into clear zones with clear responsibility. Designating the same format to family members at home (i.e., someone is responsible for taking out the trash, putting shoes away, or unloading the dishwasher on specific days) is another easy way to make sure the house stays clean. Tip #9: The overnight reset Buchanan pointed out that overnight at Disney parks, a lot is happening when guests aren’t paying attention. This includes landscaping, maintenance, and more before the next day begins. At home, the same reset can be implemented. “Not a deep clean, not an hour,” said Buchanan. But giving the kitchen a final wipe down, clearing off counters, and starting the dishwasher to ensure a fresh start for the morning can make a big difference. Tip #10: Clean in the same order Disney uses the same general cleaning sequence every time, which Buchanan thinks is an underestimated benefit that can also be done at home. “When you clean a room in different order every time, you keep having to think about what comes next,” she explained. “I like to take the ‘think’ out of everything.” She recommended creating a sequence for yourself. “For example: garbage, laundry, things that don’t belong, surfaces, floors, done.” She continued, “You can use whatever order makes sense for you. But the point is that your brain eventually learns it so it just goes on autopilot so you can just zone out.” The post Minimalist mom uses 10 tricks from ‘Disney cleaning system’ to keep her home Magic Kingdom clean appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο ειδικός στην επικοινωνία μοιράζεται το «κόλπο της Taylor Swift» για τέλεια ολοκλήρωση μιας ομιλίας σε 3 βήματα
items.titleOriginal: Communication expert shares ‘Taylor Swift trick’ for perfectly wrapping up a speech in 3 steps
items.description: Το 2022, η Taylor Swift έδωσε μια εναρκτήρια ομιλία στο Yankee Stadium σε αποφοίτους του Πανεπιστημίου της Νέας Υόρκης. Μίλησε για σχεδόν μισή ώρα και έλαβε επίσης επίτιμο διδάκτορα. Ενώ ορισμένοι μπορεί να θεωρήσουν μάλλον ανόητη την έννοια των επίτιμων διδακτορικών που δίνονται σε διασημότητες, σύμφωνα με πληροφορίες, πολλοί από τους φοιτητές είχαν μια έκρηξη. Αλλά ένας ειδικός στην επικοινωνία έχει χρησιμοποιήσει…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 2022, Taylor Swift gave a commencement speech at Yankee Stadium to New York University graduates. She spoke for nearly half an hour and also received an honorary doctorate. While some might find the notion of honorary doctorates given to celebrities rather silly, reportedly many of the students had a blast. But one communication expert has used the speech to exemplify an excellent trick for winding down a speech. Author Dorie Clark analyzed Swift’s words to illustrate how beautifully the singer crafted her speech. She noted that there are three “powerful public speaking strategies” Swift used and made it clear that these methods can be helpful for anyone who has to give a speech. Clark stated, “Taylor Swift has a trick for turning a good speech into a great one. Once you see it, you’ll want to use it every single time.” View this post on Instagram Trick for closing a speech In an Instagram clip captioned “The Taylor Swift trick for closing a speech,” Clark first introduced herself. “I taught communications at Duke University for over a decade, and I’ve coached hundreds of senior leaders from top companies. And I have rarely seen someone close a speech as well as Taylor Swift’s 2022 commencement address at NYU when she received an honorary doctorate. So watch how she closes the speech.” The clip then cut to Swift, clad in a purple (and somehow stylish) graduation gown, her cap perfectly tilted like a French beret. Swift said, “And as long as we are fortunate enough to be breathing, we will breathe in, breathe through, breathe deep, and breathe out.” Swift paused and half-smiled. “And I am a doctor now, so I know how breathing works.” This got a big laugh from the audience. Back to Clark, who broke down why Swift’s closing was so effective. “Watch what she’s not doing. Lots of speakers want to end on an ‘up’ note. So they’re too eager to assure people, ‘You can do it. It will all be fine!’ It’s too easy. Taylor didn’t do that. Instead, she used three easy, powerful public speaking strategies that you can use in your next talk. 3 public speaking strategies “First, she’s meeting the audience where they are. They’re nervous about their future. They’re worried about the direction. And she acknowledges that. Breathe in. Breathe out. It’s also a very good Easter egg, if you listen to her music.” Next, Clark noted, is humor. “Second, she ends with a joke! She’s a ‘doctor’ now. Humor always helps.” “And third, and most importantly,” Clark continued, “She shows them that she’s one of them. That’s one of the most powerful things that speakers can do. Unite people that they’re speaking to and show them ‘we are all in it together.’ That’s true whether you’re a rock star like Taylor Swift, showing you’re also just another NYU grad. Or a regular person who has influence in your company or your club or your school.” Clark reiterated that anyone can use this approach. “So the next time you give a speech, think about those three things. How can you meet the audience where they are? Use humor. And show them that we’re all in it together.” Many commenters appreciated the advice, though a few noted that Swift wasn’t exactly “one of us.” One Instagrammer did playfully point out, that while Clark’s points are helpful and true, Clark just might also be a “Swiftie.” View this post on Instagram The post Communication expert shares ‘Taylor Swift trick’ for perfectly wrapping up a speech in 3 steps appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το 1975, ένας ηθοποιός ξεδίπλωσε μια σεξιστική αγανάκτηση κατά του Τζόνι Κάρσον. Η Shelley Winters αρνήθηκε να καθίσει σιωπηλή.
items.titleOriginal: In 1975, an actor unfurled a sexist rant on Johnny Carson. Shelley Winters refused to sit silently.
items.description: Οι ηθοποιοί και οι διάσημες προσωπικότητες λαμβάνουν εκτεταμένη επίσημη εκπαίδευση στα μέσα ενημέρωσης και δημοσίων σχέσεων. Εξάλλου, τα στούντιο δεν μπορούν να κάνουν viral βίντεο με τα αστέρια τους επειδή βάζουν το παροιμιώδες πόδι τους στο στόμα τους. Αλλά πριν από μερικές δεκαετίες; Τα πράγματα ήταν πολύ πιο γρήγορα και χαλαρά. Το κοινό αποκτούσε πρόσβαση σε διασημότητες μέσω talk show και ζωντανών συνεντεύξεων για τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: Actors and mainstream celebrities today receive extensive formal media and PR training. After all, studios can’t have clips of their stars going viral for putting their proverbial foot in their mouth. But a few decades ago? Things were a lot more fast and loose. The public was gaining access to celebrities via talk shows and live interviews for the very first time. It didn’t always go smoothly and led to some pretty tense yet entertaining moments on live television . Oliver Reed goes off on “women’s liberation” and Shelley Winters responds perfectly It was September 26, 1975, when Johnny Carson welcomed renowned actor Oliver Reed to the Tonight Show stage. The English actor starred in the film Oliver! , which won an Academy Award for Best Picture a few years earlier. Reed was invited on the show to promote a new film. Shelley Winters, herself a highly acclaimed, Oscar-winning actress, was interviewed on a previous episode. In addition to her Oscar, Winters also won a Golden Globe and a Primetime Emmy and was twice nominated for a BAFTA Award. During the interview, Winters sat just off-camera, to Reed’s side. It got off to a cheeky start when Reed, talking about Americans, said, “Some of them behave themselves, and some of them are quite loud.” He then glanced pointedly at Winters. Some more good-natured banter went back and forth before Reed, feeling too often interrupted by a chatty Winters, cut her off and said, “I’m sorry, I thought it was my turn.” It was all in good fun, or at least mostly. Eventually, Winters left the stage, claiming she “had to go.” That’s when Reed began taking his shots. “She’s alright, she can’t shout at us now,” he told Carson. “So much for women’s lib.” Carson asked him about the women’s liberation movement in the U.K., to which Reed responded: “The women in England are quite good. They’re always in the kitchen, so you can’t hear them when they shout. I think most women are happy in the kitchen.” He then added that men make better chefs. The audience booed, and Reed shushed them. Carson couldn’t help but chime in with a classic quip that earned him some applause: “I think if they paid women what they pay chefs, women would love to be in the kitchen.” Reed went on to say he believed a woman’s place was to take care of “her children and her man.” He received applause for this, and a small smattering of jeers and boos. Again, he shushed the audience, even going as far as to say, “Quiet woman!” to a particular jeerer. Then, he saw Shelley making her way back to the stage. Winters dumped her drink on Oliver Reed following sexist comments Winters didn’t say a word when she returned to the stage, yet Reed seemed to know what was coming. He stood up, held his arms at his sides, and stood still as she poured an entire glass of liquid directly onto his head. Then she left the stage again, and Reed sat down to continue the interview. Reed, to his credit, took it in stride with excellent comedic timing and attempted to continue his monologue without missing a beat: “I believe that women’s liberationists…” he began, to raucous laughter. “I believe that women’s liberationists sometimes do extraordinary things,” he finished, to more laughter. But it was clear he took issue with what Winters had done: “I don’t think, in actual fact, that it gives them much armament to their cause. I mean, the fact that I have been covered in whiskey, and it is whiskey, pays no cause to the lady. There are a lot of people that watch this program that will probably laugh at that, and there will be several who will probably be quite indignant. I am not indignant, because this is indicative of the bad manners of a lot of chauvinist ladies.” Carson wrapped it all up with a sly smile. “I like this show myself,” he said. A bit? Perhaps, but Reed was open about his beliefs It’s hard to say for sure whether the conflict and the whiskey dumping were entirely authentic or played up for entertainment. However, Reed had a reputation for being outspoken against the women’s liberation movement. He was also known as something of a volatile personality. In an infamous appearance on David Letterman’s show, Reed’s interview became quite hostile and was cut short. Another talk show appearance, After Dark in 1991, devolved into chaos when Reed clashed with the female guests, tried to kiss one of them, and was ejected from the studio. Reed later discussed the incident with Winters in an interview , saying it took him off guard. “I didn’t know what to say, so I said absolutely nothing,” he admitted before adding, “She’s a showman, and I’m a showman. That’s our business.” Reed died on May 2, 1999, after a drinking contest at a bar in Malta got out of hand while he was filming the movie Gladiator . Weirdly enough, he predicted this almost exactly five years earlier, quipping that he would die of laughter in a bar after taking on a ridiculous bet. 1970s, and previous decades, were rife with sexism in Hollywood and beyond Though Shelley Winters was a beloved movie star, understanding the Hollywood she came up in helps put her actions into greater context. Hollywood was not typically a friendly place for women like Winters. Star power often rested solely on beauty, with even top-billed actresses relegated to eye-candy roles or simple tropes. Winters herself debuted in film in the 1940s, when “ casting couch ” culture was at its worst and most pervasive. Even safe, lighthearted spaces like late-night talk shows often demeaned actresses. They would be grilled about their love lives and appearance rather than their career achievements. Winters, for her part, was known for not sitting idly by and tolerating sexism or discrimination of any kind. Vanity Fair writes, “Throughout her life she was a progressive, feminist, and civil rights advocate.” She attended a Democratic National Convention and spoke at a White House Correspondents’ Dinner around 1960. She also called out John F. Kennedy, directly to his face, for his father’s antisemitic views. She died in 2006, at the age of 85, as an iconic Hollywood trailblazer. She fought for women’s rights, defied ageism in Hollywood, and stood up to any and all loudmouths who tried to stand in her way. The post In 1975, an actor unfurled a sexist rant on Johnny Carson. Shelley Winters refused to sit silently. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο σύζυγος της Debbi Fields πόνταρε ότι δεν μπορούσε να βγάλει 50 $ σε πωλήσεις μπισκότων. Μια τελευταία ιδέα μάρκετινγκ της έχτισε μια αυτοκρατορία.
items.titleOriginal: Debbi Fields’ husband bet she couldn’t make $50 in cookie sales. A last-ditch marketing idea built her an empire.
items.description: Η χρονιά ήταν 1977 και η 20χρονη Debbi Fields μόλις είχε ανοίξει το Mrs. Fields Chocolate Chippery, το ταπεινό της κατάστημα με μπισκότα στο Palo Alto της Καλιφόρνια. Το πάθος της για το ψήσιμο ξεκίνησε στην εφηβεία της και μέχρι τότε είχε τελειοποιήσει τη συνταγή της. Χρησιμοποιώντας τα 5 δολάρια την ώρα που έβγαζε ως «ball girl», αγόραζε μόνο τα καλύτερα συστατικά. Αλλά δεν ήταν μόνο το εμπόρευμα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The year was 1977 , and 20-year-old Debbi Fields had just opened up Mrs. Fields Chocolate Chippery, her humble cookie shop in Palo Alto, California. Her passion for baking began in her teens, and by then she had perfected her recipe. Using the $5 an hour she made as a “ball girl,” she bought only the best ingredients . But it wasn’t just the ingredients that made Fields’ cookies stand out. Unlike the hard, small, crumbly, mass-produced cookies common at the time, her cookies were served warm, soft-baked, gourmet-style, and oversized. Baking despite the odds Although friends and family loved Fields’ baking, no one seemed to believe it could become a business. According to the University of New Hampshire’s Rosenberg International Franchise Center , Fields had to approach several banks before finally securing financing to open her debut shop. Even Debbi’s business-tycoon husband, Randall Fields, didn’t expect it to succeed. She later told the Los Angeles Times that he predicted she wouldn’t make a measly $50 in sales on opening day. As noon approached without a single sale, it looked like Randall was right. Then, Debbi had an idea. A Hail Mary tactic that turned into a genius marketing ploy She walked out of the shop with a tray of her freshly baked signature cookies and began handing them to passersby on the street. The strategy was pretty simple. Instead of trying to convince strangers to spend money on a cookie they had never tasted, Fields gave them a reason to come inside: let them try one first. And it worked. After one sample, folks were hooked, and they went in to buy more. Fields would end up making $75 that day, surpassing her husband’s cynical expectations. And the rest is cookie history As we all know, that first-day success grew to be something much bigger. Fields continued building her business, and over the years it grew from a cookie shop to a multi-million-dollar cookie empire. Fields became a celebrity of sorts, appearing on shows like Hollywood Squares and the new Mickey Mouse Club , writing several best-selling cookbooks, and appearing as a judge and mentor on Supermarket Superstar , a reality television series where culinary entrepreneurs compete to get their product into grocery stores. Although she sold the company to an investment firm in the ’90s, she remains the brand’s spokeswoman. At its height, Mrs. Fields operated hundreds of locations across the United States, as well as in Canada, England, Japan, Australia, and Hong Kong. And that little opening-day experiment of free samples became an important (and delicious) part of the company’s identity. Fields might not have had a business background, but she certainly had a natural entrepreneurial spirit. She had no real way to know whether free cookie samples would actually resonate with potential customers. Still, she believed she had something people wanted, and she was right. Her cookies would eventually become such a familiar part of American mall culture that it’s hard to picture a trip to the mall without encountering a Mrs. Fields sample. Which, of course, has a funny way of turning into a Mrs. Fields purchase. Fields had plenty of reasons to doubt her idea, especially with everyone else doubting her. But she kept believing in it, proving that sometimes you just have to trust your own special recipe and know the result will eventually speak for itself. The post Debbi Fields’ husband bet she couldn’t make $50 in cookie sales. A last-ditch marketing idea built her an empire. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Η μισή μεταμόσχευση μυελού των οστών διευρύνει τις επιλογές για παιδιά με σοβαρή απλαστική αναιμία
items.titleOriginal: Half-matched bone marrow transplant expands options for children with severe aplastic anemia
items.description: Ερευνητές στο Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center και στο Johns Hopkins Children's Center αναφέρουν ότι η μεταμόσχευση μυελού των οστών με τη χρήση μισοταιριασμένων οικογενειακών δωρητών πέτυχε ποσοστό επιβίωσης 96% μεταξύ παιδιών, εφήβων και νεαρών ενηλίκων ασθενών με σοβαρή απλαστική αναιμία, μια σπάνια, απειλητική για τη ζωή διαταραχή του μυελού των οστών.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center report that bone marrow transplant using half-matched family donors achieved a 96% survival rate among child, adolescent and young adult patients with severe aplastic anemia, a rare, life-threatening disorder in which the bone marrow fails to produce enough healthy blood cells. The approach expands access to potentially curative treatment for patients who do not have a fully matched donor.

items.title: Πόσο αξιόπιστη είναι η ανίχνευση καρκίνου του μαστού με τεχνητή νοημοσύνη; Νέα μέθοδος μετράει την αβεβαιότητα για μεμονωμένους ασθενείς
items.titleOriginal: How trustworthy is AI breast cancer detection? New method gauges uncertainty for individual patients
items.description: Ενώ η τεχνητή νοημοσύνη προσφέρει τη δυνατότητα βελτίωσης της ικανότητας των ανθρώπινων ειδικών να διαγιγνώσκουν και να θεραπεύουν ασθένειες όπως ο καρκίνος του μαστού, τα καλά δημοσιοποιημένα σφάλματα στον ευρύτερο τομέα της τεχνητής νοημοσύνης προκαλούν ανησυχία. Μια ομάδα από το Πανεπιστήμιο του Πίτσμπουργκ χρησιμοποίησε τον κορυφαίο υπερυπολογιστή Bridges-2 της PSC για να σχεδιάσει ένα βαθύ νευρωνικό δίκτυο (DNN) που λαμβάνει υπόψη την αβεβαιότητα…
items.descriptionOriginal: While AI offers the ability to improve human experts' ability to diagnose and treat diseases like breast cancer, well-publicized errors across the broader AI field are cause for concern. A team from the University of Pittsburgh has used PSC's flagship Bridges-2 supercomputer to design a deep neural network (DNN) that takes uncertainty into account in diagnosing breast scan images.

items.descriptionOriginal: Tuesday Labs, a New York City robotics lab and design studio, has opened reservations for Voxel, a bipedal home robot meant to learn and take over routine household tasks. A $200 reservation holds a spot, while full pricing is expected to be around $20,000 when Voxel ships sometime in 2028, The Verge reported. The company calls it a “droid butler.” The Series-1 model joins other household robots, such as Weave Robotics’ Isaac 1, that aim to handle chores beyond mopping or vacuuming floors. Arms, eyes and backward knees Voxel’s main tools are two highly articulated arms with seven degrees of freedom. Each ends in a simple gripper, not the dexterous fingered hand found on machines such as Boston Dynamics’ Atlas. The arms extend from the top of a torso that also serves as the head, which has a small mouth. Pixelated, animated eyes sit near the robot’s waist, well below a hidden pair of stereo RGB cameras. A separate wide-field camera lets Voxel monitor an entire room. It walks on a pair of Z-shaped legs with knees that bend opposite to human knees. The design is intentional, allowing the robot to bend its knees for balance and to raise or lower its height while standing close to kitchen cabinets, tables and shelves. In all, Voxel is mostly humanoid, with a few liberties. It trades finger dexterity for simpler grippers and puts its face lower on its body than a human would. What it is meant to do Tuesday Labs’ website details the hardware at length but says less about capabilities and household benefits. Voxel is meant to handle basic autonomous tasks, including decluttering and putting things back where they belong. It is also meant to handle routine chores such as watering plants, fetch items like books and help locate lost objects. For example, a user could ask where Voxel last saw the TV remote. At launch, Voxel will not cook dinner or change diapers. The Verge noted that if it can reliably remember where you left your keys, people with bad short-term memories might find a reason to justify its steep price. What to know before reserving The $200 reservation is separate from the roughly $20,000 full price. Voxel is expected to ship “sometime in 2028,” the report said, so buyers would wait at least a year or more for a unit.

items.description: Τα καρκινικά κύτταρα του παγκρέατος είναι εξαιρετικά καλά στην ανάπτυξη, αλλά νέα έρευνα δείχνει ότι δύο μικροσκοπικά μόρια που υπάρχουν ήδη στο σώμα μπορεί να βοηθήσουν στην επιβράδυνσή τους. Ερευνητές στο Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) και στο College of Education and Human Development διαπίστωσαν ότι τα αυξανόμενα επίπεδα δύο microRNAs, kn…
items.descriptionOriginal: Pancreatic cancer cells are remarkably good at growing, but new research suggests that two tiny molecules already present in the body may help slow them down. Researchers at the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) and the College of Education and Human Development found that increasing levels of two microRNAs, known as miR-15a and miR-16, reduced protein synthesis and slowed the growth of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells. In a study in Physiological Reports , the researchers also shared that patients with higher levels of the microRNAs in their tumors tended to live longer, further supporting their potential as targets for new pancreatic cancer treatments. “Cancer cells continually proliferate, or grow and divide,” says James Fluckey, associate dean for research and a professor in the kinesiology and sport management department and the study’s principal investigator. “To do that, the cells need to increase processes like protein synthesis that give them what they need to grow. If you disrupt that protein synthesis, you can slow the rate at which those cells can grow.” MicroRNAs are short strands of genetic material that help regulate which proteins a cell produces. Rather than providing instructions for making proteins themselves, they can bind to genetic messages and prevent those instructions from being translated into proteins. That gives microRNAs considerable influence over what happens inside a cell. Peter Nghiem, an associate professor in the VMBS veterinary integrative biosciences department, compared their role to the brakes on a car. “Their expression can prevent something very bad from happening—like accelerating to the point where you crash or develop cancer,” he says. When levels of miR-15a and miR-16 are reduced, as the researchers observed in pancreatic cancer, that braking effect may be diminished, so the team explored what happens when those microRNAs are added back. “The whole goal with this study was not to repair the brakes but bring the brakes back into the cell to see if we can slow down the progression of these cancer types,” Fluckey says. To test that idea, the researchers increased miR-15a and miR-16 in cultured PDAC cells. Doing so reduced both protein synthesis and cell proliferation. The study builds on the team’s previous research into miR-15a and miR-16 by examining how the two microRNAs influence protein production and cell growth in pancreatic cancer. The team also used computational analysis to identify the biological processes potentially influenced by the two microRNAs, revealing connections to a broad range of genes and pathways involved in cancer, protein metabolism, cell adhesion and other cellular processes. That broad influence could be particularly important because cancer is rarely driven by a single malfunctioning process. “We would love to find that magic bullet to say, ‘This is the molecule that causes cancer,’ but we can’t,” Fluckey says. “What we can say is that these microRNAs seem to have a vital role in the protein balance of the cell. When they are in abundance, we can dramatically slow the progression of that cancer.” The researchers next turned to publicly available patient data to determine whether the patterns they observed in cultured cells were also reflected in people with pancreatic disease. They found that miR-15a and miR-16 levels were lower in pancreatic tumors than in healthy pancreatic tissue. They also found that microRNAs were also reduced in samples from patients with pancreatitis, an inflammatory condition of the pancreas. Most notably, pancreatic cancer patients whose tumors had higher miR-15a and miR-16 expression had better survival outcomes than those with lower expression. Together, the patient data reinforced the researchers’ laboratory findings, showing that the same microRNAs that slowed cancer cell growth in cultured cells were also associated with better outcomes in people with pancreatic cancer. While the results point toward therapeutic possibilities, turning miR-15a and miR-16 into a treatment will require solving a major challenge: getting them to the right cells. The researchers’ next goal is to develop a delivery method capable of restoring the microRNAs specifically in cancer cells while leaving healthy cells alone. “We’re becoming more and more confident that the miR-15a and 16 interventions may truly have therapeutic potential,” Fluckey says. “Now we just have to figure out how to get it to cells in a way that we’re only treating the cells that are cancerous.” That specificity will be critical, Nghiem says, because microRNAs also perform important regulatory functions in healthy cells. The researchers also caution that restoring miR-15a and miR-16 is unlikely to become a stand-alone cure for pancreatic cancer; instead, it could eventually provide one component of a combination of treatments targeting the many biological processes involved in the disease. “It’s just not going to be one treatment for a disease,” Nghiem says. “MicroRNA-15a and 16 can be one important arm of a treatment regimen. As we do research, we’re going to find all of the pieces that come together eventually to effectively treat and hopefully cure patients with these devastating diseases.” For Fluckey, one of the most promising aspects of the research is that those potential tools already exist naturally within the body. “The therapeutic intervention that we’re looking at is already in your body,” he says. “We just have to figure out how to get it back in working order.” Source: Texas A&M University The post 2 molecules may help slow pancreatic cancer growth appeared first on Futurity .

Blocking the enzyme restored normal brain growth in mice.

items.descriptionOriginal: Meet Kolkata’s Alpona Didi. 🌺❤️ Every year before Diwali, 74-year-old Ratnabali Ghosh steps out at 5 AM to draw intricate traditional Alponas on the doorsteps of strangers. What may look like simple patterns carries a deeper meaning. In a city where many young people have moved away and elderly parents may be left feeling alone, her colourful artwork brings unexpected joy to people’s mornings. Inspired by generations of Bengali artistic tradition, Ratnabali is doing more than decorating doorsteps. She’s helping keep a fading cultural art form alive while reminding people that even a small gesture can make someone feel noticed and valued. Her story shows us that kindness doesn’t always need grand gestures. Sometimes, it begins with a few lines of art outside someone’s door. 🎨 Know someone who would love this story? Share it with them.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Creating a More Sustainable Workplace Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Customers, employees and clients are increasingly interested in how organisations manage energy, waste and travel, but creating a greener workplace doesn’t necessarily require a dramatic redesign or a huge environmental budget. The good news is that creating a greener workplace does not always require major investment. Often, the most effective changes are simple adjustments that reduce environmental impact while improving day-to-day operations. The workspace itself can play a big part. For some businesses, this could mean looking at how they use their office space, while others are reducing unnecessary travel and allowing their staff to work from home and only meeting face-to-face for genuine reasons. Those trying to reduce travel emissions find that some cities offer flexible office space, like Leeds . These coworking and flexible office options can reduce the need for employees to travel into a permanent office every day when face-to-face collaboration is only required occasionally. Businesses that require regular in-person collaboration are increasingly choosing locations with strong public transport connections. This can help reduce reliance on car travel and make lower-carbon commuting a practical choice for more employees. Make Energy Efficiency an Everyday Habit Energy efficiency sounds like a major infrastructure project, but plenty of improvements begin with ordinary workplace habits. Lights left on in empty meeting rooms, computers running overnight and heating operating when nobody is in the building all represent avoidable energy use. Reducing energy use can lower operating costs while also helping organisations cut the emissions associated with powering their workplace. Motion-sensitive lighting, sensible heating controls and making sure equipment is switched off when it isn’t required can make an immediate difference. Businesses can also look at practical ways to reduce workplace energy consumption , including reviewing heating schedules, monitoring usage and considering smarter controls. Make Greener Commuting Easier Supporting cycling, walking and public transport can be as simple as providing secure bike storage, showers or clearer information about nearby transport connections. Flexible and hybrid working can help too. Fewer commuting journeys can also help lower transport-related carbon emissions, making hybrid working beneficial for both employees and the environment. If employees don’t need to be physically present every day, reducing unnecessary journeys may be more practical than expecting everyone to commute simply because that’s how the working week has traditionally been structured. The key is making greener choices convenient. People are far more likely to change their habits when the alternative actually works for their lives. Reduce Waste Without Making Work More Complicated Sustainability initiatives tend to lose momentum when they create additional hassle. Waste reduction works best when the greener option is also the easiest one. Moving routine documents online can reduce unnecessary printing, while clearly labelled recycling points make it easier for employees to dispose of things correctly. Reviewing purchasing habits can help as well. Ordering fewer disposable supplies, reusing equipment where possible and resisting the temptation to replace perfectly serviceable office furniture all add up. Get the Team Involved Finally, no workplace sustainability plan will get very far if it exists only in a policy document nobody reads. Employees need to understand what the organisation is trying to achieve and, ideally, feel that they have some ownership of it. That might mean creating small team targets, inviting staff to suggest improvements or simply making recycling, energy saving and sustainable travel part of everyday workplace conversations. Progress doesn’t need to be turned into a competition, but sharing the results can help people see that individual actions genuinely add up. Over time, small changes to energy use, commuting habits and waste management can reduce a workplace’s environmental impact while supporting wider sustainability goals. The post Creating a More Sustainable Workplace appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Cloud Technology Can Support Business Sustainability Goals Reading Time: 2 minutes Businesses across the UK are facing more and more pressure to reduce their environmental impact while maintaining operational efficiency. Both customers and investors are paying closer attention to sustainability commitments, and many organisations are being encouraged to look for practical ways to make a real impact with long-term environmental goals. While most initiatives often focus on transport , energy use and supply chains, technology decisions also play an important role. Many organisations are now reviewing how their IT infrastructure contributes to their wider sustainability strategy. By adopting scalable digital solutions and working with providers that offer Managed Cloud services for improved efficiency and resource management , businesses can reduce unnecessary energy consumption while maintaining the performance and flexibility needed to support growth. Reducing reliance on energy-intensive on-site infrastructure Traditional on-site IT infrastructure can require significant resources to operate and maintain. Physical servers consume electricity around the clock and often require dedicated cooling systems to prevent overheating. As equipment ages, performance can decline, leading to increased maintenance demands and higher operating costs. Moving workloads into efficiently managed cloud environments can help reduce the energy demands associated with maintaining multiple on-site servers. For example, your business may replace ageing server equipment with cloud-hosted applications and storage solutions rather than investing in additional physical infrastructure. Supporting flexible and remote working Cloud technology has transformed the way employees access business systems and collaborate with colleagues. Staff can securely access files and data from different locations, whether they are working from home or visiting client sites. This flexibility can support your objectives by reducing the need for daily commuting and frequent business travel. For example, team members can collaborate on projects remotely using cloud-based platforms. Alongside environmental benefits, flexible access can improve employee satisfaction and help organisations attract and retain talent. Businesses that support remote working and secure access to business systems can often create a more agile, environmentally friendly operating model. Making better use of business resources Another advantage of cloud technology is scalability. Unlike traditional infrastructure , businesses do not need to purchase large amounts of hardware in anticipation of future demand. Instead, you can increase or decrease capacity as requirements change. For example, a retailer may temporarily increase storage or computing resources during a busy trading period without investing in additional physical equipment that may sit unused for much of the year. This approach helps reduce waste and prevents overinvestment. Improving monitoring and reporting Accurate data is essential for sustainability targets. Cloud-based platforms often provide advanced reporting and monitoring capabilities that can help you gain better visibility into your operations. You could use cloud-based dashboards to analyse performance metrics and identify inefficiencies across different departments or locations. This information can support more informed decision-making and help businesses prioritise areas for improvement. Better access to data can also assist with reporting, making it easier to measure progress against environmental goals and demonstrate accountability to stakeholders. To summarise… While sustainability requires a broad business commitment, being fully sustainable for many businesses is not something that can be achieved quickly. Cloud adoption can be an important step towards reducing resource consumption, improving operational efficiency and supporting long-term environmental goals. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim Reading Time: 3 minutes Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim According to a study published in Patient Safety and highlighted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), diagnostic errors accounted for 26.6% of closed medical malpractice claims reviewed over a 20-year period. Among all claims related to the diagnoses, 39% were fatal. Misdiagnosis and delay in diagnoses were the most often made claims. Medical malpractices have severe implications for patients, which may range from delays in treatment to deterioration of medical conditions or even disability and death. In the USA, one is entitled to filing medical malpractice if a healthcare professional fails to adhere to the acceptable level of care, resulting in preventable harm. There are actually more malpractice cases that happen in the healthcare industry than people realize. But it’s also important to understand that not all unfavorable medical outcomes qualify as malpractice. A claim will require evidence of negligence and resulting injury. But what is an example of malpractice ? Let’s take a closer look at the common medical errors and what steps you need to take to seek a possible claim. Diagnosis Is Where Most of It Happens In the AHRQ systematic review of ED care, the rate of diagnostic errors was found to be 5.7% with an extrapolated estimate of 7.4 million diagnostic errors and 371,000 severe harms per year associated with diagnostic errors. These overall rates were based on results from three prospective studies conducted outside of the U.S. in Canada, Spain, and Switzerland. AHRQ commissioned an independent review after its publication because of the high numbers that were cited. This is an order of magnitude, not a number count. Rates of disease-specific errors have higher validity. On average, physicians fail to diagnose stroke in about 17% of patients. The list is completed by myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, spinal cord compression, and venous thromboembolism. These conditions share a profile. They present atypically often enough that a physician working quickly can reach the wrong conclusion. The Procedure Itself Surgical and anesthesia errors sit at the opposite end of the evidentiary range. Wrong-site surgery. A retained sponge. An anesthesia dosing failure during a routine case. Proof of breach in wrong-site and retained object surgeries is seldom disputed since there is evidence of negligence in the records. Firms handling this work tend to sort it by mechanism rather than by specialty. Medical malpractice lawyers in Marietta, GA , separate birth injuries such as cerebral palsy, brachial plexus injury, and hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy from anesthesia errors, emergency room errors, and surgical errors. Medication Errors More defendants get implicated in medication cases than any other type. A prescriber orders a prescription, a pharmacist dispenses the prescription, a nurse delivers the prescription, and the electronic health record alerts for a possible drug interaction or not. Wrong dosage, lack of allergy information, and drugs with similar appearances on the screen cause claims. Each individual has his own employer and his own insurance. Birth Injuries Obstetric negligence claims hinge more on timing than anything else. Whether or not someone interpreted the fetal monitoring properly. How quickly the decision was made to utilize the C-section procedure. Whether or not the procedures used were appropriate for shoulder dystocia. These cases require more time than adult claims. In fact, some states also set a separate limitations period for minors in malpractice cases that ends well before adulthood. What Turns an Error Into a Claim Expert testimony does most of the work. A plaintiff cannot establish the standard of care without a qualified physician stating what it was. A number of states, including Georgia, require a sworn expert affidavit filed alongside the complaint. That single requirement can end a case before anyone takes a deposition. Damage caps are the other structural variable. It’s important to understand, though, that these caps could shift. The non-economic damage cap in California remained unchanged at $250,000 for decades before AB 35 changed it to $350,000 for cases other than death. It is at $500,000 for wrongful death starting from 2023, increasing by $40,000 and $50,000, respectively, each year for ten years. The distance between a medical error and a malpractice claim is mostly documentary. Whether the chart recorded the symptom the patient actually reported. Whether the monitoring strip survived. Whether anybody wrote down a time. Errors are common and claims are not, and most of what fills the space between those two facts is records that either exist or do not. The post Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. A new study found that excess RNA, including the normally essential messenger RNA (mRNA), can directly disrupt mitochondria without relying on the immune system. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells.

items.descriptionOriginal: October is a good time to grow spinach on your terrace in many parts of India, as temperatures begin to ease after the summer heat. With a few containers, suitable soil, and regular care, even a small terrace can provide fresh palak for everyday meals. The key is to give the plants enough light, maintain moisture in the soil, and choose growing conditions suited to the season. Vijay Sharma, a swimming coach at SP College in Bikaner , Rajasthan, knows the satisfaction of harvesting vegetables at home. He began gardening in 2017 after noticing that the quality of market-bought cluster beans was declining. Pleased with the results, he started growing spinach, okra, chillies, and other vegetables. During the COVID-19 lockdown, he expanded his garden to cover 1,500 square feet, growing more than 150 varieties of vegetables and medicinal plants. In a conversation with The Better Indi a published in October 2021, he shared how he prepared his growing medium, reused household materials as planters, and cared for his plants. His experience offers useful lessons for those planning to grow spinach this October. 1. Choose a suitable container Spinach grows well in containers, making it a practical choice for terrace gardeners. Choose a pot or grow bag at least six to eight inches deep, with drainage holes to prevent water from collecting around the roots. A wider container allows you to grow several plants together. October is a good time to grow spinach on your terrace in many parts of India. Photograph: (The Arbor Gate) The expert found creative ways to expand his garden when gardening supplies were difficult to access during the lockdown. He reused discarded drums, old tyres, and broken plastic containers as planters. For spinach, use a clean container that allows excess water to drain freely. Avoid overcrowding the plants, as adequate space helps leaves develop well. 2. Prepare a nutrient-rich growing medium Healthy leaves begin with good soil. Spinach needs a growing medium that retains moisture without becoming waterlogged. Sharma explains that he uses soil mixed with cow dung manure or cocopeat, with these materials accounting for around half of his growing mix. For spinach, combine garden soil with well-rotted compost and cocopeat to create a loose, moisture-retentive medium. Use mature compost rather than fresh manure, which can damage plants and is unsuitable for direct application to leafy vegetables. 3. Sow seeds directly into the pot Spinach seeds can be sown directly into the container where the plants will grow. Place them in shallow furrows, cover lightly with soil, and water gently. Keep the soil moist while the seeds germinate. Once seedlings appear, thin them out if they are growing too close together. This gives the remaining plants room to develop healthy leaves. October is suitable for sowing spinach in many parts of India, particularly northern regions where temperatures begin to fall. In warmer areas, choose a cooler spot on the terrace and avoid exposing seedlings to excessive afternoon heat. 4. Give spinach adequate sunlight Spinach needs sufficient sunlight for healthy growth, but intense heat can cause it to struggle. Choose a spot that receives several hours of sunlight, preferably in the morning if your terrace becomes very hot later in the day. The gardener has observed how vegetation can influence temperatures in his garden. He explains that creepers shelter his plants from direct sunlight and help cool the garden during summers when temperatures in Bikaner can approach 50 degrees Celsius. For spinach, aim for a balance. Avoid deep shade, but provide some protection from harsh afternoon sun in warmer regions. 5. Water regularly without soaking the soil Spinach needs consistent moisture, especially during germination and early growth . Dry soil can affect leaf development, while excess water can damage the roots. Spinach grows well in containers, making it a practical choice for terrace gardeners. Photograph: (Nature & Garden) Sharma advises beginners to pay attention to watering. "Watering the plants is equally important for their healthy growth," he says. Check the soil regularly and water when the surface begins to dry. Water gently around the base of the plants, allowing excess moisture to drain through the container. Pots exposed to strong sunlight or dry winds may need more frequent checks. 6. Feed the plants and keep an eye on their leaves A growing medium enriched with compost gives spinach a good start. If the plants remain in the same container for several weeks, add a light layer of mature compost around them to replenish nutrients. Inspect the leaves regularly for holes, discolouration, or pests. Remove damaged leaves and avoid overcrowding, which can restrict airflow. The gardener advises beginners to grow seasonal vegetables and says that plants need occasional trimming. For spinach, remove damaged foliage while leaving healthy leaves and the central growing point intact. 7. Harvest without uprooting the plant Once the outer leaves are large enough to use, harvest them carefully while leaving the central growing point undisturbed. This allows the plant to continue producing leaves. The first harvest may be ready in around four to six weeks , depending on the variety, temperature, and growing conditions. For a more regular supply, sow small batches of seeds at intervals rather than planting everything at once. For spinach, use a clean container that allows excess water to drain freely. Photograph: (Gardener's Path) Sharma's terrace garden shows how growing vegetables at home can begin with a simple experiment and expand over time. For beginners, a couple of spinach containers are a good starting point. TBI Gardening Calendar brings together what to plant, grow, and care for each month of the year, helping home gardeners make the most of their balconies, terraces, backyards, and small growing spaces. Each story focuses on seasonal plants and crops, with simple, practical guidance on when to sow or plant, how to care for them, and what to expect as they grow.

items.title: Είμαστε πολύ πιο κοντά στην προστασία του 30% του πλανήτη από όσο γνωρίζαμε. Αλλά υπάρχει μια σύλληψη.

items.description: Πρώτον, τα καλά νέα: Ο κόσμος μπορεί να είναι πολύ πιο κοντά από ό,τι πιστεύουμε σε έναν διεθνή στόχο προστασίας του 30% της γης έως το 2030. Τα κακά νέα: Μάλλον δεν είναι η σωστή γη. Τα έθνη του κόσμου έχουν θέσει προστασία στο 27% περίπου των χερσαίων μαζών του πλανήτη, πολύ περισσότερο από το 19% που πιστευόταν προηγουμένως, σύμφωνα με έρευνα που δημοσιεύθηκε πρόσφατα…
items.descriptionOriginal: First, the good news: The world might be a lot closer than we think to an international goal of protecting 30% of land by 2030. The bad news: It’s probably not all the right land. The nations of the world have placed protections on roughly 27% of the planet’s land masses, far more than the 19% previously thought, according to research recently published in Nature . There has been much hand wringing among conservation-minded folks that countries were woefully behind on land protection pledges made in 2022 to shield 30% of Earth’s land and 30% of the ocean from development as part of an update to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the main international agreement aimed at the current extinction crisis. But “our analysis suggests that much more of the land is in some type of conservation area than currently recognized,” said lead author Helen O’Neill, a postdoctoral researcher at the United Kingdom’s Institute of Zoology, London. The official tally tracking protected lands is a database at the Protected Planet website , a collaboration between the United Nations and the International Union for Conservation of Nature. While this is the authoritative source, it’s incomplete. Some protected land hasn’t been registered there by countries. And it doesn’t include significant acreage that falls into a kind of gray area – land that isn’t formally protected chiefly for wildlife, but where regulations provide many of the same benefits. Known as “other effective area-based conservation measures” or OECMs, this might include land protected as sacred by Indigenous groups or managed to improve water quality. O’Neill and 35 other scientists from across the globe set out to tally this overlooked land to create a more complete picture. To reduce the massive effort required to scrutinize the status of every piece of land on the planet, the researcher selected pieces totaling 10% of all the world’s land masses. That included terrain scattered across the world and covering major types of ecosystems, from the Rocky Mountains in Montana to the Amazonian jungle to the desert of the Arabian Peninsula. .IRPP_ruby where regulations and management practices made them good candidates for being OECMs. The scientists used the results to create a computer model that estimated how this pattern would apply to the entire world. The result was the encouraging estimate that 26.8% of all land is protected, at least on paper. But that doesn’t mean conservationists can cruise across the 2030 finish line with their arms raised. Because the research also revealed troubling holes in where these lands are being conserved. Of the 173 different ecological regions scientists have mapped around the world, fewer than 100 have greater than 17% of their land protected, the scientists estimated. Regions that are primarily ice and rock – polar and alpine landscapes – are significantly overrepresented in the catalog of protected areas. That’s not a big surprise, since those regions are often less attractive for human settlement or exploitation by farming or other activities. By contrast, deserts, woodlands, grasslands and temperate forests all fall below the 30% target. Then there is the question of whether land that’s conserved on paper is really being protected . The new research points to the potential gains that can be made, particularly with the recognition of the conservation potential of these OECMs. But “conserving 30% of land and seas is not sufficient on its own,” said Heather Bingham, a co-author who heads the Protected Planet Initiative. “The target also calls for these areas to be managed effectively for positive biodiversity outcomes, and to be placed where they will have the greatest impact on biodiversity.” O’Neill, et. al. “ Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates .” Nature. items.title: «Thermocol Out, Clay & Shola In»: Αυτά τα είδωλα Durga των καλλιτεχνών της Καλκούτα δεν θα πνίξουν το Hooghly This Pujo
items.titleOriginal: ‘Thermocol Out, Clay & Shola In’: These Kolkata Artisans’ Durga Idols Won’t Choke the Hooghly This Pujo
items.description: Στο Joy Durga Bhandar, ένα εργαστήριο στο Kumartuli της βόρειας Καλκούτα, ο Koushik Ghosh ξεκινά ένα είδωλο με ένα πλαίσιο από μπαμπού και ξύλο δεμένο μεταξύ τους με σχοινί από γιούτα. Από αυτή τη βάση προέρχονται οι γλυπτές φιγούρες, οι διακοσμήσεις και τα στρώματα χρώματος που βλέπουν οι θιασώτες κατά τη διάρκεια της Durga Puja. Ο Koushik ξέρει καλά αυτή τη διαδικασία. Για γενιές, οι τεχνίτες στο Kumartuli φορούσαν…
items.descriptionOriginal: At Joy Durga Bhandar, a workshop in north Kolkata's Kumartuli, Koushik Ghosh begins an idol with a framework of bamboo and wood tied together with jute rope. From this base come the sculpted figures, decorations and layers of colour that devotees see during Durga Puja. Koushik knows this process well. For generations, artisans in Kumartuli have worked with bamboo, straw and clay, shaping idols by hand for Kolkata's Durga Puja celebrations. Over time, many workshops also adopted thermocol decorations, synthetic paints and plastic ornaments because they were quicker or cheaper to use. Koushik is looking for ways to bring more traditional materials back into his work. "The frame, the clay, the straw, those were always ours. The thermocol and the chemical colours came later, because they were cheaper and faster. I am going back to what was here before," he says. The straw framework gives the idol its shape before artisans add the first layers of clay. He is working towards idols decorated with natural clay, shola (the soft pith of a plant used for delicate ornaments) and natural colours instead of thermocol. Every year, after Durga Puja, thousands of idols are immersed in the Hooghly River and other water bodies. In 2025, around 5,200 idols were immersed across 34 major Hooghly ghats and approximately 30 other water bodies in Kolkata and nearby suburbs, according to The Times of India . Civic workers clear debris from immersion sites, but thermocol and plastic decorations need careful collection and disposal because they can persist in the environment. Neel, a volunteer who has spent several seasons cleaning the Hooghly's banks near Babughat, remembers finding thermocol floating on the surface, coloured residue near the banks, and plastic decorations gathering along the ghats. Kumartuli's workshops have produced clay idols for Kolkata's Durga Puja for generations. For Koushik, the challenge is to make the decorations less wasteful while keeping the craft affordable for the families who depend on it. From bamboo frames to Durga's eyes: Inside the craft of Kumartuli Walking through Kumartuli's narrow lanes, the smell of wet clay is difficult to miss. The neighbourhood, whose name comes from kumor (potter) and tuli (neighbourhood quarter), has been home to idol makers for more than three centuries. Its workshops stand between Rabindra Sarani and the Hooghly, the river that has long supplied the fine alluvial soil used in their craft. Traditionally known as Ganga maati , this clay is softer and finer than ordinary earth, allowing artisans to sculpt delicate features. Artisans shape clay over the bamboo-and-straw framework before adding finer details and colour. At Koushik's workshop, everything begins with the kathamo (a framework made from bamboo and wood). "The frame is not just engineering," he explains. "It is the first thing she stands on." The structure must support the central Durga figure, accompanying figures, a lion and other sculpted elements. Next comes khar bandha (tying straw around the frame). Carefully shaped bundles of straw form the arms, waist, chest and other features. If the straw is tied incorrectly, the figure may lose its balance or the clay may crack. The first clay layer is entel mati (sticky clay mixed with tush , or rice husk). It takes about three to four days to dry. Straw and clay form the idol's limbs, which must be balanced before the finer layers are applied. Artisans then apply bele mati (finer, smoother clay), allowing another five or six days for drying, depending on the weather. Any cracks are repaired with fresh mud. Faces, hands and other delicate parts are often made separately using chhach (moulds), helping workshops manage the large number of orders they receive. The final detailing includes chokkhudaan (painting the eyes). Some artisans specialise in this stage because even a slight difference in the brushstrokes can change the expression of the figure. This process has remained largely familiar across generations. A Durga idol includes accompanying figures and a lion, all assembled before the final decoration. The changes have come in the materials used for decoration and finishing. Earlier, artisans relied on bamboo, straw, jute, shola and natural pigments. Tamarind-seed gum, chalk powder and starch made from boiled arrowroot were used to prepare and finish colours. As demand grew, thermocol became popular for chaal (decorative backdrops), mukut (crowns) and ornaments. Synthetic paints offered brighter colours, while plastic jewellery entered some workshops. These alternatives were quicker, cheaper and easier to work with when deadlines were approaching. The extra work behind a natural finish Gopal, a veteran artisan who remembers making idols before thermocol became common, understands why workshops adopted it. He recalls decorating traditional sabeki pratima (traditional-style idols) with shola, cloth, zari and daaker saaj (traditional decorative work). Handmade clay figures require repeated shaping and drying, adding to an artisan's working hours. "Shola was beautiful, but it took time. Thermocol came because it was fast and cheap. If you remove thermocol now and don't give me shola at the same price and within the same time, I am just working slower for the same money," he says. Thermocol is lightweight, easy to cut and relatively inexpensive. Shola, jute, handmade paper, paper pulp, bamboo and clay ornaments may require more time and skill, and sometimes cost more. Natural colours create another difficulty. Asha, who manages colouring and finishing work at a Kumartuli studio, says buyers have grown accustomed to the bright, uniform finish of synthetic paints. "Natural colour is more beautiful if you know how to look at it. But the buyer is standing under LED lights in the pandal. They want brightness. Softness looks like less work to them, even when it is more," she explains. Colouring and decoration come after sculpting, with buyers often expecting a bright, even finish. This expectation has financial consequences. Koushik points to raw-material prices, labour, drying time and the risk of damage as factors that can raise the cost of working with natural materials. Handmade decorations take more hours. Natural colours need careful application. During the monsoon, wet clay can also take longer to dry. In the final weeks of a season, artisans often work long hours to meet delivery dates, using fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions. Koushik has not lost an idol to rain, but the possibility remains with every order that needs additional drying time. Artisans use fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions while working to Puja deadlines. The bigger challenge is recovering these expenses. There is no fixed price for a Durga idol. The cost depends on its height, design, decorations, arrangement of figures and the buyer's budget. Even two idols of the same height can have different prices. Costs differ by design, materials and year, so there is no single price difference between idols using natural decorations and those made with synthetic alternatives. For a small workshop, even a modest unplanned expense can make a difference. "If the idol has to be eco-friendly and the client wants the same finish as a synthetic-painted one, one of us has to absorb the difference. Usually, it is us," Asha says. The cost of an idol depends on its size, design, decorative materials and time spent finishing it. A South Kolkata Puja committee organiser, who requested anonymity, describes the buyer's dilemma. His committee relies on contributions from neighbourhood families, so any increase in an idol's price or change in its appearance must be discussed with the people paying for it. Gopal believes buyers and artisans should agree on materials and costs when placing an order. That would help workshops plan their purchases without bearing unexpected expenses themselves. After the idols are immersed, what is left in the Hooghly? Idol immersion is an important part of Durga Puja. The environmental concern lies with synthetic decorations and paints that may enter the water or be left on the banks unless they are removed and collected. Thermocol and plastic do not biodegrade easily and can break into smaller fragments that remain in the environment. Some synthetic paints contain heavy metals that can affect water quality. Decorative paints and plastic ornaments may leave residues that require post-immersion collection. A Central Pollution Control Board study conducted between 1993 and 1995 estimated that idol immersions released 32 tonnes of colours and 16.8 tonnes of varnish and garjan oil annually into the Hooghly during that period. These colours contained metals including lead, mercury and chromium, according to findings reported by Down To Earth . These are historical findings, not a measure of present-day pollution. They help explain why safer materials and careful post-immersion clean-ups matter. The CPCB's revised guidelines of May 2020 call for natural, biodegradable idols, discourage toxic synthetic paints and restrict thermocol, plastic and plaster of Paris. CPCB guidelines favour biodegradable idols and discourage thermocol, plastic and toxic paints. West Bengal's 2018 immersion rules require natural clay and bamboo, prohibit plaster of Paris and toxic colours, and place responsibilities on Puja committees and local authorities. Decorative thermocol has also been prohibited under national single-use plastic restrictions effective from July 2022. For workshops, switching materials works best when decisions are made before production begins. In August 2025, The Times of India reported that police were conducting awareness drives and inspections at Kumartuli and other idol-making centres. West Bengal's immersion rules call for natural clay and bamboo and prohibit toxic colours. Artisans interviewed for that report asked for guidance six to eight months before Durga Puja, when orders and material choices can still be changed. Koushik agrees that natural decorations need to be planned from the start. A 25-YO idol maker puts paper pulp & plant colours to the test A few workshops have already begun experimenting with alternatives. Ritwik, a 25-year-old third-generation idol maker, has been testing paper pulp for ornaments and plant-based colours for the faces of idols. After attending an awareness workshop, he brought back samples of gerua (an earth-based red pigment), turmeric-based colours and dyes derived from plants. He began trying them on small clay surfaces before using them on larger figures. "The look is different. Not worse, actually; I think it is more beautiful. But it is older-looking. Some clients like that. Some think I made a mistake. It depends on whether they know what they are seeing," he says. Artisans testing plant-based pigments say their finishes can look different from synthetic paints. The softer, slightly uneven appearance resembles the finish of traditional idols made before synthetic paints became widespread. There is no reliable figure for how many Kumartuli workshops have completely moved away from thermocol. During the reporter's visits, thermocol decorations and synthetic paints were still visible in workshops. Experiments with natural alternatives were promising, but had yet to become the norm. With thousands of idols made in Kumartuli each season, these material choices can add up. According to a September 2026 report in The Telegraph , around 166 studios produce close to 8,500 idols in a season, with turnover exceeding ₹200 crore in the previous year. A 2026 report estimated around 166 Kumartuli studios making close to 8,500 idols each season. Koushik and other artisans say a broader shift will depend on affordable traditional materials, clear specifications from buyers and guidance shared well before production begins. A reliable supply of shola, jute and natural pigments would also make it easier for workshops to plan ahead. What a painted tile shows about the choice At Gopal's workshop, a painted tile offers another way to compare the materials. One strip was coloured with synthetic paint, the other with natural pigment. Gopal left both exposed through the previous monsoon to see how they changed. The synthetic strip remained uniform; the natural one developed warmer, slightly uneven edges. Gopal did not declare either better. For him, the contrast shows how a natural finish may differ from what buyers are accustomed to. Natural pigments can create a different finish, while handmade ornaments take time. These differences need to be part of the discussion when an idol is commissioned. Traditional clay figures are moulded and dried before receiving their colours and decorations. Koushik is working to bring more of the materials his craft has long relied on back into use. Buyers can help by agreeing on materials and budgets early; timely guidance and access to affordable supplies could help more workshops do the same. Behind every idol are weeks of skilled labour. Choices about paint, decorations and post-immersion waste collection matter both to the artisans and to the river near their workshops. For Koushik, the goal is practical: honour an old craft, reduce the amount of synthetic waste entering the Hooghly and make sure artisans can still earn a fair living. All images courtesy Akhil Rajarathinam
