items.descriptionOriginal: Flying cars are once again taking over the internet, with Tesla's plans fuelling conversations about a future where people could travel through the air instead of sitting in traffic. But in Almora, Uttarakhand, an innovator has spent 13 years working towards a similar idea, driven by a problem much closer to home. Ravi Tamta grew up in the mountains of Kaflikhan village near Jageswar Dham, where reaching a hospital could mean hours on winding roads. He began wondering if there was another way to travel through the hills, one that did not depend on roads or require an airport. Inspired by the challenges of reaching hospitals in the hills, Ravi Tamta spent 13 years developing a flying vehicle that can take off and land vertically. Photograph: ( Zee News) That question led him to build HAPIDA SKYNeX, an electric flying vehicle prototype that can take off and land vertically. After years of experiments, the vehicle completed its maiden test flight in August, taking off from an army helipad in Almora and remaining airborne for nearly a minute. A mountain problem sparked the idea For people living in hilly regions, distance is not always measured in kilometres. Winding roads and difficult terrain can turn a relatively short journey into a long trip, particularly when someone needs medical attention. Tamta began exploring whether a flying vehicle could help people cover such distances faster. His idea was to develop a vehicle that could rise vertically, travel over difficult terrain, and land without needing a runway. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The aim is to make air travel more accessible in hilly regions, particularly during medical emergencies and in areas that are difficult to reach by road. Developed under his venture, Hapida Sky Private Limited, the HAPIDA SKYNeX combines modified, scaled-up multirotor drone technology with an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) system. In simple terms, it uses the same basic principle that lets a multirotor drone take off and hover, but applies it to a prototype designed to carry a person. Unlike conventional aircraft that need a runway to gain enough speed for take-off, an eVTOL vehicle is designed to lift off and land vertically. This could make the technology particularly relevant to mountainous areas, where finding suitable space for runways can be difficult. How the flying vehicle works HAPIDA SKYNeX uses multiple electric motors and propellers mounted on external arms to generate lift. Working together, these components are designed to raise the vehicle off the ground, sustain a hover, and help control its movement through the air. This multirotor arrangement is similar in principle to the technology used in drones, although scaling it up to carry a person presents additional engineering and safety challenges. The prototype also features a lightweight frame, a cockpit designed for a single pilot and a transparent canopy. Its electric propulsion system is battery-powered, eliminating direct exhaust emissions during operation. From a mobile-charging shoe to a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, Ravi Tamta's earlier inventions also focused on solving practical, everyday problems. Photograph: ( Business Today ) However, its practical flight range, battery endurance, and overall efficiency will depend on factors such as the battery capacity, the vehicle's weight, and the power required to sustain flight. The intended use is short-distance travel across difficult terrain. According to the reported project details, a journey of around 40 kilometres that takes approximately 90 minutes by mountain road could potentially be completed in 10 to 15 minutes by air. This is an intended travel-time goal, rather than a demonstrated operational capability at this stage. Thirteen years of learning through experiments Tamta did not have an engineering degree or access to a fancy laboratory. Instead, he turned to the internet to learn, relying on his parents' support and repeated experiments to develop his idea. Over 13 years, the concept gradually took shape under his venture, Hapida Skynex. The maiden flight was an important step in testing whether his idea could work beyond the drawing board. The single-seater prototype features a lightweight frame, a cockpit for one pilot and a transparent canopy, with multiple electric motors and propellers designed to generate lift. Photograph: ( Influencer Book of World Records ) The prototype is still at an early stage and requires further testing. While the test flight offers a glimpse of what the vehicle might eventually do, it is too soon to know how it will perform in regular use. Before a vehicle of this kind can be used for routine passenger travel, it would need to demonstrate reliable flight control, sufficient battery performance, structural stability and safe responses to component failures. Operating in mountainous terrain would bring additional considerations, including changing weather, wind conditions, landing-site availability and emergency procedures. From everyday inventions to flying vehicles The flying vehicle is not Tamta's first attempt at solving practical problems through invention. His earlier creations include shoes that charge mobile phones on the go, a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, a bamboo-splitting machine and firefighting equipment. Ravi Tamta hopes HAPIDA SKYNeX will one day make travel across Uttarakhand's mountains faster and more accessible. Photograph: ( Instagram/@ravi_tamta3 ) Each project began with a practical challenge, leading him to explore how a device could make a task easier. HAPIDA SKYNeX has a longer journey ahead before it can carry passengers or help people reach hospitals faster. For now, its first flight marks a step forward for an idea shaped by life in the mountains. As conversations about flying cars continue online, Tamta's work offers a different way to look at the technology: not just as a futuristic mode of transport, but as a possible answer to the everyday challenges of getting from one place to another. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup Reading Time: 4 minutes From a Dutch teenager’s question in 2013 to 50 million kilograms of debris removed, Ocean Cleanup proves ingenuity can still tackle one of the ocean’s most overwhelming problems. Our oceans cover 71% of the planet’s surface, plunging down nearly 11,000 meters at their deepest point in the Mariana Trench, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Below the waves lies home to billions of species spread across coral reefs, mangrove forests, seagrass beds, and hydrothermal vents. The deep-sea bed alone hosts an estimated 500,000 to 10 million species, with scientists believing 91% of ocean species remain unclassified to this day. Despite this astounding biodiversity, humans continue to put large portions of it at risk with persistent detrimental activities. In 2023, the 5 Gyres Institute, set up by Marcus Eriksen and Anna Cummings to carry out in-depth research on plastic pollution, published data revealing that 82-358 trillion plastic particles currently float on the ocean’s surface, equal to between 2.4 and 4.9 million tonnes. However, this figure is only the portion of plastic that floats; the United Nations Regional Information Centre for Western Europe (UNRIC) estimates that in total from rivers, lakes and oceans, between nine and 23 million tonnes of plastic waste reach aquatic ecosystems annually. These are the statistics that led Boyan Slat, at the age of only 18, to ask himself why no real progress was being made to tackle the plastics that had found their way into our world’s seas. In 2013, Slat set up Ocean Cleanup, which has now grown into a globally recognized non-profit organisation that utilises sustainable innovation to systematically clear non-biodegradable waste from oceans. The idea was brought to life when the Dutch innovator designed a system that harnesses the natural movement of waves and currents to push plastic into the curve of a U-shaped inflatable barrier which floats on the ocean’s surface, with both ends steered by a boat. Once the retention zone is full, it is detached from the main inflatable system, emptied into a third boat and replaced, continuing the process. The plastics on board the collection boat are taken back to shore and recycled. At 18, Boyan Slat designed a U-shaped floating barrier that uses natural wave and current movement to concentrate ocean plastic into a collection zone, creating the foundation of what Ocean Cleanup has become today. Photo courtesy of Ocean Cleanup . A perfected process now allows the organization to use an Automated Debris Imaging System (ADIS), which not only keeps track of plastic collected, but also monitors and maps the distribution of plastic debris using embedded AI. This helps to plot where to place their cleanup systems as efficiently as possible. The crew onboard also includes independent observers to monitor interactions with marine life, such as protected turtle species or whales. The key to the design is that ocean animals can easily swim under or around the system without harm. The retention zone has numerous inbuilt safety measures, including acoustic deterrents, escape aids for any animals caught up in the rubbish, and breathing hatches for mammals to ensure they can access a clear patch of ocean surface. In 2025, Ocean Cleanup launched System 03, which is almost three times larger than previous systems and measures up to 2.2km long, hoping to make even more impact on the effects of the climate crisis. The organisation has found that ocean plastics accumulate mainly in five different zones called ocean garbage patches, the biggest of them all being the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. This is bounded by the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, a network of ocean currents, which rotates clockwise around an area of 20 million square kilometres. As the currents churn the plastics piled up in the Patch, they break down further, becoming microplastics which are known to build up in food chains that are reaching humans. Turtles are eating plastic bags mistaking them for jellyfish, albatrosses are feeding resin pellets to young instead of fish eggs, and a phenomenon known as ‘ghost fishing’ is becoming ever more common as marine mammals get tangled in discarded plastic fishing nets. This is why this Patch has become a main target zone for the organisation. However, by weight 70-80% of ocean plastic actually arrives there by rivers, with studies suggesting that just a few major rivers are the worst offenders. This is why Ocean Cleanup tackles the root of the problem as well, working with government leaders, individuals and private companies to set up interceptors at points along some of the most polluted rivers, like the Sandy Gully in Kingston, Jamaica. These interceptors include barriers, barricades, guards and the Interceptor Original: an autonomous, 100% solar powered craft that utilises a conveyor belt to continuously extract debris and distribute it evenly between containers that can store up to 50m 3 of trash combined before needing to be emptied. All of which work together to drastically reduce the trash flow from rivers into the wider sea. In March 2026, Ocean Cleanup reached 50 million kg of debris removed. This organization is living proof that with perseverance and ingenious solutions we can come together to tackle some of our world’s largest problems. But how can you play your part to help reduce plastics in our oceans? So how can you help reduce plastic in our oceans? Every little bit counts. Refuse single-use plastics like straws, and bring reusable bags when you shop. Recycle properly, following your local program’s rules closely. Avoid microbeads in products like face scrubs, usually listed as “polyethylene” or “polypropylene” on ingredient labels. Share what you’ve learned with others. Support organizations fighting plastic pollution. Join a river or beach cleanup, and never flush non-biodegradable items down the toilet. The post The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis Reading Time: 3 minutes Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts in Mexico’s Chihuahuan Desert are reviving ancient pools and returning bison to the land, offering a model for desert restoration worldwide. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation begins in a valley most people have never heard of. Tucked into the Chihuahuan Desert in Coahuila, the basin holds hundreds of crystal-clear pools called pozas that Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has spent years working to protect. These pools support life found nowhere else on the planet. The valley became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2006. It spans more than 413,000 hectares, an area larger than Los Angeles. Within that space live over 800 plant species and roughly 360 animal species, many found only here. The pools themselves hold something even stranger. Scientists have traced microbial life in the pozas back nearly 500 million years. Researchers believe these microbes descended from an ancient sea trapped underground when mountains rose around the basin. Some pozas also contain stromatolites, layered rock structures built by microbial colonies. Scientists consider them living relatives of some of Earth’s earliest life forms, similar to formations found in Australia’s Shark Bay. Few places on the planet still host stromatolites forming under natural conditions today. Mexican scientists Valeria Souza and Luis Eguiarte made that discovery, turning a quiet desert valley into a living laboratory. Their work found more bacterial diversity in a single pool than scientists had documented across China’s entire Pearl River. The find helped convince Mexico to take the area’s protection more seriously. Protection came just in time. Decades of irrigation for alfalfa farming, much of it feeding dairy operations, drained the aquifer feeding the pozas. Nearly 90 percent of the valley’s surface water has disappeared since the 1960s. Churince, once the basin’s largest lagoon, dried up completely in 2016. That loss sparked a wave of local action. In 2018, conservationists won a court order forcing officials to close a canal draining two major pools. The ruling marked a turning point for regional water policy. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has since built on that momentum, becoming the driving force behind on-the-ground Cuatro Ciénegas conservation. The nonprofit works to protect the valley’s water, restore native habitat, and support ranching methods that use less water. Its programs also train local students in environmental science, turning former skeptics into active partners in the valley’s recovery. That shift in local support matters. Many families once saw conservation as a threat to their livelihoods. Years of education and dialogue changed that view for many residents, who now see healthy pozas as tied to their own future. The clearest sign of progress arrived in December 2025. Forty-four American bison arrived at a reserve called El Santuario in Coahuila, marking a major step in Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts. The animals came from a managed herd at Rancho El Uno in Chihuahua’s Janos Biosphere Reserve, overseen by the conservation group Cuenca Los Ojos. American bison graze on restored grassland in Coahuila, part of a new Cuatro Ciénegas conservation effort to bring the keystone species back to northern Mexico. Photo courtesy of Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas . Bison do more than roam grasslands. Their grazing improves soil structure and helps native plants recover. Unlike cattle, bison tolerate drought well, making them a natural fit for a region growing hotter and drier. The project brought together Mexico’s environment ministry, SEMARNAT, along with its national parks commission, CONANP, and several conservation groups. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas partnered with the N’dee/N’nee/Ndé Indigenous nation to open reserve land for the herd. The Mexican Fund for the Conservation of Nature also supported the effort, reflecting the broad coalition needed to pull off a reintroduction of this scale. Officials involved called the partnership a model for Cuatro Ciénegas conservation going forward. Government agencies, scientists, ranchers, and Indigenous communities rarely align this closely. Their shared success offers a template other desert regions could follow. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation still faces real challenges. Water rights in Mexico remain tangled in overlapping laws, and some irrigation canals draining the basin remain open. Full recovery of dried lagoons like Churince could take years, if it happens at all. Even so, the signs of resilience are hard to ignore. Researchers have found that dormant microbes can survive in dry mud for years, springing back to life once water returns. A desert valley that nearly vanished is showing what patient, collaborative Cuatro Ciénegas conservation can achieve. Scientists study its microbes, ranchers adjust old habits, students learn to protect their backyard, and American bison once again roam land shaped by their ancestors. What happens next in Cuatro Ciénegas may show the rest of the world how to save a dying ecosystem before it is too late. The post Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes Reading Time: 3 minutes An urban food forest thrives 51 floors above Singapore’s streets, proving hyperdense cities can grow far more than ornamental greenery. Permaculture educator Andrew Millison traveled to Singapore to answer a deceptively simple question: how much food, greenery, and habitat can a hyperdense urban environment actually produce? What he found reshaped his understanding of what cities can grow. At the top of one Singapore skyscraper sits what is described as the world’s highest rooftop farm, an urban food forest producing roughly a ton of organic food annually on the 51st floor. Bananas, mulberries, star fruit, and water apples grow alongside pumpkin vines. Bees pollinate crops despite the extreme elevation, including kadong , a native fruit with a tart, green-apple flavor whose edible leaves are traditionally used in local salads. A nearby miracle berry temporarily transforms sour flavors into sweet ones, delighting visitors encountering the effect for the first time. Unlike conventional rooftop farms arranged in single horizontal rows of vegetables, this urban food forest layers vertically within a tight footprint. Tree layers rise above shrub layers, herbs fill the understory, and vines climb through the structure, creating a legitimate multi-tiered food production system rather than a novelty garden. The restaurant sourcing from this rooftop describes the space as inseparable from its culinary philosophy, using every part of each harvest to minimize waste while drawing creative inspiration directly from what grows above the kitchen. Beyond this single example, Millison explored how urban food forest principles could scale across Singapore’s built environment. The island nation has almost no farmland and imports nearly all of its food, yet government policy already mandates extensive greenery integration. A landscape replacement policy requires developers to replace any land they build on with equivalent greenery elsewhere on the structure, driving widespread adoption of vertical gardens and rooftop plantings across the city. One striking example of this policy in action covers roughly 200% of its building footprint in combined horizontal and vertical greenery, effectively treating the high-rise as a small mountain, with the ground extending upward through multiple stories. The landscape architect behind the design explained that root space is the central engineering challenge, requiring sufficient soil depth or widened planters, root barriers to prevent structural damage, built-in drainage systems, maintenance walkways, and anchor cables to stabilize mature tree canopies as they grow denser over time. Currently, Singapore maintains roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space, but most of this greenery consists of exotic ornamental plants rather than food-producing species. The country spends approximately one billion dollars annually managing this urban vegetation. Replacing ornamental plantings with productive alternatives, while maintaining the same underlying infrastructure, could transform this investment into a genuine urban food forest network spanning the entire city, rather than a purely decorative one. Singapore’s landscape replacement policy has created roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space citywide, with Edible Garden City working to transform this largely ornamental urban food forest infrastructure into a genuine perennial food production network using resilient native and traditional crops. Photo by Cyrill on Pexels. Edible Garden City, a Singapore-based urban farming social enterprise, is actively developing the plant genetics needed to make this transition possible. At Gardens by the Bay, the organization experiments with diversified, multi-tiered plantings that move away from monoculture rows toward genuine food forest design. This approach reduces pest pressure by diluting concentrated crops across diverse species, minimizes pesticide use, and incorporates flowering plants that attract pollinators while producing edible blooms. Perennial plants form the backbone of this urban food forest model, since street-side and terrace plantings cannot practically be tilled and replanted annually like conventional vegetable plots. Species proven successful at the test site are introduced to industry partners and community gardens, spreading resilient, low-maintenance crops including lemongrass, pandan, cassava, sweet potato, and Brazilian spinach, alongside traditional vegetables once grown by earlier generations before industrial food systems replaced them. Singapore currently allocates only about 1% of its land to farming, yet its extensive rooftop and vertical greening infrastructure suggests far greater capacity remains untapped. The research, plant trials, and structural engineering needed to convert ornamental cityscapes into a genuine urban food forest have already been completed and proven at scale within the city itself, requiring policy rather than new invention for wider implementation. What makes Singapore’s example significant extends beyond any single rooftop or building. The city demonstrates that food production and dense urban living are not inherently incompatible, provided cities are willing to reimagine landscaping budgets, structural design, and plant selection around productivity rather than appearance alone. An urban food forest at this scale offers a template other hyperdense cities worldwide could adapt, transforming skylines already covered in decorative greenery into genuine sources of food, habitat, and community resilience. The post Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Emanuel Kuntzelman has a special relationship with trees. Sitting in an apple tree at the early age of six, he decided to dedicate his life to serving the universe. Under an oak in college, he formulated an idea to unite people in a common purpose. Reading under a weeping willow, the name Holomovement came to him for that common purpose, a movement he later helped realize. People also appeared along the way as if on cue to point him in a direction when he didn’t know which way he was going. “Sometimes the universe makes things so easy for us — if you're on that quest for truth, and you're willing to say it here and there.” Emanuel believes each person has a calling, a purpose, and trees and people are there to help us as long as we keep learning and seeking. In doing so, all can join in the Holomovement “to unite humanity through our collective purpose.”

items.descriptionOriginal: In November 2018, conservationists working in North Bengal's Dooars region raised an alarm about a barrier that was increasingly obstructing elephants: razor-sharp fencing around tea estates. The Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) reported on a series of stakeholder meetings organised by its conservation partner, the Society for Protecting Ophiofauna and Animal Rights (SPOAR), between 11 and 16 November that year. It described how randomly installed razor-blade fencing was forcing elephant herds to divert from their usual routes. The organisation reported that the sharp wires caused serious injuries to elephants and other wildlife, and that some animals died while attempting to cross the fences. The report did not identify individual animals or provide a tally of razor-wire injuries . But it highlighted a problem that extended beyond the fences themselves: when elephants could no longer follow familiar routes, their movement could bring them into closer contact with people. In August 2026, WTI and SPOAR brought tea estate representatives, government agencies and conservation organisations together in Chalsa, Jalpaiguri, to discuss elephant-friendly management. Photograph: (csmonitor) Seven years later, a reassessment by WTI and SPOAR would offer a measurable indication of how much the landscape had changed. Between 2019 and 2026, the length of razor-wire fencing mapped across the assessed tea-estate landscape fell from approximately 134.7 km to 34.8 km, a reduction of 74.2%. The change followed years of engagement with tea estate management, local communities and government agencies. It also raised a question: how much safer can an elephant's journey become when a landscape begins to accommodate its movement? A corridor is not always a forest Across North Bengal's Terai and Duars, elephant movement does not stop at the edge of a forest. Routes run through forest patches, tea plantations, worker settlements, roads and railway lines. These connections allow elephants to move between habitats in search of food, water and space. But when land is divided by fences, trenches and other obstacles, a familiar passage can become difficult or dangerous to navigate. For tea estates, fencing may be intended to protect workers, crops and property. Yet barriers placed across elephant movement routes can also redirect herds towards labour lines, roads and settlements, creating risks for people and wildlife alike. To understand the extent of the problem, WTI and SPOAR conducted a year-long field survey in 2019 across eight identified elephant corridors in North Bengal. The survey documented how elephants used tea estates and identified barriers that could impede their movement. From a survey to a shared commitment The findings became the starting point for discussions with those managing the landscape. On World Elephant Day in August 2019, nearly 50 representatives from tea estates, the Forest Department , tea associations, the administration and conservation organisations gathered for a consultative workshop on securing elephant passage through tea gardens. The discussions focused on practical measures such as identifying problematic barriers, keeping movement routes open and reducing losses for both people and elephants. Camera trap footage of a wild #elephant herd crossing the Apalchand-Kalimpong corridor via the Meenglass Tea Estate in North Bengal. These cameras were installed by WTI's Green Corridor Champion (GCC) partner in the landscape, @SPOAR_India https://t.co/ZF4RgSGE3a — Wildlife Trust of India (@wti_org_india) November 22, 2024 Some tea estate representatives shared examples of areas being left open for elephants. Others discussed commitments to remove existing razor wire or to avoid installing it in the future. WTI, SPOAR, the Forest Department and tea estate management continued engaging with the landscape, while awareness initiatives helped workers and residents understand elephant movement and the risks posed by obstructed routes. What changed between 2019 and 2026? A reassessment by WTI and SPOAR in 2026 offered a way to measure changes in the fencing landscape. In 2019, the survey had mapped 291.7 km of fencing across the assessed area. By 2026, the total had fallen to 104.5 km. The decline in razor-wire fencing was particularly notable in 2026: from 134.7 km to 34.8 km. However, the figures do not mean that all the missing fencing was deliberately removed. WTI's account attributes the reduction to a combination of removal, deterioration and fencing not being reinstalled. Nor do the figures establish how many elephant injuries or h uman-elephant encounters have been prevented. They measure a change in the physical barriers across the landscape, not a verified reduction in casualties. Still, the reassessment suggests that estate practices have changed over time, following sustained engagement and discussions about safer elephant movement. The next danger is overhead The same reassessment identified another concern: low-hanging electrical infrastructure. The survey documented 54 power lines below a height of 13 feet, with 47.4% hanging below 10 feet. These were flagged as serious hazards to elephants. An elephant may be able to move past a fence only to encounter a low electrical line or another obstacle along its route. The findings are intended to guide joint verification and corrective action involving tea estate management, the Forest Department, the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (WBSEDCL) and conservation partners. A charter for coexistence In August 2026, WTI and SPOAR brought tea estate representatives, government agencies and conservation organisations together in Chalsa, Jalpaiguri, to discuss elephant-friendly management. The consultation introduced the Elephant-Friendly Tea Estate Charter. The proposed framework focuses on keeping known elephant routes open, reviewing hazardous fencing , improving electrical safety, preparing workers and residents for encounters, managing crowds and strengthening monitoring. The fall from 134.7 km to 34.8 km of razor-wire fencing is a measurable change. It is not, on its own, proof that elephants are safer. Establishing that will require continued monitoring of injuries, deaths, movement patterns and encounters with people. Sources: 'SPOAR lobbies to Mitigate Human-Elephant Conflict in Elephant Corridors of Dooars in Northern West Bengal' : By WTI 'From Commitments to Change: How North Bengal's Tea Estates are Making Space for Elephants' : By Upasana Ganguly, Published on 8 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: "Earlier, it was very difficult for me," says Bengaluru resident Rashmi Sampath, recalling every family outing with her 16-year-old daughter, Deeksha, who has spinal muscular atrophy. "She weighs 55 kilograms, and lifting her into the car was exhausting. But now, since the seat rotates 90 degrees, it is very comfortable." The difference has been more than convenience. A journey that once demanded careful planning, physical effort, and frequent compromises has become something the family can look forward to. Last year, they drove nearly 1,000 kilometres from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari without the travel itself becoming an obstacle. "She was very comfortable throughout," Rashmi says. "We took just two breaks. She could even sleep on the seat. Earlier, we couldn't have imagined travelling such a long distance like this." For millions of Indians living with disabilities or age-related mobility challenges, the hardest part of a journey often begins before the vehicle even starts moving. Getting into a car can require multiple people, unsafe lifting techniques, or simply deciding that the trip isn't worth the effort. It is this overlooked challenge that Bengaluru-based TRUE Assistive Technology set out to address. Founded by engineers Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre, the company designs assistive mobility solutions, including swivel seats, portable ramps, transfer systems, and wheelchair-accessible vehicle modifications, that make everyday travel safer and more accessible. TurnPlus rotates towards the car door, making it easier for passengers to get in and out with less physical strain. Since beginning its journey, the company says it has enabled mobility for over 1,000 users across India, supporting people with conditions ranging from paralysis and Parkinson's disease to post-polio complications and age-related mobility issues. A project that uncovered a larger problem Neither Naina nor Anand had initially planned to build an assistive technology company. Both spent over two decades working as engineers — Naina in software and compliance engineering, Anand in the automotive sector. Their journey into accessible mobility began unexpectedly in 2013, when Toyota approached them with a project to design a swivel seat for the Corolla Altis. The prototype was showcased at an auto show, but it failed to gain traction because of its high cost. "We went on to see how we could bring the solution to the Indian market," recalls Naina. Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre spent years developing mobility solutions that work with existing cars, without permanent modifications. The idea had also been shaped by another experience. Having lived in the United States before returning to India, the couple had seen people with disabilities participating independently in everyday life. "We had seen a lot of people in the US who were disabled but still living day-to-day life with full potential. We thought we should do something similar in India," she says. The path, however, was anything but straightforward. Without external funding, they bootstrapped the venture using income from consulting assignments. "Sometimes we had money but no people, and sometimes we had people but no funds," Anand recalls. "That's why it took about four years to bring the whole thing together." Interest slowly began building after an article about their work led families to reach out directly. Once they had served their first hundred customers, the founders realised there was a genuine demand for accessible mobility solutions in India. They expanded the design to fit nearly 80 percent of Indian car models before formally establishing TRUE Assistive Technology in 2022. Designing for Indian conditions As Anand began designing the products, one principle remained non-negotiable. "I didn't want to do anything like jugaad ," he says. Instead of permanently altering vehicles, the founders focused on creating solutions that could fit existing cars without affecting warranties, insurance, or resale value. Their flagship innovation, TurnPlus , is a patented swivel-seat mechanism that transforms an existing car seat into one that rotates outward. Rather than climbing or being lifted awkwardly into the vehicle, the passenger can first sit on the seat while it faces the door. The seat then swivels back into the cabin, making transfers smoother for senior citizens and people with conditions such as paralysis, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, post-polio complications and spinal injuries. Unlike many vehicle modifications that require structural changes, TurnPlus uses the car's existing seat. The mechanism is installed beneath it, allowing the seat to rotate without permanently altering the vehicle. TRUE Assistive Technology's portable ramps and transfer systems help wheelchair users navigate everyday barriers at home and on the move. "We didn't want people to leave their vehicles in garages for days," Naina explains. "You don't have to leave the vehicle with us. We bring the product to your doorstep." Because the original seat remains intact, the system can also be removed later if the owner decides to sell the vehicle, helping preserve its resale value. As they worked with more users, the founders realised that mobility challenges rarely end once someone gets into a car. Some wheelchair users needed a safer way to enter vehicles without being manually lifted. Others struggled with small staircases outside homes, clinics or public buildings. That led to the development of RamPlus , a lightweight portable ramp that can be carried in a vehicle and unfolded whenever a step or raised entrance blocks wheelchair access. The company later introduced TransPlus and HoistPlus , assistive systems and transferring devices that help caregivers lift and transfer people safely between wheelchairs, beds and vehicles, reducing physical strain for both users and families. For individuals who require more extensive support, TRUE also undertakes end-to-end vehicle modifications, including wheelchair ramps, hydraulic lifts and roof-height adjustments that convert standard vehicles into wheelchair-accessible ones. Before reaching users, every solution undergoes automotive safety testing, including front and rear crash tests, seat belt anchorage testing and durability assessments across temperatures ranging from minus 20 C to plus 60 C. The above tests are only for their products and not for vehicle modifications. "If I had to sell it across India , it had to be as reliable as the vehicle itself," Anand says. 'To be dependent on anybody is very painful' For Amritsar resident Jatin Gandotra, the technology came into his life after someone close to him suffered a stroke. His relative, now in her 60s, has severely restricted mobility and has spent nearly two years confined to bed. Jatin first discovered TRUE Assistive Technology while reading about a collaboration with Maruti Suzuki. "I found the technology very fascinating because my close relative is a stroke patient," he says. "I wanted to see how we could help her." After a relative suffered a stroke, Jatin Gandotra turned to accessible mobility to make family outings easier for her. Today, the family uses TurnPlus to help her get into the car more comfortably. Speaking about the emotional impact, Jatin says it goes far beyond the physical act of travelling. "To be dependent upon anybody is very, very painful," he says. "When you look through the patient's eyes, you can see that satisfaction that they are being cared for." For him, accessible mobility is ultimately about giving families more choices. "See what freedom you can bring to their life," he says. More than easier journeys The founders say stories like these continue to reinforce why they chose this path. Among their earliest customers was a woman who completed her PhD sooner because she could travel to college more frequently after installing the mobility solution. Another user, Vijay Kannan, fulfilled a long-held dream of driving his parents to Ayodhya after equipping his vehicle with an accessible ramp. "It's not just for the person using it," says Naina. "It helps the entire family. When they see how conveniently they can travel together, it changes things for everyone." Rashmi has witnessed that change firsthand. "The more we socialise these children, the happier they become," she says. "We shouldn't confine them to a single room." Her daughter now plans trips with the confidence many teenagers take for granted. "She says, 'We'll go anywhere. We'll explore this place.' She feels nothing is limited for her anymore." For families like Rashmi's, accessible mobility means fewer limitations, more shared experiences and the freedom to explore the world beyond their homes. According to the Census 2011, India is home to over 2.68 crore persons with disabilities, alongside a rapidly growing elderly population. Yet for many, something as ordinary as getting into a vehicle remains one of the biggest barriers to participating in everyday life. For families like Rashmi's and Jatin's, accessible mobility is not simply about modifying a car. It means visiting relatives without anxiety, travelling to school or work more comfortably, taking a long-awaited road trip, or stepping outside after months of staying indoors. Sometimes, restoring independence begins with making the first step into a vehicle a little easier. All images courtesy True Assistive Technology team

items.descriptionOriginal: Frankie Robertson had spent years helping families navigate premature birth. But nothing could have prepared her for sitting in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) with her own newborn daughter. Robertson had spent nearly a decade in leadership at March of Dimes, an organization whose work includes premature birth prevention. She had listened to parents’ stories, supported families and cried alongside mothers whose babies arrived too soon. But experiencing it herself was entirely different, revealing a gap often overlooked in conversations about pregnancy and childbirth: Mothers need care and support long after their babies arrive. It’s a critical need that philanthropists Olivia and Tom Walton are working to address. In September 2026, the couple announced an initial $100 million commitment over five years to Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America , a national initiative aiming to cut the country’s maternal mortality rate in half by 2031. The investment is intended to help states expand promising approaches to maternal healthcare, particularly in rural and underserved communities where women face significant barriers to care. That includes expanding access to virtual appointments for women who live far from healthcare providers, training more midwives and community health workers, and strengthening postpartum care during the critical first year after childbirth. Olivia Walton's 0 million dollar commitment to maternal health Rather than creating an entirely new healthcare system, the initiative aims to help states put proven solutions into practice on a larger scale. The Waltons’ $100 million commitment will support state matching grants, partnerships, and improvements in healthcare infrastructure , with the goal of attracting additional public and private investment to sustain those efforts long after the initial five years. The ultimate measure of success is ambitious but straightforward: cutting the nation’s maternal mortality rate in half by 2031. The risks aren’t the same for every mother The United States has one of the highest maternal mortality rates among wealthy nations, and those risks aren’t shared equally. In 2024, non-Hispanic Black women were more than three times as likely to die from maternal causes as non-Hispanic white women, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This disparity is driven by a combination of systemic inequities in healthcare, including unequal access to quality prenatal and postpartum care, higher rates of certain underlying health conditions, and racial bias within the medical system. Research also shows that Black women’s concerns about their symptoms are sometimes dismissed or inadequately addressed by healthcare providers, potentially delaying lifesaving treatment. Geography matters, too. In rural communities, women may have to travel long distances to reach maternity care, making consistent prenatal and postpartum support difficult to access. Robertson, who has spent much of her career advocating for maternal health equity in Louisiana, believes improving outcomes also requires recognizing the circumstances women bring into pregnancy. Researchers call one aspect of this weathering : the cumulative physical toll of chronic stress, discrimination and systemic inequities. First proposed by public health researcher Arline Geronimus , the hypothesis explores how these experiences may contribute to poorer health outcomes over time. “It’s not simply about experiencing an isolated act of discrimination,” Robertson explained. “It’s about the overall effect, physiological toll of navigating just environments where you constantly have to confront, recover from inequities, or anticipate them.” Improving maternal health means looking beyond medical emergencies and recognizing the importance of consistent care, emotional support and access to resources before, during and after childbirth. What if better maternal care looked like this? Imagine a new mother returning home from the hospital, exhausted and overwhelmed. She’s anxious, struggling to sleep and unsure whether what she’s experiencing is a normal part of recovery or a sign that something is wrong. Now imagine someone comes to check on her. A postpartum home visit could help identify complications, answer questions and connect her with additional care. A midwife or community health worker could help another mother navigate appointments and find needed resources. A doula could provide emotional and practical support during childbirth, helping a woman understand her options and communicate her needs. Photo by Sarah Chai For mothers experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety, better access to mental health services could mean receiving help before symptoms become a crisis. These are among the approaches Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America hopes to help states expand, building on programs already showing promise rather than starting from scratch. In October, the initiative announced its first state-level investments: $10 million each for Arkansas and Kentucky over five years. The grants are intended to strengthen maternal healthcare access, particularly in rural communities, through workforce development, postpartum support and improved maternal health data. The initiative hopes successful approaches can eventually be adopted in other states. Photo by Healthy Moms and Healthy Babies America The investments are still in their early stages, and it will take time to see how many families benefit and whether improvements can be sustained. The Waltons hope their commitment will also attract additional public and private funding to help effective services reach more communities beyond the initial five years. Helping mothers find joy, even when pregnancy doesn’t go as planned For Robertson, the importance of having someone looking out for mothers is deeply personal. Her experiences with postpartum recovery and her daughter’s premature birth inspired her to become a doula and establish Black Joy Doula Firm, a maternal health practice focused on supporting Black women through pregnancy and childbirth. Her goal is to help mothers facing unexpected complications manage their fears, understand their options and hold on to some of the joy they felt when they first imagined becoming parents. “I wanted to be a doula to work with moms who get this news and then show them how to protect their peace, help them with coping mechanisms, help them slow down, help them maintain that joy,” she explained. It’s a philosophy that reflects what meaningful maternal care should look like: someone who listens, recognizes when a mother needs help and understands that her well-being matters, too. Frankie Robertson at the Joyful Birth Advocacy session with expectant moms, partners, and families at the Community Baby Shower Robertson knows firsthand that even mothers with extensive knowledge and resources can find themselves overwhelmed by the unexpected. But protecting maternal health shouldn’t be a responsibility women carry alone. That’s what makes the Waltons’ investment an opportunity worth watching. If it helps more communities provide consistent, compassionate care, fewer mothers may have to navigate pregnancy and recovery without the support they deserve. Because when a baby arrives, a mother’s need for care doesn’t end. A healthier start for families begins with making sure someone is looking out for her, too. The post Who takes care of mom after the baby arrives? appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall, something happens in the body before it happens in the mind. The smell of wood smoke drifting through a cracked window, the particular weight of October light slanting across the floor, and suddenly you’re somewhere else entirely, back in a kitchen you haven’t thought about in years, or feeling fourteen again for no apparent reason. Then you reach for the show you always watch this time of year, or the book with the cracked spine, and the evening softens. If that pull toward the familiar feels like something you should probably resist, it isn’t. Mental health professionals describe what happens each autumn as a predictable response to something real: the season changing registers in your nervous system as a small form of loss. The nostalgia that follows isn’t a distraction from fall; rather, it’s a part of how you move through it. Seasonal transitions are a form of small loss “Transitions mean something is changing, and change inherently means something is being lost,” says Janna Sayfie , L.M.S.W., co-founder and psychotherapist at Urban Mind Psychotherapy. “These ‘endings,’ however small, register to us as a form of loss. Looking back at something familiar anchors us to a sense of continuity and stability that we try to find when it feels like the ground is shifting beneath us.” That sense of loss takes different shapes for different people. For a lot of adults, the end of summer is the end of a looser way of moving through the week, a rhythm that’s harder to hold onto once September arrives. For parents, back-to-school season carries a weight that’s difficult to articulate, the passage of time made suddenly visible. And even without children in the picture, fall tends to settle in with a certain pressure attached: fresh starts implied, intentions expected, a vague sense that you should be doing more with the season than you are. Matt Sosnowsky , L.C.S.W., founder and psychotherapist at Philadelphia Talk Therapy, compares it to New Year’s, with all the same weight and none of the festivities. Your body recognizes fall before your brain does Part of why autumn nostalgia can feel so sudden and strange is that it often bypasses the thinking mind entirely. Sarah Haugh , L.M.H.C., founder of North Shore Professional Therapy, describes these as somatic memories: body-based recall that surfaces through sensory cues before any conscious recognition has kicked in. “Even before we know what these triggers remind us of, we’re swept away into visceral or nervous system memory,” Haugh says. She explains that this kind of implicit memory, a felt sense rather than a story you can retrieve, is the same part of the memory system that holds experiences from before we had language. Fall is unusually thick with these triggers. Wood smoke through a cracked window. The low angle of October light that somehow reads as different from September even when the temperature hasn’t shifted. Damp leaves, a candle you only bring out once a year, the sound of a school bus on a Tuesday morning. Any of these can pull a decade-old feeling into your chest before you’ve had a chance to ask where it came from. Why reruns feel better than something new Once the nervous system has registered the season as a kind of ending, it tends to steer toward the known. Sayfie puts it plainly: “Our brains tend to favor the predictable over the unpredictable.” We associate the unknown with risk, and when things are shifting, even in the small seasonal way they do every year, the familiar offers something new experiences can’t: you already know how it ends. Revisiting a favorite show or book is one way of meeting that need without quite naming it. The characters feel like company you trust. There’s no uncertainty about whether it will be good. Sosnowsky describes this as a form of safety-seeking, not a failure to engage with what’s ahead, but a way of steadying yourself so that you can. Nostalgia as a tool, not just a feeling Sosnowsky calls nostalgia “an engine for positive emotions,” pointing to research showing that wellbeing draws from three sources: anticipating the future, savoring the present, and looking back at the past. “Taking time to sink into a memory with gratitude and appreciation can help us elevate seminal experiences of joy, connection, and deep meaning,” he says. Nostalgia works that third channel. Don’t think of it as wallowing but as a return to something that still has something to give. Sometimes it carries grief alongside the warmth, which is its own kind of usefulness. A young person packing for college while their mind keeps wandering back to high school. A parent watching a kid start middle school while some part of them is still at kindergarten drop-off. Someone moving through a first round of holidays without a person they love. Looking backward in these moments isn’t getting stuck; it’s how the past gets processed. “Looking back, though sometimes difficult, helps us to integrate our past and make meaning from life,” Sosnowsky says. “In this way, we benefit from the people, places, and experiences that helped shape our lives by recognizing what remains a part of us as we move forward.” So when October settles in, and you find yourself scrolling down to the same playlist, reaching for the same worn-out novel, or clicking on the same show you’ve already seen more times than you can count, that pull isn’t something to override. It may be your nervous system holding onto who you are while the season changes around you. Remind yourself that you can gift yourself that return. At some point, when you’re ready, you can always put something new on. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached full height in Germany. GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall from base to blade tip, making it Germany’s second-tallest structure after Berlin’s TV tower . Official commissioning is set for November. Higher altitude, stronger winds Higher up, winds are faster and more reliable. That translates to more hours of generation per year, and GICON says its design could produce roughly twice the electricity of a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. One thing to flag: that’s a claim about cumulative generation over time, not rated power. The turbine’s rated capacity is 3.8 megawatts; future versions are designed to go past seven. The rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground. Building that high required rethinking construction. A crane capable of reaching 1,197 feet wasn’t realistic, so GICON used a telescoping tower instead. A specialized lifting system raised an inner tower through a surrounding lattice structure, then locked it at full extension. “365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.” A second tier for existing wind farms GICON and its funder, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND), aren’t pitching these turbines as replacements for existing wind farms. The plan is to stack them above. A “second tier” of tall turbines with their rotors spinning above those of conventional turbines already in the ground, adding generation without touching any new land. Germany’s existing wind farms could potentially fit up to 4,000 of them, per the companies’ own estimate. That’s a significant amount of added capacity without a single new wind farm permit. The Schipkau turbine is still a pilot, and the yield projections haven’t been proven in operation yet. GICON and SPRIND are in talks with wind energy companies about commercialization, with series production as the goal. Everything depends on what the numbers look like once it’s running. items.descriptionOriginal: A married California couple has made it their mission to photograph all 40 wild cat species on Earth — and they only have one more to go. The stunning images serve to raise awareness about the animals, many of which are vulnerable or endangered. So far, Sebastian Kennerknecht and Rachel Tobias have traveled to 33 countries across five continents and photographed 39 species in the Felidae family, often using camera traps in forests, deserts, and grasslands where the elusive cats roam. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht The San Francisco-based duo has captured images of a cheetah in Tanzania, a tiger in India, and an ocelot in Panama. The only species they have yet to cross off the list is the northern oncilla, found in Central America. It’s a rarely seen animal, and one of smallest wild cats in the Americas. View this post on Instagram Kennerknecht, 41, has been photographing cats since college: He studied ecology at the University of California, Santa Cruz, to understand animals and became particularly interested in bobcats. Tobias, 37, grew up loving wildlife and was always drawn to the ocean and photography. The two met online, and they instantly connected over their love of nature. Fittingly, their first date was searching for bobcats. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht In 2024, Kennerknecht realized he had photos of 30 of the world’s wild cats, so he and Tobias decided to go for the full 40. In addition to photography, the couple run cat expeditions together, taking out small groups to observe the felines in their natural habitat and learn how to photograph them. They’ve raised hundreds of thousands of dollars through their work. One photo of a Borneo Bay cat brought in $120,000 for conservation efforts, and they collected around $70,000 per year for five years to protect lion species in Zambia’s Kafue National Park. They are partnered with Panthera, the world’s leading wild cat conservation organization. Kennerknecht told Talk to the Press that the couple’s work is “99% frustration and 1% joy,” noting that they’ve seen elephants crush their expensive camera traps, insects get into them, and humidity fog up lenses, rendering images unusable. “We set up a studio in the forest,” Tobias explained, adding: “In Malaysia, we set up six traps; we had to sleep in the jungle full of bugs and carry 60 pounds of gear.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Despite the project’s challenges, the couple is dedicated to ethical photography. They don’t use any bait or lures to attract the cats towards the cameras, so they can observe their natural behavior. “It’s much more successful for telling a story about the species,” said Tobias. “Telling a story between the viewer and the animal is really powerful for conservation.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht A large part of their aim is to introduce the world to the 33 small wild cat species that are relatively unknown, so more can be done to protect them. “If you protect small cats, you protect big cats,” she added. The pair also wants to prove humans can coexist with big and small wild cats. “There are lots of human activities that might negatively impact cats without people knowing,” Tobias said. “People want to protect natural spaces and help with coexistence.” View this post on Instagram In Paraguay at the time of this writing, the team has had camera traps set up since April to capture the northern oncilla, with a ground crew frequently checking on them, but the cat has remained elusive. View this post on Instagram “It’s been pretty incredible,” Kennerknecht said, “but measuring local awareness has been tough.” They’ve set up billboards in areas with wild cats, featuring pictures of the local cats with the slogan, “I’m your neighbor.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht As for their favorite species, Kennerknecht said his is a bobcat, as that’s the feline that launched his photographic journey in Santa Cruz. But for Tobias: “There’s nothing more beautiful than a female leopard.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Below are the cats they’ve photographed so far: Lion — Zambia Jaguar — Brazil Tiger — India Snow Leopard — Kyrgyzstan Leopard — Zambia Mainland Clouded Leopard — Malaysia Sunda Clouded Leopard — Malaysia African Golden Cat — Uganda Caracal — Yemen Serval — Tanzania Geoffroy’s Cat — Argentina Southern Oncila — Brazil Andean Mountain Cat- Argentina Pampas Cat- Bolivia Ocelot — Panama Margay — Panama Marbled Cat — Malaysia Borneo Bay Cat — Malaysia Asiatic Golden Cat — Indonesia Bobcat — U.S. Canada Lynx — Canada Eurasian Lynx — Kyrgyzstan Iberian Lynx — Spain Mountain Lion — Chile Cheetah — Tanzania Mainland Leopard Cat — Malaysia Sunda Leopard Cat — Malaysia Flat-Headed Cat — Malaysia Rusty-Spotted Cat — India Fishing Cat — Thailand Pallas’s Cat — Mongolia Jungle Cat — India Sand Cat — Western Sahara Black-footed Cat — South Africa European Wild Cat — Spain Afro-Asiatic Wild Cat — Botswana Chinese Mountain Cat — China Jaguarundi — Location Unconfirmed/South America Güiña — Location Unconfirmed/Chile/Argentina This article was originally written by William Ormes Roder for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.titleOriginal: A Harvard scientist followed ‘shy’ babies for 13 years. What he found is a goldmine for parents.
items.description: Ο ψυχολόγος του Χάρβαρντ Τζερόμ Κάγκαν είχε μια άκαμπτη άποψη για τη φύση εναντίον της ανατροφής νωρίς στην καριέρα του: «Μπήκα στην ψυχολογία γιατί ήθελα να ανακαλύψω πόσο ισχυρό ήταν το περιβάλλον και ήμουν πολύ απρόθυμος να αναγνωρίσω τον ρόλο οποιωνδήποτε βιολογικών διαφορών μεταξύ των παιδιών», λέει σε μια συνέντευξη στο κανάλι YouTube The Brainwaves Video Anthology.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Harvard psychologist Jerome Kagan had a rigid view on nature vs nurture early in his career: “I entered psychology because I wanted to discover how powerful the environment was and I was very reluctant to acknowledge the role of any biological differences between children,” he says in an interview with The Brainwaves Video Anthology YouTube channel. But the more he studied upbringing, family life, and other environmental factors, the more he felt he was missing a piece of the bigger picture of what shapes a child’s temperament, whether they are shy or outgoing. Harvard psychologists followed infants and toddlers for years to uncover the roots of shyness Kagan says he could see differences between infants of different nationalities at just 3 months old, which led him to realize that our natural temperament must have a biological underpinning. So in the late 1970s, he launched a series of studies following what he called both “high reactive” and “low reactive” children. Researchers screened infants as young as four months for how much they reacted to unfamiliar stimuli. This could be as simple as introducing a new toy or mobile, or taking them to an unfamiliar place. “High reactive” kids would cry and flail, while “low reactive” kids would be mostly unbothered. The most extreme cases on both ends of the spectrum were selected for long-term follow-ups over the course of several years, with many children being studied well into their adolescence, and some into adulthood. All-in-all, Kagan studied temperament for decades, and much of what he discovered helped write the so-called book on shy kids. Here are a few of the most interesting bits of his research: Being “shy” is mostly physiological Kagan found that infants only three or four months old could be easily sorted into the high or low reactive bucket. His research eventually revealed that shyness, or high reactivity, stems from an overactive or hypersensitive nervous system. Physical differences in brain makeup and neurochemistry make some people more attuned to stimulation. Kagan could quite literally see the difference through activity in the amygdala, the part of the brain responsible for our survival instincts and fight-or-flight response. Previous research had pegged shyness as a fixed personality trait, but Kagan’s long-term studies revealed that it is often biologically based and inherited, which is a total game-changer. In some cases, he found that people could “develop” shyness over time due to trauma at home or other environmental factors. But shyness, or being “inhibited,” is not locked in place One of the most fascinating parts of Kagan’s long-term research was how it clearly showed that shyness can change over time. Even though its basis lies in our nervous system and brain chemistry, the children he studied sometimes became less shy and reactive over time—and sometimes more. “I would say, if you start with 10 very shy children at age 1, you’ll end up with 3 who are very shy as adolescents,” he said in 1991, per The Harvard Crimson . The most extreme cases were the least likely to change. Shy kids can learn to be bold adults, but the brain markers remain One major follow-up in Kagan’s work was doing brain scans, some 20 years later, on some of the children he identified early on as shy or highly reactive. He found that many of those kids had become less “fearful” as adults. They had learned to overcome their shyness and be bolder. However, their brains still showed a highly active, sensitive amygdala upon scanning. This not only supported his original theories that shyness is biological, but it also showed that many of these kids eventually learned coping strategies and social skills that helped them overcome their natural temperament. The key to parenting a shy child Understanding shyness as an inherited but flexible physiological trait, and not a rigid one, goes a long way toward understanding kids who are more sensitive than their peers. It helps us see that reserved kids aren’t being difficult or stubborn—they just have a stronger physical reaction to things that wouldn’t faze an “uninhibited child.” However, parents, teachers, and anyone else who regularly interacts with kids want to know the best way to engage a shy child. Kagan says pushing them too hard and forcing them out of their comfort zone is the worst thing you can do. “You have to be sensitive. You don’t want to put too much pressure on such children to join the group and be sociable,” he said in the Crimson . However, gentle encouragement and help building scaffolding for social skills, coping strategies, and confidence can go a long way. Kagan specifically advocated making the unfamiliar familiar: meeting the teacher in advance, touring a new classroom before the first day, and exposing students to new things whenever possible. Shy brains may always tell a person that the world is threatening, but they can learn to adjust the way they act on that feeling. There’s a correlation between shyness and blue eyes The shy kids Kagan studied were also more likely to have blue eyes, he noted. He even theorized that the genetic factors that determine our eye color may be the same ones that influence how sensitive our nervous system is to stimulation. However, follow-up studies have either failed to find the same correlation or found it fairly weak. Kagan also found that the inhibited kids he studied were likely to grow up tall and thin and suffer from conditions like hay fever and eczema due to higher levels of stress hormones. The magic number for parents Shyness isn’t inherently bad; Kagan was careful never to treat it as a disorder or something that needed fixing. In fact, a shy temperament often helps people succeed in fields that value being measured, careful, and a good listener. In extreme cases, however, a sensitive temperament can lead to adults who are fearful, isolated, or who suffer from anxiety disorders. Moreover, modern society tends to reward people who are outgoing, bold, and extroverted. Kagan says the key to helping a child overcome a shy temperament is early intervention, ideally before age 7. “The general rule [is], you change a lot between birth and age 7. After age 7, you don’t change very much. If you’re extremely shy and fearful at 7–the odds are about two-thirds of those kids will be shy as adolescents,” he says. A stigma still remains around people who are labeled as shy. People often conflate shyness or reserve with fear, weakness, or a lack of confidence. Kagan’s work went a long way toward clearing up misunderstandings about what shyness is and isn’t, but we could all use a bit of a refresher. A shy temperament is the result of a brain that’s hypersensitive to danger, not a failure of parents to socialize or a child being stubborn or difficult. But temperament and behavior are two different things, and with the right support, many extremely shy kids can go on to become highly social and successful adults. The post A Harvard scientist followed ‘shy’ babies for 13 years. What he found is a goldmine for parents. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Pets are pawing at screens to watch this South Korean cartoon. Experts explain the science behind it.
items.description: Τα σκυλιά συνεχίζουν να χτυπούν τα πόδια στην τηλεόραση κατά τη διάρκεια ενός συγκεκριμένου καρτούν του Netflix… που δεν ήταν φτιαγμένο για αυτούς. Μια γυναίκα από το Όρεγκον είπε στον Guardian ότι α…
items.descriptionOriginal: Dogs keep pawing at the TV during a specific Netflix cartoon … that wasn’t made for them. A South Korean cartoon about a colony of seals has turned into an unexpected hit with animals, and social media is full of videos of dogs standing inches from the screen, tilting their heads and batting at the glass . One Oregon woman told The Guardian that a clip of her two goldendoodles watching it pulled nearly 10 million views. “The minute the seals started drumming, Benny sat up, and Myrtle had these subtle head tilts,” she said. The show is Sealook , a wordless slapstick series co-produced by The Pinkfong Company and Million Volt. It premiered in South Korea in 2022 and later landed on Netflix, where it’s listed as a TV-Y kids’ comedy. It was made for children. “Seeing cats and now dogs as well, becoming so absorbed in Sealook has been a fun and unexpected surprise,” Leah Yeon, Pinkfong’s communications lead, told The Guardian . She said they didn’t set out to make a show for animals, but what they did make is pretty (and accidentally), perfect for one. Dogs and cats are dichromatic , meaning they see blues and yellows well but struggle to distinguish reds and greens. Sealook is pale ice, blue water, and brightly colored seals, so almost the entire color palette falls inside the range an animal can actually distinguish. Netflix noted in its own feature on the show that viewers started pointing this out in late summer, and that it’s a coincidence rather than a design choice. Then there’s the movement on the screen. “Cats and dogs are particularly interested in movement because they are instinctively drawn to chasing a mouse or other prey,” David Williams, an associate lecturer in veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Cambridge, told The Guardian . Freya Mowat, a veterinary ophthalmologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, put it more plainly to the paper: “Cartoons are great content for dogs: high contrast, lots of movement, nice fun music, it’s the whole package.” The sound may matter as much as the picture. Emily Blackwell, a companion-animal behavior specialist, told The Guardian that the noises the seals make could register as prey sounds or as squeaky toys. Williams suggested an easy at-home test: turn the sound off and see whether your dog stays interested. A 2024 study in Applied Animal Behaviour Science surveyed 1,246 dog owners and found that 86% said their dogs watched screens, with 90% of those owners citing movement as what grabbed the dog’s attention and 78% citing sound. However, that study is about dogs and screens in general, not this show—and it says nothing about cats. Nobody has actually tested Sealook on a representative sample of animals. But what does exist is a pile of videos of pets that do appear to be watching, and a reasonable enough theory about why. Of course, plenty of dogs don’t care at all. As one commenter put it: “I put this on for my dog, and she’s watching me instead.” The post Pets are pawing at screens to watch this South Korean cartoon. Experts explain the science behind it. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Η Hilary Swank ανταποκρίνεται τέλεια στη γυναίκα που λέει ότι είναι πολύ μεγάλη για να κάνει παιδιά
items.titleOriginal: Hilary Swank responds perfectly to woman who says she’s too old to have kids
items.description: Η ηθοποιός Hilary Swank περιμένει το τρίτο της παιδί. Η 52χρονη σταρ του Boys Don’t Cry ανακοίνωσε την εγκυμοσύνη της στο Instagram στις 14 Οκτωβρίου μαζί με τον σύζυγό της, Philip Schneider, και τα δίδυμα (γιος Ohm και κόρη Aya). Η Swank έγινε για πρώτη φορά μαμά στα 48. Κατά τη διάρκεια μιας πρόσφατης εμφάνισης στο The Drew Barrymore Show, η Swank μίλησε για το πώς είναι να είσαι έγκυος…
items.descriptionOriginal: Actress Hilary Swank is expecting her third child. The Boys Don’t Cry star, 52, announced her pregnancy on Instagram on October 14 alongside her husband, Philip Schneider, and twins (son Ohm and daughter Aya). Swank became a first-time mom at 48. During a recent appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show , Swank opened up about what it’s like to be pregnant at 52. “I just entered my third trimester,” she told Barrymore. Swank’s pregnancy at 52 As the two sat down together, Swank shared that the last time she appeared on Barrymore’s show, she was 12 weeks pregnant with her twins. “Now with this baby I’m 28 weeks,” Swank said before adding, “Just one this time!” They continue to talk about Swank’s pregnancy cravings (which include Rice Krispies Treats and a vegan alternative to Cheetos) before Barrymore reiterates how “beautiful, glowing, gorgeous” Swank looks. “It’s amazing what women’s bodies can do, and it’s just such an extraordinary privilege and honor and blessing to carry life. It’s a dream come true and I love being a mom,” said Swank. Barrymore asks Swank to share more about what it was like to share her first pregnancy with the world at an “older age.” “This was the right time for me. Although not everything happens in our own time. We have ideas for timelines for ourselves, and getting pregnant isn’t always in our own timeline, right?” Swank shared. “You can hope and pray for certain things, and things happen when they’re supposed to happen. I was very excited, and it was a good time for me because I feel like I had this career that was a ‘baby’ of mine that I really wanted to give to and devote my time to and not share. And now I can totally devote [myself] to my children.” View this post on Instagram “Backlash” for older pregnancies Swank continued, “What’s interesting and beautiful is a lot of people say, ‘This has given me hope that I can get pregnant too, and it’s something that I really want in my life,’ because for a lot of women it’s a ticking clock. It’s not the same for men.” Swank then talked about the “backlash women get for having children older but not men, which is interesting.” Barrymore chimed in that men “have babies in their 80s,” and when Swank had babies in her 40s, “people weren’t always gracious about it.” Swank responded with a story about criticism she received from a woman who told her, “How dare you! You’re too old. You won’t be [young] enough when your kids are older. My dad was my favorite person, and he died when I was in my early 20s. And it’s just devastation.” She added that she “related” to the woman’s story and was “drawn to it” after her father died at a young age as well. But then she thought to herself, “I would rather be born and have that person and experience that than not at all.” View this post on Instagram Becoming a mom at 48 In a 2024 interview with PEOPLE , Swank opened up about why getting pregnant at 47 and welcoming her twins at 48 was right for her. “I was 47 when I got pregnant, and I feel like I have a lot more patience, and I’ve done a lot of my own personal work to be the type of mother I want to be, whereas it would’ve just been different in my twenties and thirties,” she told the publication. “I don’t think I would’ve had the patience and the grace that I hopefully can bestow a little bit more [of] now, and a self-awareness in a different way that I don’t need to focus on myself anymore in the way that I did at that point,” she said. “I can give differently.” The post Hilary Swank responds perfectly to woman who says she’s too old to have kids appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Όποιος έχει παίξει Monopoly ξέρει πώς πάει συνήθως: αυτό που ξεκινά ως διασκεδαστικό παιχνίδι μετατρέπεται αναπόφευκτα σε ένα ατελείωτο slog μέχρι να συμφωνήσουν όλοι να ανακηρύξουν κάποιον νικητή.
