Ένας YouTuber που περνάει από το @sblga εξηγεί ότι, παρά το fo…
items.descriptionOriginal: Anyone who’s played Monopoly knows how it usually goes: what starts as a fun game inevitably turns into an endless slog until everyone agrees to declare someone the winner . As it turns out, we’ve brought this agony on ourselves by not actually following the official Monopoly game rules . A YouTuber who goes by @sblga explains says that, despite following all kinds of made-up “house rules,” most of us neglect one simple, official Monopoly rule that makes the game go much faster. It’s known as the “auction rule,” and it’s literally a game-changer. (By the way, he also shares the game’s absolutely wild history, which is definitely worth sticking around for.) How the ‘auction rule’ in Monopoly changes the game Several scenarios can trigger the auction rule. The primary rule, however, is that when a player lands on a property and doesn’t want to (or can’t) buy it, the property immediately goes up for auction, and all players can bid on it. There is no minimum bid, so bidding can start at just $1. Theoretically, if a player lands on Boardwalk and doesn’t buy it, another player (or even that original player) could nab it for far less than its $400 value through a bidding war. Players flush with cash can create monopolies simply by outbidding their opponents. This rule means properties get picked up much more quickly, so the game doesn’t stall. It also forces players to strategize differently with their property purchases and money management. Can you imagine playing a full game of Monopoly in 30 minutes and having someone actually win? It’s possible with the auction rule. Who knew? Monopoly money changing hands. Photo credit: Canva Monopoly ‘house rules’ ease the game’s ruthlessness So if the auction rule has always been part of the standard game rules, why don’t more people use it? Theories abound, but one big one is that most people just don’t read the official rules. Gameplay often gets passed down by family and friends, and for Monopoly in particular, “house rules” often trump official rules. Some popular Monopoly house rules include: Free Parking jackpot, in which all tax payments go to the center of the board instead of to the bank. When someone lands on Free Parking, they collect the jackpot. Double salary landing on GO. First-lap immunity, meaning no one can buy property on their first lap around the board. No rent in jail, meaning if a player is in jail, they cannot collect rent when other players land on their properties. People may not even realize that house rules aren’t standard. Someone likely eliminated the auction rule at some point to slow the game’s pace and/or reduce its brutality, and it spread and stuck. What’s interesting about Monopoly house rules is that they often ease the game’s ruthlessness, which is ironic, considering why the game was created in the first place. Monopoly’s origin story: A caution against unbridled capitalism In January of 1904, a woman named Lizzie Magie patented a game called the Landlord’s Game. The game had two sets of rules: one used a single land tax and distributed wealth among players, resulting in a collective win, and the other let players build monopolies and ruthlessly fleece opponents. It was meant to be a lesson, an indictment of unbridled capitalism. However, a heater salesman named Charles Darrow took a particular liking to the game and its monopoly rules. Without crediting the Landlord’s Game, Darrow created Monopoly as we know it and sold it to Parker Brothers. “What Magie intended as a forecast of disaster became Monopoly’s sole objective,” Public Domain Review notes. A criticism of greed and power imbalance became a celebration of free-market capitalism. In 1935, Parker Brothers bought Magie’s patent for $500 and no royalties . Meanwhile, Darrow became a millionaire. The tendency to add house rules to make Monopoly more fun and fair for everyone is a good sign. It may not be the original creators’ intention. Still, many prefer a “compassionate capitalism” version of the game (even if it does take five hours and no one really ever wins). The post Man explains the official Monopoly rule no one uses that ends the game way faster appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Γνωρίστε το πρώτο πουλί στον κόσμο με 3D-εκτυπωμένες προσθέσεις άνω και κάτω ράμφους
items.titleOriginal: Meet the World’s First Bird With 3D-Printed Upper and Lower Beak Prostheses
items.description: Η ζωή είναι λίγο πιο εύκολη τώρα για ένα νότιο κέρας στην Ολλανδία, χάρη στις τρισδιάστατες προθέσεις για το πάνω και το κάτω ράμφος του. Το πουλί στο μέγεθος της γαλοπούλας στον Βασιλικό Ζωολογικό Κήπο ARTIS του Άμστερνταμ υπέστη σοβαρό τραυματισμό που έσπασε και τα δύο τμήματα του λογαριασμού του και του άφησε δύο κολοβώματα, δυσκολεύοντάς του να πάρει φαγητό και να περιποιηθεί τον εαυτό του.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Life is a little easier now for a southern ground hornbill in the Netherlands, thanks to 3D-printed prostheses for his upper and lower beak. The turkey-sized bird at the ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo suffered a severe injury that broke both sections of his bill and left him with two stumps, making it difficult for him to pick up food and groom himself. “He managed reasonably well with them, but he could no longer do everything a hornbill naturally does,” ARTIS veterinarian Martine van Zijll Langhout said in a press release . To improve his well-being, the team perfected custom prostheses that are “virtually identical” to his original beak. “A bird uses its beak all day long, to pick up food and, for example, to preen its plumage. Especially with a young bird that can still live to a very old age, we felt it was important to see if we could improve its quality of life,” van Zijll Langhout added. ARTIS Although several birds have been fitted with artificial beaks, this hornbill is believed to be the first to receive replacements for both the upper and lower beak. Should the beak parts continue to function well for the long-term, the team plans to publish a scientific paper detailing exactly how they created the prostheses, so veterinarians around the world can help similar patients. The process is technically complex, as every bird has a unique beak that perfectly aligns to its skull and other anatomy. If the shape isn’t exactly right for either part of the bill, the animal will struggle to use the prosthesis. To ensure their creation would be a success, van Zijll Langhout and her colleagues performed a CT scan of the bird’s head as well as the broken beak pieces. The prostheses were then 3D-printed from plastic, and orthopedic surgeons meticulously attached them using titanium components. View this post on Instagram One of the biggest risks with a procedure like this is that the bird will reject the new beak, which could result in the animal refusing to eat. The zoo staff planned for that possibility and were prepared to have the prostheses removed if need be — but so far, all is going well: The team reported the bird settled in right away after the beak attachment operation and even appeared to be “smiling” afterward . And the day following the surgery, he began eating independently. “That was an incredibly important moment for us,” said van Zijll Langhout. “He understood that he could use his beak and began to discover for himself what was possible with it.” RELATED: From a Dolphin’s Tail to a Bird’s Beak: 7 Innovative Prosthetics That Have Helped Animals

items.descriptionOriginal: The treatment delivers a light-sensitive algae protein to the retina. Paired with special goggles, it can restore limited vision and lasts for years. The patients sit perfectly still as a needle inches toward one of their eyes. After the injection, they’ll no longer be completely human. The syringe is filled with a gene therapy that installs a light-sensitive algae protein into failing retinas and could reboot some lost vision. When scientists first proposed using algae proteins to restore human eyesight, the idea seemed like science fiction. Could alien proteins integrate into our intricate visual system? Even if they did, could the brain translate the resulting signals into sight, rather than nonsensical bursts of light? A new study suggests yes, with caveats. The team treated people with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that gradually destroys light-sensing cells in the retina. Seven of ten patients showed improved light sensitivity. After patients donned goggles that deliver pulses of light to activate the algae proteins, the team tested their eyesight. Roughly half could reach for and touch objects or identify the orientation of a black bar, a common test of visual recovery. The treatment is still far from restoring full vision. What patients saw was too blurry and the field of view too narrow to discern texture or fine detail. The boundaries of objects looked squiggly. But those who responded to the treatment continued to improve over roughly five years. One participant, whose story made headlines in 2021 , can now recognize and count different objects, and white stripes on a crosswalk pop out. The study, called PIONEER , is an ambitious clinical trial combining gene therapy with optogenetics. The first goal was to assess safety, and it met the mark. Most participants experienced a brief bout of inflammation in the eye receiving the injection. The only patient to suffer a severe side effect was quickly treated with medication. The findings suggest the initial success wasn’t a fluke. The study “represents an important milestone for optogenetic vision restoration,” said study author Stefan Futterknecht at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel, in a press release . Setting Sights High Around two decades ago, Karl Deisseroth was hunting for new ways to control brain cells. Electrical bursts and chemicals, which are how neurons communicate, seemed like obvious choices. But nature had something stranger to offer: algae. Algae produce a protein called channelrhodopsin. When activated by light, the protein changes neuron activity using a mechanism that works similarly in mammalian cells. In a foundational paper , Deisseroth’s team inserted the protein into rodent neurons, and voilá—the neurons could now be controlled using light. The technology, called optogenetics, revolutionized neuroscience. By genetically tagging specific neurons with channelrhodopsin, scientists can now dial the cells’ activity up or down like a dimmer switch. Optogenetic experiments have revealed brain circuits that shape feelings, memory, and cognition with unprecedented precision. Researchers panning for more genes in different algae strains struck gold again. One channelrhodopsin variant they found, ChrimsonR, was particularly exciting. Unlike the classic version that’s activated by blue light, ChrimsonR responds to amber light, which penetrates tissues better and is less damaging. More recently, scientists have begun to use generative AI to redesign natural proteins to make them even more sensitive to light. “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, when the technology won the coveted prize this year. Still, it has mainly been considered a research tool. Light It Up Retinitis pigmentosa gradually robs people of their eyesight. Researchers have linked over 100 genetic variations to the condition, which kills off light-sensitive cells in the retina. “The replacement (or editing) of a single gene would not help most persons,” wrote Deisseroth in the New England Journal of Medicine . Instead, adding channelrhodopsin could offer a more universal solution by rewiring surviving neurons. Early successes bolstered the idea. In one study , scientists equipped cones—a type of retinal light-sensing cell—with channelrhodopsin in mice with retinitis pigmentosa. The therapy boosted their light sensitivity. It also reactivated cones that had stopped responding to light in human retina samples. The new study took a different approach. In advanced disease, cones may have already degenerated beyond the point at which they could be saved. So instead, the gene therapy targeted ganglion cells. These cells process signals from light-sensitive cells and pass that information to the brain, but don’t detect light themselves. Ganglion cells are, however, more resilient than cones. Add channelrhodopsin, and they could become substitute light sensors. The team packed genetic instructions for ChrimsonR into a harmless viral delivery system and injected it into the poorer seeing eye of 10 patients aged 40 to 73. All were legally blind, and each received one of three escalating doses. As the patients gradually built up levels of the algae protein in their eyes, the team faced another challenge: Translating visual scenes from the outside world into amber light that the engineered ganglion cells could recognize. They developed specialized goggles that look a bit like Apple’s Vision Pro. The goggles use a camera to scan the field of view thousands of times per second, monitoring for light changes in every pixel. When the device detects a change, it pulses amber light from that pixel into the eye. Because our eyes naturally dart around—often without us noticing—this dynamic method may better mimic normal vision. With the goggles on, 6 of 10 participants showed clinically meaningful improvement in light sensitivity, with more than a fourfold boost over baseline readings. One participant improved over 62-fold. Of the eight who agreed to further eyesight tests, roughly half could touch a notebook, grab a small staple box, and detect changes in a rotating bar. Of those who initially responded to the treatment, improvements lasted for years. Their brains also seemed to adapt to the alien light sensors. In one test, participants were asked to open or close their eyes while looking at a tumbler. Electrical brain signals related to vision were more coherent with eyes open, suggesting their perception depended on improved visual input. Any gene therapy carries risk. In an already worsening eye, inflammation and other side effects could cause further damage. Overall, the injection appeared relatively safe. Most participants experienced a temporary increase in eye pressure, but no detectable side effects throughout the body. The retina’s overall structure remained unchanged. One person suffered a blockage in a major eye artery that cleared within minutes after treatment with an FDA-approved eye drop. For now, the participants still can’t read or see faces. The therapy reaches only a fraction of their ganglion cells, making sharper vision harder to restore. More advanced versions of channelrhodopsin with greater light sensitivity may increase resolution. As for the hardware, the team is working on versions of the goggles that deliver more accurate and timely stimulation. Potential upgrades include an eye tracker, software to preprocess visual scenes, and even holographs . “Overall, although optogenetic methods have been developed primarily for basic science discovery,” wrote Deisseroth, they’re now heading towards “diverse therapeutic approaches.” The post Blind Patients Recover Partial Vision in Gene Therapy Trial appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.description: Αν έχετε δει ποτέ φωτογραφίες του γάμου ενός ξένου και σκεφτήκατε: "Φαίνεται καλή στιγμή! Μακάρι να μπορούσα να ήμουν εκεί", αυτό το άρθρο είναι για εσάς. Και αν είστε στην αγορά για να παντρευτείτε και ανησυχείτε μήπως το πληρώσετε, ίσως να θέλετε να δώσετε προσοχή επίσης. Ιδού το σενάριο: τις εβδομάδες ή τις ημέρες πριν από τον γάμο τους, ένα ζευγάρι στ…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you’ve ever seen pictures of a stranger’s wedding and thought, “That looks like a good time! Wish I could’ve been there,” this article is for you. And if you’re in the market to get married and worried about paying for it , you might want to pay attention as well. Here’s the scenario: in the weeks or days leading up to their wedding , a couple finds that a handful of their guests have canceled. They’ve already purchased the meal, and arrangements have already been made for their attendance. The couple will have to eat the cost, and with weddings already averaging over $30,000 , who can afford the waste? What if there were a simple solution to that problem? View this post on Instagram Having strangers pay to attend your wedding Not a Wedding Crasher might be one of the most unique wedding businesses ever. The website describes the premise as “A thoughtful way to share the seats that would otherwise go empty. “ “Nearly every wedding has guest cancellations or venue minimums that need to be met. The flowers are arranged. The meals are paid for. The music still plays,” the site explains. “Not a Wedding Crasher helps couples thoughtfully invite verified guests to experience a celebration that would otherwise have empty chairs, creating connection, energy, and unforgettable memories along the way.” People’s initial reaction to strangers paying to attend a wedding might be, “No way, that’s too weird.” But in reality, especially if your wedding is large, you likely have people on the guest list you don’t know very well anyway. (Your distant cousin’s new boyfriend, for example.) What’s adding a couple of vetted strangers to the mix if it helps cover the cost of cancellations? View this post on Instagram Who would want to pay to go to a stranger’s wedding? If you’re asking, “Who would do this?” you’re likely not someone who would sign up for this service. But some people love weddings, love a good party, love dressing up and dancing, and are perfectly willing to help a stranger out in exchange for the fun of it all. In fact, the couple who founded the site, Jeff and Karina Besen, said the idea first came to them because they were looking for a unique date night. As a long-time married couple, they value going on dates—and what better date is there than attending a wedding? “You can’t just go to a wedding, at least not morally,” Jeff told WGN News . “So we connected a few dots…maybe there’s now a way to attend a wedding intentionally.” The Besens explained that many people who sign up as guests on their site are planning to get married themselves (and are looking for ideas for their own weddings) and work in the wedding industry (and are always working at weddings and rarely get to enjoy them as guests). Others have never been to a wedding and want to experience one, while others just love celebrating love. (Note: Stranger-guests have to be verified by the site, and couples have to manually approve them before they can attend, so there are some guardrails in place to weed out potential weirdos.) Are couples really using the site to fill seats? As of this writing, 24 upcoming weddings were listed on notaweddingcrasher.com . Prices range from $25 to $150 per seat, and each listing includes details about the wedding, dress code, meal, music, and other information. Exact locations aren’t listed, only the city where the wedding will take place. The couple sends pertinent details to guests after verification and approval. Some couples who’ve used the service have shared that having strangers at the wedding brought in fun energy. As one bride wrote , having a stranger-guest “amped up the vibe” of the event. Imagine folks who love to dance rolling in and getting the party started on the dance floor. It could change the whole atmosphere in minutes. It’s definitely not everyone’s cup of tea. But for those who love a wedding and don’t mind “crashing” one, it can be a total win-win for them and the couple who “invites” them. You can check out the current wedding spots available here. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips Reading Time: 3 minutes Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips If you’re wondering, “Where can I buy peppermint oil in bulk?”, you have many options, including specialist wholesalers, ingredient distributors, and online marketplaces. Wholesale Botanics, Bulk Apothecary, and Bulk Natural Oils are just a few options worth considering. Walmart also lists larger bottles, while Amazon is another marketplace to check. The best starting point depends on the quantity of the product you need. A larger bottle may suit occasional soap making, but regular production calls for a reliable supplier. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Specialist Suppliers for Bulk Peppermint Oil Consider these suppliers if you’re looking to buy peppermint oil in bulk. Wholesale Botanics Wholesale Botanics lists peppermint oil in 5, 25, 100, and 400-pound sizes, with custom quotes for larger quantities. Buyers have the option to choose between Mentha piperita and Mentha arvensis variants. Wholesale Botanics’ essential oil wholesale service offers consultations and sample packs, enabling you to discuss requirements before placing an order. You can also request a sample of the variant you want to purchase and confirm that testing documents are also provided. Bulk Apothecary Bulk Apothecary offers Japanese and Supreme peppermint oils in 5, 25, and 400-pound options. Shipping is calculated at checkout, so bear that in mind when purchasing. The smaller bottles allow you to test a variety before moving to a larger order. It helps to ask the company’s team about quantities beyond the listed options. New Directions Aromatics New Directions Aromatics offers its Peppermint Essential Oil (Supreme) in sizes that extend up to 396 pounds. This is the Mentha piperita variation, but it also has organic peppermint listings. Availability and dispatch arrangements differ between sizes, so it helps to confirm the selected pack is available. Bulk Natural Oils Bulk Natural Oils offer Piperita and Arvensis peppermint oils as well as organic options. The website lists a minimum spend of $150 on a combination of products. This option might suit businesses purchasing several ingredients together. Shay and Company Shay and Company is a good choice for smaller buys as it offers peppermint oil in smaller bottles in 5- and 10-pound sizes. Orders over 25 pounds require an email inquiry. Its Willamette Valley listing identifies Oregon as the origin, making it worth exploring when sourcing location matters to your product. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Can You Buy on Amazon or Walmart? Walmart’s online listings include peppermint oil in 16-ounce bottles as well as one-gallon containers. This might suit smaller projects that don’t have a large wholesale commitment. Ensure that you check the individual seller, ingredients, and documentation instead of relying on the retailer’s name alone. If you want to purchase peppermint oil on Amazon, search for the quantity you need and check who sells and ships the product. Double-check that the listing describes essential oil and not fragrance oil, extract, or a diluted blend. Check the Oil Before Comparing Prices You would typically come across two main variants: Mentha piperita, which is peppermint, and Mentha arvensis, commonly called cornmint or Japanese peppermint. While both appear in peppermint ranges, their aromas and chemical profiles differ. Make sure that you match the botanical name to your formula instead of substituting whichever costs less. Where possible, request a certificate of analysis, an available batch-specific GC/MS report, and a safety data sheet. These cover specifications, handling hazards, and chemical composition. Request the relevant certification and confirmation of suitability for certified organic, food, or oral care application. Remember that “pure” alone doesn’t establish that an oil meets your requirements. Compare Delivered Cost and Order Size In your comparison between products, factor in shipping, taxes, import charges, and membership fees. Check whether the ounces refer to weight or fluid volume. For international orders, check that the selected quantity can actually be shipped to your country and clearly establish who pays the customs charges. Drum deliveries can involve freight shipping, so ask about unloading requirements as well. For occasional purchases, compare membership savings with subscription costs before signing up for a wholesale plan. Always test a sample in the finished product before scaling up, as peppermint oil can irritate skin, and cosmetics and candles require appropriate safety or performance testing. Confirm lead times, return conditions, and remaining shelf life before paying. Store the oil tightly sealed, away from heat and light, and order only what you can realistically use. Choosing Where to Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk Amazon and Walmart are worth exploring if you want to purchase a large bottle as a one-time thing. For regular production, specialist suppliers give you more options to discuss specifications and quantities. Start by requesting a sample and a quote for the oil you need. Once you test it in your formula, you can decide whether the pricing, documentation, and availability make it a practical choice for future orders. The post Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: From being body-shamed in school to starring in a Netflix special, Sumukhi Suresh is turning the judgements women face into comedy. She gave up dancing for fear of being laughed at, but eventually found her voice through stand-up comedy. She went on to create and star in Pushpavalli and create Motormouth to make more space for women’s stories. In her Netflix special Hoemonal, Sumukhi tackles body image, dating, being single and the societal pressure on women to become mothers. Through humour, she brings conversations often brushed under the carpet into the spotlight, challenging the expectations women are constantly asked to live up to. Her journey is a reminder that you don’t have to shrink yourself to fit into someone else’s idea of who you should be. Sometimes, the most powerful way to challenge judgement is to laugh at it, speak up and tell your story on your own terms. What do you think women are judged unfairly for the most: their bodies, their age or being single? items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in Spain have shown that a modular tire in which tread and casing are designed as separate pieces stays together while in use, provided that it’s properly inflated. “This is an encouraging step toward a more sustainable tire architecture, where the worn tread could potentially be replaced while the main tire structure is reused,” says study team member Farshad Afshari , a PhD researcher at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M) and Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM).. A modular automobile tire could be easier to recycle compared to conventional ones, which require time- and labor-intensive separation of rubber treads and sidewalls from steel belts and bead cores. It would also use materials more efficiently, since there would be less material to replace at any given time. A modular tire could also be better for the environment . Conventional rubber tires are a prominent source of microplastic pollution because tiny rubber particles degrade due to friction and enter the air and waterways. But the modular design could open up the possibility of making each component of the tire from safer and more easily recyclable materials. It’s a compelling idea in theory, but would the components of a modular tire actually stay together in practice? Afshari and his collaborators built a scaled-down prototype of their ECOTIRE modular tire concept, in which tread and casing are mechanically interlocked through a series of bumps and hollows like the two halves of a waffle iron. They tested the tire on a custom-built rolling test rig in the lab to see how the tire would fare while varying parameters such as load, turning radius, inflation pressure, and slip. items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking through Ziro's lush green forests, hearing birds call from the treetops and spotting colourful butterflies fluttering along the trail. Now imagine someone helping you put a name to the birds and butterflies you see! Most of us know Arunachal Pradesh's Ziro Valley for its famous music festival, sprawling paddy fields and beautiful landscapes . But its forests have a fascinating world of wildlife waiting to be explored. And this October, 630 people got a chance to discover it. At the valley's first Ziro Bird and Butterfly Festival, students, local residents and wildlife enthusiasts headed into the forests for four days of birdwatching, butterfly spotting, nature treks and hands-on learning with conservation experts. Organised by the Hapoli Forest Division alongside the 72nd Wildlife Week, the festival had a simple idea at heart: help people discover the wildlife around them and understand why it needs protecting. And what better place to begin than the forests themselves? Beyond the music, what makes Ziro's forests so special? Ziro's music may draw visitors from across the country, but its surrounding forests have plenty worth exploring, too. Located in Arunachal Pradesh's Lower Subansiri district , the valley is part of the biodiversity-rich Eastern Himalayan landscape, home to a remarkable variety of birds, butterflies, moths and other wildlife. Some are easy to spot. Others require a little patience, curiosity and someone who knows where to look. That's where the festival came in. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Ireland in India (@irelandinindia) Led by Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) Tilling Takar, with support from Deputy Commissioner Oli Perme, the initiative brought forest officials, scientists, schools and community organisations together. The idea was to help people get to know the wildlife living around them. After all, when you can recognise a bird by its call or identify a butterfly fluttering past, even a familiar walk can become an exciting discovery. And the organisers wanted children to be part of that experience from the very beginning. It started with paintbrushes, poems and a promise Before anyone headed into the forest, students from local schools were invited to participate in wildlife-painting, poetry and essay-writing competitions. Organised in collaboration with the Apatani Students' Union, these activities encouraged children to think about nature in their own creative ways. The opening programme at Saint Claret College brought together over 450 people and representatives from 19 local organisations. Together, they pledged to protect the valley's natural heritage. There were exhibitions showcasing local plants and animals, along with sessions on wildlife laws and how to stay safe around reptiles. Traditional music performances, boxing and martial arts demonstrations by local youth groups added to the celebrations. It was a lively start, bringing people of different ages and interests together around a shared love for nature. But the most exciting part was still ahead. From bird calls to butterfly trails, the real adventure begins On the second day, participants swapped the college grounds for a forest trail. Deputy Commissioner Oli Perme flagged off a trek from Manipolyang towards Pange Camp in Tale Wildlife Sanctuary. There was one important rule for the journey: keep it plastic-free and leave no waste behind. It was a practical reminder that enjoying nature comes with the responsibility of looking after it. At Pange Camp, wildlife experts introduced participants to the fascinating world of birds, butterflies and moths. There were exhibitions showcasing local plants and animals, along with sessions on wildlife laws and how to stay safe around reptiles. Photograph: (Nature Web) Specialists associated with Bird Count India, the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), and the Wildlife Trust of India helped guide the activities. Over the final two days, participants joined early-morning birdwatching walks and butterfly-identification sessions along the Orchid Trail. Think about it. How often have you heard a bird calling from a tree but had no idea which one it was? Or spotted a beautiful butterfly without knowing anything about it? Here, participants had experts to help answer those questions. They learnt how to observe wildlife, recognise different species and understand the habitats these creatures depend on. The evenings brought research presentations and wildlife documentaries, helping connect what participants had seen outdoors with the importance of conservation. And there was plenty to learn. Birds, butterflies and moths all have important roles in nature. Many help plants reproduce through pollination, while others are part of the food chain. Studying them can also help scientists understand changes in forest habitats. Getting to know these creatures is one way to begin caring about their survival. The festival is over. But will the curiosity stay? After four days of activities, the festival concluded at Pange Camp, where competition winners and participants received certificates and awards. During the closing ceremony, DFO Tilling Takar expressed hope that the Ziro Bird and Butterfly Festival would become a regular part of Arunachal Pradesh's annual calendar. And that could make a meaningful difference. A four-day festival cannot protect an entire forest. Wildlife conservation needs continued effort from forest officials, researchers and the communities who share their surroundings with these creatures. But imagine what this experience could mean for a child who has learnt to identify a butterfly for the first time. The next time they spot one near their home, they might stop for a closer look. Someone who attended a birdwatching walk might become curious about the birds visiting their garden. And a traveller who learnt to leave no waste behind might carry that habit into their next forest adventure. These may seem like small things, but they are the kind of awareness the organisers hope to encourage. For now, Ziro will continue to draw visitors with its music, culture and breathtaking landscapes. But its newest festival has given people another reason to explore: to look up into the trees, follow a bird's call, pause for a butterfly and discover the wonderful wildlife that has been here all along. Source: 'Ziro Concludes First Bird and Butterfly Festival with 630 Participants' : By Arunachal24, Published on 10 October 2026 'Ziro Bird and Butterfly Festival begins' : By Arunachal Times, Published on 5 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree Reading Time: 3 minutes Greening upwind of cities may offer a simple fix for urban heat, with new research showing strategically placed suburban forests can cool more than half a metropolitan area. Greening upwind of cities draws on a centuries-old planning idea. Researchers behind the new study found inspiration in traditional Chinese village design , where settlements were built backed by mountains, facing water, and surrounded by forest. That layout, known as the mountain-water-forest framework, helped villages stay naturally cooler. Shi-Jie Cao, director of the Center for Sustainable Built Environment at Southeast University in Nanjing, led the team exploring whether this ancient pattern could work for modern megacities. Many cities have already tried planting trees within urban cores to combat heat. Results have often fallen short, leaving some cities sweltering through increasingly hot summers despite those efforts. Cao’s team wondered if location mattered more than volume. Placing vegetation strategically outside a city, rather than scattering it inside, might produce better cooling results. Testing that idea required a different approach than simply counting trees planted downtown. Researchers built a computer model to simulate temperature changes in urban cores during hot summer days. They tested what would happen if suburban land upwind of two Chinese cities, Beijing and Shanghai, were converted into either forest or built-up development. The two cities offered contrasting geography, with Beijing sitting on a plain near mountains and Shanghai positioned along the coast. Results revealed a clear mechanism. Greening upwind of cities creates a mass of cooler air in the surrounding suburbs. Prevailing winds then carry that cooler air directly into the city, lowering temperatures across the urban core without requiring any changes inside city limits. Encouraged by these findings, researchers expanded their analysis to six additional megacities worldwide. Cairo, Kinshasa, São Paulo, Houston, Sydney, and London each represent vastly different climates and urban layouts. Testing across such varied conditions helped determine whether the cooling strategy held up beyond China’s borders. Across all eight cities studied, greening upwind of cities produced an average cooling effect of 0.4 degrees Celsius. That temperature drop applied across at least half of each city’s total area during peak summer heat. Exact results varied by location, but the underlying cooling pathway remained consistent everywhere researchers tested it. A city skyline rises beyond green suburban land, illustrating the wind pathway researchers studied when greening upwind of cities to reduce heat. Photo by Andy Lee on Pexels. Shanghai’s results illustrated the strategy’s limits alongside its potential. Cooling effects there were more modest and localized than in Beijing. Shanghai’s cooling sea breezes simply don’t align well with the areas where suburban trees could realistically be planted, reducing how effectively wind carries cooled air into the city. That finding carries an important caveat for city planners. Cao emphasized that this approach isn’t a blanket call for planting trees everywhere possible. Success depends on cities having consistent wind patterns and available space specifically positioned upwind of urban centers. Available space presents its own complication in many real-world settings. Suburban land upwind of major cities often already hosts housing developments, roads, and industrial facilities. Implementing this strategy would require creative, multi-functional land-use planning rather than simply clearing space for new forests. Local governments and other stakeholders would need to coordinate closely to make such changes possible. Getting buy-in across multiple jurisdictions and property owners adds real-world complexity that no climate model can capture. Political and logistical hurdles may prove just as challenging as the science itself. Beyond the specific temperature findings, Cao pointed to a broader lesson drawn from traditional village design. Cities benefit from thinking about vegetation, wind, topography, and water as one interconnected system rather than isolated green spaces scattered without coordination. That systems-level thinking represents a meaningful shift from how most urban cooling efforts currently operate. As global temperatures continue rising, cities will likely need every available tool to manage heat exposure for residents. Greening upwind of cities offers city planners a research-backed strategy that works with existing wind patterns rather than against them. The approach won’t work everywhere, but where geography cooperates, it could meaningfully ease the burden of urban heat without requiring dramatic changes to how city centers themselves are built. The post Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: There Are Ways to Reduce Campus Sexual Assaults. Will More Colleges Use Them?
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το The Understory. Όταν ήμουν φοιτήτρια στο Πανεπιστήμιο Cornell, διάβασα το βιβλίο «Fraternity Gang Rape» της Peggy Reeves Sanday για μια από τις τάξεις μου. Αυτό το βιβλίο γράφτηκε το 1990, που ήταν πολύ καιρό πριν. Αλλά και πάλι, ήταν; Σήμερα έβγαλα το βιβλίο από το ράφι μου. Ξεφυλλίζοντας το, παρατήρησα ένα νοσηρό patte…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by The Understory . W hen I was a student at Cornell University, I read the book “Fraternity Gang Rape” by Peggy Reeves Sanday for one of my classes. That book was written in 1990, which was a long time ago. But then again, was it? I took the book off my shelf today. Paging through it, I noticed a sickening pattern. Parts of it felt ripped from the allegations coming out of the Cornell investigation today: Long nights saturated in alcohol. Women who spend days tunneling through layers of self-blame and shame before concluding they’ve been raped. Prosecutors who do not pursue charges. One example: a 19-year-old woman at a small Midwestern college drank alcohol, had sex with her boyfriend, “fell asleep and the next thing she knew she awoke with a man she didn’t know on top of her.” The more things change, apparently, the less any goddamn thing changes. But wait. At moments of despair like this, I have learned to stop and ask myself: Is it actually true that nothing has changed? There has been some extraordinary reporting done about the Cornell case, including by The Cornell Daily Sun , the student-run newspaper that gave me my first reporting job many years ago. But as usually happens with terrifying news stories, it’s very hard to figure out how to assess the threat — and find proven solutions. How typical was this case? Is sexual assault happening more or less over time? In other words, what is the denominator for whatever fresh horror we are worried about? Most importantly, what actually works to make sexual assault more rare? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] To answer these questions, I’m going to uncomfortably set aside many other important questions — about accountability, humanity, legality, fairness and barbarity. Those are questions being interrogated in many other places. Here at The Understory, we’re trying to fill gaps that we see in traditional journalism. And one of those gaps is almost always context: How often are horrible things happening, and what can be done to make them more rare? These are the kinds of questions that we know humans need answered, in order to stay sane and take meaningful action in a time of relentless news battering us from near and far. So in that spirit, here is what I have learned so far: Rape reports have been declining in the U.S. since 2021. For 2025, the FBI estimates that 36 rape offenses were reported for every 100,000 people. The number of rapes that get reported to law enforcement each year has been gradually declining every year since 2021 , based on FBI data. This data comes with giant caveats, though. First, the number of actual sexual assaults is far higher than the number that get reported. (Only about 24 percent of sexual assaults were reported to authorities in 2024, according to the National Crime Victimization Survey .) Second, the FBI broadened its definition of rape in 2013, so it is hard to compare statistics going back any further than that. (The current definition includes “penetration, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with any body part or object, or oral penetration by a sex organ of another person, without the consent of the victim.”) In general, definitions of rape and sexual assault vary from place to place, making it harder than it should be to track changes over time and to find which cities, states or countries have unusually low (or high) rates. Sexual assault remains appallingly common on college campuses. In 2019, 13 percent of college students reported that they’d experienced some form of sexual assault since they’d arrived on campus. This category is broader than the FBI definition of rape; it includes nonconsensual penetration, attempted penetration, sexual touching by force or inability to consent. This data comes from the 181,752 students who responded to the 2019 Campus Climate Survey (conducted by the Association of American Universities). Importantly, the odds vary tremendously depending on who you are. The rate of sexual assault for women and transgender or nonbinary students was 20 percent — or four times the rate for men. Credit: Zhuoyao Song / Shutterstock The Cornell case is typical in some ways. In most campus sexual assaults, both the victim and the offender have consumed alcohol or drugs. Typically, rape victims are girls and very young women, and the vast majority of perpetrators are male. Victims usually know their perpetrators. At colleges, assaults primarily happen in residences or fraternity houses, according to the Campus Climate Survey (and Cornell’s own 2025 survey on sexual assault). And if a victim reports the offense, official responses are slow and unsatisfying, generally speaking. In all these ways, the Cornell case seems fairly typical. The Cornell case is atypical in other ways. Most sexual assault cases involve just one perpetrator, not multiple, making the Cornell allegations unusual. The other rarity is that the woman in this case reported the incident. And she has continued to push for a reckoning in a civil suit filed this year. To date, none of the accused men has been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing. Something can be done. And is being done. There is a lot of speculation happening right now about what leads to rape. Can we blame always-accessible, violent porn? Or campus hookup culture and frat-boy privilege? I have hunches about this, like everyone else. But I’m more interested in evidence of change. What actually works to reduce the number of rapes? And guess what? We now have some answers — answers we did not have when I was a student at Cornell. A 2014 study led by Laura Salazar at Georgia State University randomly assigned 743 college men to receive something called the RealConsent online training or a generic online health program. RealConsent featured six 30-minute modules about informed consent, intimate communication skills, the role of alcohol and male socialization in sexual violence, empathy for rape victims and bystander education. Six months later, the men who had received the special training reported intervening more often to stop a peer from engaging in sexually violent or inappropriate behavior. And, most importantly, they reported engaging in less sexual aggression themselves. “The odds for perpetrating among RealConsent participants were 73 percent lower than participants in the comparison condition,” according to the study. The attitudes of these men changed, too. They had greater empathy for rape victims, less hostility toward women and less comfort with other men’s inappropriate behaviors. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Another program, which has been studied even more extensively, first appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2015. The researchers, led by Charlene Senn at the University of Windsor, randomly assigned a group of first-year female students at three Canadian universities to receive a special training program for resisting sexual assault. The control group got general brochures on sexual assault instead. The training program, known as EAAA (for Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act) featured four three-hour sessions. Students were taught how to assess risk, overcome emotional barriers in acknowledging danger and engage in effective verbal and physical self-defense. In all, 451 women received the EAAA training, and 442 women got the brochures. One year later, the researchers checked in on the women. Get this: women in the training group were 46 percent less likely to report having been raped than women in the control group. They were also 63 percent less likely to report attempted rapes. A subsequent study found that the benefits continued, even two years later. “The program significantly reduced the risk of completed and attempted rape, attempted coercion, and nonconsensual sexual contact over the entire follow-up period,” the study concluded, “yielding reductions between 30 percent and 64 percent at 2 years.” Women who still became victims of sexual violence, despite the training, were less likely to blame themselves than women in the control group. The U.S. Air Force Academy has adopted the program for first-year female cadets. So have many colleges, including Stanford University. Interestingly, Cornell University has tried out this program, too. Cornell facilitators piloted the EAAA program in 2019 and 2020. Then the pandemic came along and on-campus training stopped . Which means it’s unlikely that the students involved in the 2024 case got this training. Last year, Cornell revived the EAAA program with sorority members, as well as a parallel program for fraternity members. You might wonder: Why isn’t every high school student getting proven training like this? There are many reasons, but one reason is that too few people know about these options. When rapes get covered in the media, the reporting almost never includes research like this. It can feel like this kind of violence is inevitable — or the fault of some inherent flaw in the perpetrators. But violence is never inevitable. We, as a society, tend to focus on holding perpetrators accountable after the fact. And this is important, but tragically late. It would be great if laws were clearer, data collection was consistent and police and prosecutors had excellent, trauma-informed training. But it would be infinitely better to prevent more rapes from happening at all. “Despair demands less of us, it’s more predictable, and in a sad way safer,” Rebecca Solnit wrote in Hope in the Dark. “Authentic hope requires clarity — seeing the troubles in this world — and imagination, seeing what might lie beyond these situations that are perhaps not inevitable and immutable.” The post There Are Ways to Reduce Campus Sexual Assaults. Will More Colleges Use Them? appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.titleOriginal: From 5 Rhinos in 1984 to a Free-Ranging Experiment: What Dudhwa Is Teaching India
items.description: Για δεκαετίες, η διατήρηση των ρινόκερων στο καταφύγιο Dudhwa Tiger στο Uttar Pradesh χτίστηκε γύρω από προστατευμένα περιβόλια. Η προσέγγιση βοήθησε έναν πληθυσμό να ανακάμψει μετά την εξαφάνιση του είδους από την περιοχή, αλλά το επόμενο ερώτημα είναι πιο δύσκολο: μπορούν αυτά τα ζώα να ζήσουν, να αναπαραχθούν και να επιβιώσουν ως ένας πραγματικά ελεύθερος πληθυσμός σε μια λειτουργική γη Terai…
items.descriptionOriginal: For decades, rhino conservation in Dudhwa Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh was built around protected enclosures. The approach helped a population recover after the species had disappeared from the region, but the next question is harder: can these animals live, breed and survive as a genuinely free-ranging population within a functioning Terai landscape? That question is now being tested. In March 2026, four greater one-horned rhinos were moved out of Dudhwa's fenced rehabilitation area into suitable grassland habitat in the reserve. The release took the number of mature rhinos free-ranging in Dudhwa to eight. The state's longer-term plan is to explore the feasibility of having 10 rhinos free-ranging as an initial phase of a wider conservation strategy. The latest census, conducted in June 2026, counted 53 rhinos in Dudhwa: 17 adult males, 25 adult females and 11 calves older than one year. Eight of them were among those released from the rehabilitation enclosures to improve genetic diversity and reduce inbreeding. But the significance of Dudhwa is not simply that there are more rhinos here than there were four decades ago. It is that the reserve is now becoming a test ground for a much larger question: what does it take to move from reintroduction to a resilient rhino population that can sustain itself across the wider Terai? From five rhinos to a larger experiment Dudhwa's rhino story began in 1984, when five rhinos were brought in as part of a reintroduction programme . The population has since grown, demonstrating that the Terai can once again support the species. But numbers alone can conceal the harder ecological questions. A population can grow while remaining vulnerable to genetic limitations, habitat pressures, disease, predation or a lack of connectivity with other populations. For a large herbivore such as the greater one-horned rhino, a viable future depends on much more than a protected patch of land. Amit Sharma, National Lead, Rhino Conservation at WWF India, sees the current phase in Dudhwa as a shift in that direction. "It is a great achievement for rhino conservation in Dudhwa as the rhinos have been allowed free range outside the enclosed area after almost four decades. Even though the initial plans are to release 10 rhinos, the objective should be more than releasing the 10 rhinos — it should be establishing an ecologically functional, demographically viable and genetically resilient free-ranging rhino population." The test now is whether the landscape can support the next generation, and the one after that, without conservation managers having to intervene constantly. What does a rhino need from a landscape? The Terai is a landscape of grasslands, wetlands, swamps, rivers and forests. Rhinos depend heavily on productive grasslands and water, while the mosaic of habitats allows them to feed, wallow and move through the landscape. Dudhwa already has much of this. "Dudhwa already has a successful reintroduction history and the basic ecological foundation : extensive terai grasslands, wetlands, swamps and riparian habitats are already in place," Sharma says. He points to a 2022 analysis which estimated that around 20% of Dudhwa was under grasslands and another 3% under wetlands, marshes and swamps, habitat classes that are critical for a flourishing rhino population. But having these habitats on a map is only the beginning. Instead of asking how Dudhwa can maintain one population, planners may eventually need to ask how Dudhwa, Valmiki, Nepal's Terai and other suitable habitats can function as parts of a larger rhino landscape. Photograph: (WWF India) "The natural water flows must be maintained, and perennial water sources must be secured to maintain the habitat standards. Further, the grassland extent and quality also must be managed to support a good herbivore population, especially for a mega-herbivore like the rhino." That makes habitat management one of the central lessons of Dudhwa. A rhino recovery programme cannot be separated from the health of the grassland itself. If grasslands degrade or natural water flows are disrupted, simply adding more rhinos will not solve the problem. And so the experiment in Dudhwa is also about learning how to manage a landscape before attempting to expand a population beyond it. The real test begins after release There is another difference between rhinos in an enclosure and rhinos that range freely. Once animals move through a larger landscape, conservation managers have to understand where they go, what they eat, how they reproduce, which calves survive and what causes mortality. Sharma says this requires long-term monitoring rather than periodic population counts alone. "For long-term viability of the population through active management, it will be necessary to undertake systematic monitoring for individual identification, reproductive success, calf survival, mortality, home-range use, forage availability and genetic diversity. Non-invasive DNA and technology-based approaches can strengthen population monitoring." In other words, Dudhwa's success will need to be measured in biological terms. Are females producing calves? Are those calves surviving? Are animals using suitable habitat? Is the population genetically healthy? Are rhinos able to expand their range? And can the population continue growing without continual human supplementation? These are the indicators that could determine whether Dudhwa's experience can inform future conservation in the Terai. The landscape does not end at Dudhwa The Terai does not follow state boundaries, and wildlife does not recognise them either. Dudhwa sits within a wider ecological system connected to other forests and protected areas in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal. Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar is another important rhino landscape, while rhinos also move across the India-Nepal border. A 2025 Wildlife Institute of India study on the Western Terai Arc Landscape highlighted how roads, development and other land-use changes can disrupt wildlife corridors, affecting the movement of large mammals and potentially isolating populations. Research and modelling under the project have specifically examined rhino and tiger habitat connectivity, and the areas where linear infrastructure could interfere with movement. For rhinos, that connectivity has consequences beyond movement. (1/3) Four greater one-horned rhinos have been released into the wild at Dudhwa Tiger Reserve, taking the free-ranging population to eight and strengthening conservation in India's Terai landscape. @moefcc @DudhwaTR @ManpowerGroupIn @experisitindia #WWFIndia https://t.co/vBt5uekU30 — WWF-India (@WWFINDIA) March 24, 2026 "A landscape-level approach is essential for the long-term recovery of rhinos in the Terai," Sharma says. "Rhinos do not recognise administrative boundaries, and the Katerniaghat–Bardia and Valmiki–Chitwan systems are ecologically interconnected." He points to a pattern already visible on the ground. "Studies have confirmed rhino movement across the India–Nepal border as a natural process to meet ecological requirements. Rhinos from Nepal are observed across the border on the Indian side at Pilibhit, Katerniaghat and Valmiki almost regularly." That changes the conservation question Instead of asking how Dudhwa can maintain one population, planners may eventually need to ask how Dudhwa, Valmiki, Nepal's Terai and other suitable habitats can function as parts of a larger rhino landscape. "It is thus essential to consider the entire area as one conservation unit and manage the rhino population as one single metapopulation or rather as a rhino landscape in the terai belt." But connectivity is not the only challenge. The same landscape that can support rhinos is also under pressure from infrastructure, human activity and climate-related changes. "The omnipresent risk to any rhino population is the threat of poaching arising out of the demand for the rhino horn and, to some extent, its body parts in the international market," Sharma says. But he points to another risk that may become harder to manage because it affects the habitat itself. "However, the predicted risk is the impact that a rapid change in the climate can exert in the region, which can lead to widespread effects in the fragile Himalayan system; the recent floods in Nepal during 2026 are indicative of the likely impacts." For rhinos, climate change is therefore not an abstract future threat. Changes in rainfall, flooding and water availability can alter the grasslands and wetlands on which the species depends. "The habitats in the terai are already under stress due to degradation and any deviation from the climatic pattern may result in drastic changes in the composition and condition of the habitats that may put the survival of the rhinos at risk." Then there is the human landscape around these habitats. "Again, due to multiple developments in the border areas and expansion of human activities, the connectivity with Nepal facilitating safe and active movement of rhinos and wildlife is under increasing threat. Any blockage in the natural connectivity will pose a huge challenge for rhino conservation in the entire Terai region." That means expanding rhino populations will require more than habitat protection. It will also require communities to be part of the conservation landscape. What happens when rhinos meet tigers? Dudhwa has another lesson to offer, and it is less comfortable. In March 2026, a 30-year-old female rhino named Rajeshwari was found dead in a water body in the reserve, with a tiger on her carcass. A post-mortem confirmed that she had died from injuries sustained in the attack. Reports said two sets of tiger pugmarks were found near the site. The incident raised an obvious question: if Dudhwa is trying to build a larger free-ranging rhino population, what happens when those rhinos share the landscape with a strong tiger population? Sharma says predation is part of the ecological reality, but adult rhino predation remains unusual. Dudhwa sits within a wider ecological system connected to other forests and protected areas in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal. Photograph: (Indian Express) "Tiger is an apex carnivore in the Indian forest, and it is quite natural for them to prey even on large animals like the rhino or the elephant." "In a park like Kaziranga, where tiger presence ten years back was not that dense, yet the rhinos falling prey to them was not uncommon. However, tigers preying on a healthy adult rhino are relatively rare, as it has been observed that they mostly attempt to attack the calves." For Dudhwa, however, the demographic consequences matter. "Rhino predation by tigers is not new to Dudhwa, and the death of the adult female rhino Rajeshwari in Dudhwa indicates that active predator–prey interactions are an integral component of managing a recovering rhino population within a tiger landscape with a high tiger population." But there is a limit to how much mortality a small or recovering population can absorb. "The rhino population in Dudhwa is limited and still aims for growth; as such, a high rate of predation will negatively impact the demography and population dynamics." Dudhwa's biggest lesson: release is only the beginning A rhino reintroduction cannot be treated as the finish line. "Dudhwa exemplifies a conservation story of return, resilience and the long road from reintroduction to rewilding," Sharma says. "The key lesson from Dudhwa is that reintroduction should be viewed as the beginning of population recovery; it teaches us to plan holistically to achieve a viable free-ranging population." A population of 50, 100 or 200 rhinos can remain vulnerable if it is isolated. For Sharma, resilience means several things happening at once. "The ability of the population to grow without continual human supplementation and connect naturally to be considered as a meta population including Nepal terai and communities to persist without perpetual intensive conflict will also be within the vision." That is why the 10 rhinos proposed for Dudhwa matter less as a number than as a beginning. The real test will come later, when rhinos are counted as members of a connected Terai population that can move, breed, survive, and coexist across a changing landscape.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News River Rights Movement in the UK Gains Ground as Communities Rally to Protect Local Waterways Reading Time: 3 minutes The river rights movement in the UK now connects around twenty grassroots groups working to give rivers legal standing. The river rights movement in the UK is growing steadily, uniting campaigners, co-ops, and community groups behind one shared goal. They want rivers to have real legal standing. Around twenty river groups now work together across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. The River Rights Network connects these local efforts under one umbrella. Instead of working in isolation, groups now share strategies, successes, and lessons learned. That collaboration has helped the river rights movement in the UK move faster than any single campaign could alone. Funding from an Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) Curiosity grant has helped the network expand. The grant supports four events, each hosted by a different member group, giving campaigners a direct chance to learn from each other. The first major event took place in Cambridge in September 2024. Friends of the River Cam hosted a workshop focused on rights. A second workshop followed in Sheffield in April 2025, hosted by OPUS Independents, exploring how rivers and their communities get a genuine say in decisions. Network members also joined the March for Clean Water in November 2024. Thousands turned out to call for healthier rivers nationwide. That visibility helps keep the river rights movement in the UK on the national agenda. Local campaigns make up the backbone of this effort. Groups like Love Our Ouse, Friends of the Medway, and Sacred Severn each focus on a specific waterway. Others, including Voices of Water and the Bioregional Learning Centre, bring creative approaches to river advocacy. Love Our Ouse offers one of the clearest examples of what the river rights movement in the UK can achieve. The group helped develop the first Charter of Rights for a UK river to gain formal council backing, with the River Ouse in Sussex officially recognized as a living entity by the Lewes District Council. That milestone shows local advocacy can lead to real institutional change. The river rights movement in the UK reached a milestone when Love Our Ouse helped secure Lewes District Council’s formal recognition of the River Ouse in Sussex as a living entity, making it the first UK river charter to gain official council backing and proving that local advocacy can drive real institutional change. Photo by Mike Bird on Pexels. The Ouse case also highlights why this work matters. Data from the river tracker Top of the Poops recorded sewage pollution there 63 times in 2023 alone, exposing the waterway to 442 hours of contamination across four monitoring sites. Supporters hope the charter will help hold polluters accountable. Josh Levene, who leads the network’s Rivers of Hope project, has spent over 25 years working with river communities worldwide. He directed Love Our Ouse before taking on this wider role. His experience now helps guide new communities through similar processes. Rivers of Hope is the network’s flagship initiative for scaling up this work nationally. The project runs workshops with communities, catchment partnerships, and local councils to help people reconnect with their local river and explore what a rights-based approach could look like. The project follows five clear steps. It raises awareness about what river rights mean in practice and showcases tools, such as river charters and nature guardian programs, that communities can adapt. It also works to reconnect people with rivers they may have grown distant from. From there, Rivers of Hope helps communities weigh their options. Every river faces different pressures, so no single solution fits all. Finally, the project strengthens the broader movement, since each new charter adds weight to the next community’s case. This model already has global precedent to draw from. Rivers in New Zealand, India, and Ecuador have received forms of legal personhood in recent years. Campaigners behind the river rights movement in the UK are adapting those ideas to fit British law and British rivers. The stakes remain significant nationwide. Many English rivers face pollution from sewage overflows, agricultural runoff, and aging infrastructure. Giving rivers a stronger legal voice could change how those long-standing problems finally get addressed. Nearly 20 rivers, from the Dart in Devon to the Tyne in the northeast, now have active local campaigns tied to the network. Some focus on legal recognition, while others prioritize education or council engagement. All share the belief that rivers deserve protection as living systems, not just resources. The success at the River Ouse has already inspired similar efforts elsewhere in England. New groups are welcome to join the river rights movement in the UK at any point. The network continues to grow as more communities decide their rivers are worth fighting for. What began as scattered local campaigns has become a coordinated national effort. Communities are learning from each other, sharing tools, and building a stronger case together. As more rivers gain formal recognition, the movement’s influence on UK water policy looks set to grow. items.title: Ήθελε τα παιδιά να καταλάβουν τον καρκίνο. Έτσι το μετέτρεψε σε παιχνίδι
items.titleOriginal: He Wanted Kids To Understand Cancer. So He turned It Into A Game
items.description: Όταν ο Daniel Zhang ήταν εννέα, είδε τη γιαγιά του να χάνει τα μαλλιά της λόγω χημειοθεραπείας και δεν μπορούσε να καταλάβει γιατί η ιατρική μπορούσε να μοιάζει τόσο πολύ με κακό. Αυτή η σύγχυση δεν τον εγκατέλειψε ποτέ, και όταν αργότερα ο παππούς του διαγνώστηκε με καρκίνο -- και ο Ζανγκ είδε την ίδια σύγχυση στο πρόσωπο της επτάχρονης αδερφής του -- έγινε ο σπόρος του…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Daniel Zhang was nine, he watched his grandmother lose her hair to chemotherapy and couldn't understand why medicine could look so much like harm. That confusion never left him, and when his grandfather was later diagnosed with cancer -- and Zhang saw the same bewilderment on his seven-year-old sister's face -- it became the seed of something purposeful. He and his classmate Zachary Tou, both 17, built *Tumor Tactics*, a Pok mon-inspired card game that teaches children cancer biology through the same mechanics they already love -- where, as Zhang explains, "chemotherapy can be a really powerful treatment, but you have to roll a die to determine how effective it is, and you might have to skip your next turn to recover from its side effects." What began as one boy trying to translate grief into language a child could hold has grown into a student-led nonprofit running workshops across San Diego schools, reaching kids from kindergarten through eighth grade. Perhaps most quietly remarkable is what happens at the end of each session: Zhang and Tou open the floor for discussion, and children -- unbidden -- begin sharing their own family stories, needing not just explanation, but the invitation to be heard.

items.descriptionOriginal: At 74, Ratnabali Ghosh wakes up at 5:30 AM to bring smiles to Kolkata’s streets, one Alpona at a time! Known for creating traditional Bengali Alpona designs outside doorsteps, she began with a simple idea: surprise people and brighten their day. What started as a small initiative has grown into a beautiful mission to preserve Bengal’s cultural heritage. From decorating dilapidated houses to bringing joy to elderly couples and slum residents, her art reminds us that beauty and kindness belong everywhere. Inspired by her grandmother and Rabindranath Tagore’s artistic legacy, Ratnabali hopes to revive a fading Bengali tradition and pass it on to future generations. Her story carries a powerful message: modernisation matters, but our cultural roots deserve to be cherished, too. Sometimes, preserving a tradition begins with one person, a little creativity and the desire to make someone smile. Do you think traditional Indian art deserves more space in our modern cities? items.descriptionOriginal: Growing vegetables and herbs on a balcony can be rewarding, but a healthy-looking plant does not always translate into a good harvest. Despite regular watering and adequate sunlight , tomatoes may yield fewer fruits than expected, herbs may struggle to grow, and vegetables may lack the flavour gardeners hoped for. The problem could lie in the conditions specific to the balcony. Dr Mayur Mandrah, an ex-Army major who shares gardening advice on Instagram as @plantwithmayur , has highlighted three common mistakes that can affect the growth of edible plants in containers. His advice focuses on understanding what plants need below the soil as well as the conditions in which they grow. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dr Mayur Mandrah, Ex Army Major (@plantwithmayur) 1. Choose the right soil for your pots Garden soil and potting mix serve different purposes. According to Mayur, using ordinary garden soil in containers can cause problems because it tends to compact over time. This reduces the air available to the roots, making it harder for plants to absorb the nutrients they need to grow. He recommends using a good-quality potting mix with adequate drainage instead. A suitable mix helps maintain airflow around the roots while allowing excess water to drain away. For balcony gardeners, choosing the right growing medium is an important first step towards healthier plants and a better harvest. 2. Give your plants enough room to grow The size of a pot matters beyond how well it fits into a balcony garden. A plant may appear healthy above the soil while its roots struggle for space in a shallow container. The gardener recommends providing tomatoes with at least 12 inches of soil depth and peppers with at least 10 inches. Even herbs such as basil can benefit from having sufficient room for their roots to develop. Before planting, check whether the container is deep enough for the crop you intend to grow. A pot that looks attractive may not necessarily offer the space the plant needs to survive. 3. Pay attention to your balcony's microclimate Balconies can expose plants to conditions that are different from those in a garden bed. Wind can dry out potting mix more quickly, while walls and floors absorb heat during the day and release it later. These changing conditions can place plants under stress and affect their growth and flavour. Mayur advises gardeners to spend time observing their balconies at different points throughout the day. Notice which areas receive direct sunlight, where the wind is strongest, and which spots become particularly hot. Based on these observations, move pots to locations that better suit their needs. A little attention to the conditions around the plants can help gardeners make better decisions about where to place them. Growing vegetables and herbs on a balcony can be rewarding, but a healthy-looking plant does not always translate into a good harvest. Photograph: (Ruff Day Vet + Pet Gym) Start with these three changes A productive balcony garden depends on more than regular watering and sunlight. The soil must support healthy roots, containers must provide enough depth, and plants need to be placed where they can cope with the surrounding conditions. By addressing these three factors, balcony gardeners can give their edible plants a better chance of growing well and producing a more satisfying harvest.
