items.titleOriginal: The Tourism Industry Is Slowly Waking Up to Solo Travelers’ Needs
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Peter McGraw, καθηγητή μάρκετινγκ και ψυχολογίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Colorado Boulder, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Τα σόλο ταξίδια αυξάνονται — και μια βιομηχανία…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Peter McGraw , a professor of marketing and psychology at the University of Colorado Boulder, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Solo travel is surging — and an industry still largely built for two is taking note. Google reported in April 2026 that online searches involving “solo travel” hit an all-time high this year, with queries for “women solo travel” reaching a 15-year peak. Hilton’s 2026 trends report found that 26% of travelers planned to take a trip alone this year, and that nearly half said they planned to add solo days to the front or back of a family trip. The issue isn’t new. In 1992, marketing researchers identified the solo consumer as an underserved market . But as tourism researchers have documented , the accommodation sector treats double occupancy as the default unit of consumption, which often slaps a “single supplement” charge on customers when they travel without a partner. The industry essentially penalizes travelers for arriving without a second body to fill the other half of a room they aren’t using. The reason why so many hotels, cruise lines, and tour operators still base prices on double occupancy is that their costs — the room, the berth, the coach seat, the guide — don’t fall by half when the second person fails to materialize. But the supplement isn’t just a pricing convention. It’s the clearest signal the industry sends about who it built the product for. I’m a scholar who studies what I call the solo economy : how institutions and markets adapt, or fail to adapt, to the rise of single living. I’ve written before about how retail and restaurants still design for pairs. Travel is further along than most in recognizing this cultural shift. It’s also a useful case because the industry has started on the easy part of the problem but barely touched the rest. Demographics Matter, but Not the Way You’d Think The broader shift toward solo living is real. In 2025, 39.7 million Americans lived alone . That’s 29% of all households, up from 20% in 1975. Married couples, meanwhile, fell to 47% of households from 66% 50 years earlier. Those numbers alone don’t explain solo travel. Some of that decline went to people living alone; some went to unmarried couples, who are still a party of two on a booking page. Married people take trips alone. Single people travel with friends, siblings and parents, and plenty of them have logged serious hours as an extra wheel. Living alone and vacationing alone are different behaviors with different causes. What connects them is the erosion of a single assumption: that every adult arrives with a plus-one. That assumption is weakening at home, and it’s now encountering the booking page. Price Is the Easy Rung One response by the travel industry has been to shave the single supplement. For example, the tour operator Tauck announced this year that it’s waiving the single supplement on a class of its riverboat cabins across more than 250 European river cruise departures and reducing it by up to US$600 on 105 land departures. Another touring company has taken a more committed approach to adjusting its offerings: Aurora Expeditions sets aside 10 dedicated solo cabins on every sailing across its three ships, with no single supplement, through its 2026 and 2027 seasons. Then there’s Norwegian Cruise Line, which was early to the shift. In 2010, it introduced Studio staterooms aboard Norwegian Epic: small cabins designed for one passenger, sold at single-occupancy prices and arranged around a keycard-access Studio Lounge reserved for solo travelers. The trade-off is less private space, but at a price for one, with access to a room full of fellow travelers going it alone. Norwegian then expanded solo categories in 2024 from nine ships to its full 19-ship fleet. But on ships without Studios, much of the expansion was relabeling. Cruise Critic reported that standard double-occupancy rooms would likely be reclassified rather than retrofitted. And by Norwegian’s own account , the Studio Lounge is reserved for guests in Solo Studios — so the fleetwide solo categories come with the discount but not the room full of other solo travelers. That’s the difference between repricing and redesigning. The 2010 Studio was a purpose-built 100-square-foot (9 square-meter) cabin that cost Norwegian something to construct. The 2024 categories are, in many cases, the same rooms as before, with a new label and a discount. The solo traveler pays less than two people would, but it’s still more than half for a room sized and built for two. A cabin sold to one occupies the same space as a cabin sold to two, and the industry still counts berths. There’s a cleaner approach. Yotel sells a room type it calls Solo — 114 square feet (about 10 square meters) in New York City, maximum occupancy one, at the bottom of its price range. Nothing was subtracted to make it. It was built at that size, for that guest, and priced accordingly. That’s what designing for one looks like, and it’s rare enough that a tiny room counts as progress. alvarez—E+/Getty Images Many solo travelers seek control over their experiences and schedules, but they still seek a social component. Traveling Alone Doesn’t Mean Being Alone A common mistake in designing for solo travelers is assuming that solitude is the product. It isn’t. In the same 2026 data showing record interest in solo travel, Google found that searches for “travel groups” and “tour groups” also hit record highs . A Mastercard survey of more than 15,000 consumers across 11 countries found that 39% of international travelers had already taken a trip alone — and 7 in 10 international leisure travelers were interested in solo experiences built to connect them with like-minded people. The contradiction makes sense when you acknowledge that privacy and isolation are two different things. A person can want total control over where to go, when to eat, and when to return to the room — and still want company at dinner. The issue with double-occupancy pricing is that it assumes the customer brings their own company. But when only one person books, the operator has to address the pricing problem — whether or how to discount; and a product problem — how to supply a social component. Waiving a solo supplement solves the first issue, but it ignores the second. Norwegian understood this in 2010 by creating its lounge for solo travelers. The Pitch Is Easier When the Product Is for One For all these changes, travel advertising often still runs on couples: two glasses of wine, two lounge chairs, two silhouettes against a sunset. Sandals Resorts built an entire resort category around the premise. When solo travel does appear, it gets a different script. The traveler is adventurous, on a journey of self-discovery. AARP’s current solo-travel guide emphasizes personal growth and self-reliance. Even Norwegian closes its solo pitch by reassuring the reader that “you’re pretty good company.” The effect is to mark solo travel as exceptional at precisely the moment it stops being exceptional. Nobody reassures a couple that they will enjoy the balcony. Calling a solo traveler “brave” can be a compliment, but it can also reveal the assumption that traveling alone is abnormal, even when that’s changing. That all said, parts of the tourism industry have taken big steps over the past 15 years. But treating solo travelers as an audience rather than an accommodation is harder. It’s about selling them what they have already said they want: control over the trip, and access to other people, on their own terms. Marketing researchers named this opportunity in 1992. Thirty-four years later, the industry is still learning to build for one. Meanwhile, the solo traveler is standing at reception, holding a credit card, waiting for someone to design a room. Η Respyre, μια ολλανδική startup, εργάζεται από την αντίθετη αρχή. Η εταιρεία έχει αναπτύξει το Mosscrete, μια βιοδεκτική επίστρωση σκυροδέματος που δημιουργεί τις συνθήκες για να αναπτυχθούν βρύα απευθείας σε κάθετα…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. A 300-square-meter (about 3,230-square-foot) noise barrier in Hoofddorp, the Netherlands, is being used to test passive greening: moss growing from natural moisture alone, no watering involved. The porous structure of moss may also help absorb sound, which makes the noise barrier a natural fit for the technology. A 260-square-meter (about 2,800-square-foot) social housing facade in Purmerend was one of the first practical applications. Traditional greening options were rejected there as too expensive and maintenance-heavy, and the project helped Respyre work out how bioreceptive facades are best designed and applied. In Haarlem, a 313-square-meter (about 3,370-square-foot) commercial renovation combined Mosscrete with insulation, aiming to both green the facade and improve thermal performance. Research published in June 2026 in the journal Science of the Total Environment found the effect is moisture-dependent: wet moss creates a cooling effect through evaporation, while dry moss can overheat in direct sunlight. In Amsterdam, the technology is being tested on bridge piers where graffiti has been a persistent problem. Moss-covered surfaces are less appealing as targets, and since the site has no irrigation, the project is also tracking how moss develops under ordinary conditions of rain, shade, and humidity. Designing for change Respyre is betting on a different idea of what building materials should do. Most are made to resist change, to stay gray and sealed for decades. Mosscrete is made for the opposite: it works best when moss gradually takes over. Urban greening helps manage stormwater and heat in dense cities, and there’s evidence it supports local biodiversity too. But a building slowly covered in moss doesn’t look like neglect. It looks like something is alive there. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Pumpkin spice lattes, jack-o’-lanterns, and Thanksgiving pies : pumpkins are the unofficial mascots of fall. But behind their seasonal charm lies a deeper, more complicated story that winds through language, history, agriculture, and even a little insult comedy. “ Pumpkins are more popular than ever,” says Cindy Ott , associate professor of history at the University of Delaware and author of Pumpkin: The Curious History of an American Icon. But our obsession with this humble gourd, she notes, is tied less to flavor and more to a nostalgic longing for simpler, rural times. “People are buying these things, even pumpkin spice lattes, because of these attachments, these very old-fashioned ideas about reverence of the small family farm.” A name with roots that twist like a vine The word “pumpkin” has always been more conceptual than botanical. According to Logan Kistler , curator of archaeobotany at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, the term refers to squash varieties bred to resemble the round, orange gourds we associate with fall. “Pumpkin isn’t exactly a botanical group,” he explains. Linguistically, the word has had quite a journey. Fiona McPherson of the Oxford English Dictionary traces it from the Greek pepon to the French pompon , which eventually morphed into the English “ pompion ” in the 1500s. “Pumpkin,” as we know it today, first appeared in print in 1647, ironically in reference to the meager diet of early settlers. But while the word took a European path, the plant itself is deeply American. Indigenous peoples across North, Central, and South America cultivated early pumpkin ancestors, domesticating different types of Cucurbita as far back as 10,000 years ago in Mexico. “Pumpkins are part of this genus Cucurbita,” says Kistler, noting that they were farmed widely throughout the Americas long before colonists arrived. From insult to endearment Surprisingly, it didn’t take long for the word “pumpkin” to go from dietary staple to verbal jab. By the late 1600s, it was being used as an insult. “It really did not take long for it to develop this figurative use,” says McPherson. Pumpkin became a shorthand for someone who was conceited, dim-witted, or full of hot air. Cindy Ott adds that gender played a role in the insult’s direction. For women, pumpkin imagery was linked to the body and “natural urges,” seen as a lack of refinement. For men, it implied an empty head. “It’s been used for politicians for hundreds of years,” she notes. A symbol of imagined agrarian purity By the late 19th century, the pumpkin was undergoing a cultural rehabilitation. It shifted from insult to affection, and from staple crop to nostalgic icon. “So Americans move out of the country, into the city, but they like to imagine themselves farmers at heart, many of them,” Ott explains. As industrialization transformed the U.S., the pumpkin came to symbolize the pastoral life being left behind. In poetry, paintings, and festivals, it became a stand-in for tradition and a romanticized vision of national roots. Today, that symbolism is being put to work, literally. Pumpkins are once again supporting small farmers, not as dietary staples but as attractions. Ott calls them “agrarian wonderlands,” where farms market autumnal experiences that hinge on the iconic gourd. “The cool thing about the whole story,” Ott says, “is that these very romantic ideas and myths that a lot of Americans tell themselves about their origin stories are actually helping to rejuvenate the very thing it represents: a small family farm.” Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs Reading Time: 3 minutes How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs Commercial buildings waste about 30% of their energy, and that’s just an average, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. In practice, that means part of your utility bill is probably paying to heat empty rooms, cool unoccupied offices, light parking lots after everyone has gone home, or keep equipment running on an outdated schedule. While that’s a remarkably high number for energy waste, it’s surprisingly easy to lower it significantly. Often, you can start with low-cost fixes before investing in more sustainable and energy-efficient upgrades. All that is really needed is a fresh, honest look at how the building actually operates. Find Out Where Most of the Waste Goes Before replacing any equipment, look at your data: where does the building actually use energy? Review your utility bills, demand charges, operating schedules, and, where available, interval data from smart meters. Look specifically at peak demand times; staggered startup schedules can significantly reduce demand charges. Also compare energy use against occupancy and production schedules. If consumption barely changes between a busy Monday and an empty Sunday, something deserves investigation. An energy audit or retro-commissioning study can take this further. In plain terms, you are checking whether the building still operates the way its designers intended. Get Serious About Building Controls According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), high-performance control strategies can reduce annual HVAC energy use by 30% across a range of commercial building types. Of course, this doesn’t mean every building will cut its HVAC bill by that exact amount, but it shows why controls deserve more attention than they usually get. Look at temperature setbacks, occupancy schedules, ventilation rates, economizer operation, and simultaneous heating and cooling. A building automation system is only as useful as its programming. If the system has sophisticated controls but nobody checks whether they still match actual occupancy, you have an expensive computer making the wrong decisions. Upgrade Lighting and Control It LED retrofits remain one of the more straightforward commercial efficiency projects, particularly in buildings with old fluorescent or high-intensity fixtures. But swapping fixtures and calling the job finished misses half the opportunity. Add occupancy sensors where spaces sit empty for long periods. Use daylight controls near windows and skylights. Put exterior and parking-lot lighting on appropriate schedules rather than relying on someone to remember to flip a switch. This is also where electrical expertise matters. Whether you operate a warehouse in Texas, an office in Colorado, or need an Albuquerque electrical contractor for a New Mexico facility, look for a provider that can handle both the electrical work and efficiency side of the project. Look Beyond the Big Systems Some of the easiest savings are hidden in ordinary equipment. Plug loads can become a significant energy drain in efficient buildings, particularly where computers, kitchen equipment, vending machines, and other devices remain powered outside working hours. Smart power strips, automatic shutdown schedules, and better equipment procurement can help. This is a good reason to use submeters in larger facilities. Instead of seeing one enormous monthly electricity number, you can separate major loads and identify what changed. Use Maintenance as an Energy Strategy A dirty filter, poorly calibrated sensor, worn weatherstripping, or failing motor doesn’t just create a maintenance problem. It can make equipment work harder and longer. Build energy checks into preventive maintenance rather than waiting for an obvious failure. Inspect: HVAC controls and sensor calibration, Lighting and setback schedules, Equipment operating outside occupied hours, Door seals and building envelope air leaks, Unusual shifts or spikes in consumption. DOE research has found that properly tuned controls alone can produce substantial savings, partly because controls in existing buildings often drift away from their intended settings over time. Not every green upgrade deserves a blank check. Rank projects by expected energy savings, installation cost, maintenance savings, useful life, demand reduction, and available utility incentives. The post How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Kolkata's 74-year-old Ratnabali Ghosh aka "Alpona Didi" wakes at 5:30 AM everyday to draw alpona outside strangers' doors, just to make them smile. every day to draw traditional Bengali alpona outside strangers' doorsteps, just to make them smile. Inspired by her mother, Ratnabali believes art is about making people feel welcome, valued and less alone. Even as age and arthritis make her work harder, she refuses to give up. This Durga Puja, discover how Alpona Didi is keeping Bengal's fading folk art alive, one doorstep at a time. From residential buildings to shopfronts and restaurant entrances, her traditional alpona designs greet people as they step out in the morning. Her story is a reminder that traditions survive when someone chooses to carry them forward and that kindness matters, even when nobody is watching. Know someone who'd love this story? items.descriptionOriginal: "Archana ma'am!" The voice comes from one corner of the classroom. "Ma'am, I have a question." Another hand goes up. Archana Jaisal turns, listens and answers. Then comes another doubt, and another. In a rural Uttar Pradesh classroom, these may seem like ordinary questions. But to Archana, every child who feels comfortable enough to ask one represents something bigger: the opportunity to learn close to home. It is the kind of classroom she wished more village children could have. She knows what it means when education depends on circumstances : whether a family can afford coaching, whether a good teacher is nearby, or whether someone offers the right opportunity at the right time. "I realised that the children were studying, but their studies were not really helping them," she recalls of what she saw in villages. Inspired by her late father, Jagdish Ram, who studied while pulling a rickshaw, Archana grew up seeing how education can change a family's future. That realisation eventually led her to start Shiksha Saathi, a rural education and livelihood startup that now runs over 78 learning centres across six districts of Uttar Pradesh, reaching more than 7,650 students with 67 teachers. But the story began long before the first centre opened. It began with her late father, Jagdish Ram. From rickshaw puller to railway employee Archana grew up in Ghazipur, where her father's own childhood had been shaped by hardship. Her grandfather died when her father was young, leaving the family struggling to survive. There was also pressure to get his sisters married. With little money coming in, her father had to make a difficult choice. At 17, he began pulling a rickshaw. Yet he continued his education alongside the work. "In the beginning, he thought he would have to leave his studies and drive a rickshaw," Archana says. "But gradually, he continued studying while working." He eventually completed his graduation. His routine revolved around driving the rickshaw while finding time to study. One day, he struck up a casual conversation with a fellow rickshaw puller who had noticed him studying diligently over the past few months. The man asked him, "Why don't you apply for a railway job?" Jagdish took the suggestion seriously. "He didn't know what to do next, but he applied for a railway job. He got the job and moved to Varanasi," Archana recalls. That one opportunity changed the family's circumstances. In Varanasi, he also found different ways to support the family while waiting for his career to settle. He painted boards and banners, made portraits and even wrote names and numbers on T-shirts. "He used to make portraits and earn some more income. That is how my father survived in the city," Archana says. Through Shiksha Saathi, Archana works to address learning gaps among children who attend school but often struggle to understand their lessons. But perhaps the biggest thing he brought back from that struggle was a belief that his children should have a different life. "My father did not want his children to grow up in the same circumstances he had," she says. A couple of months later, he brought his children to the city. They studied, built new lives for themselves, and for a while, it seemed the family had finally moved beyond those difficult years. When another challenge hit the family Archana was still young when her father passed away. His death left the family without the person who had worked so hard to give his children a more secure future. Her mother was supposed to take up his railway job, but she was not in a position to do so. With little support and no stable income, the family of five sisters and a brother found themselves facing financial difficulties once again. They continued living in the railway quarters, but meeting everyday expenses was becoming difficult. And with money running short, continuing their education — something their father had worked so hard to make possible — was now uncertain. The siblings had to find ways to support one another. It was during this difficult period that Archana's elder sister stepped in. "After a few months, my elder sister began earning and helped pay for groceries and tuition," she adds. "That gave us a means to continue studying and sometimes practising teaching along the way." For Archana, that support meant she could pursue her education despite the difficulties at home. She eventually went on to complete her graduation and post-graduation in Economics from Banaras Hindu University. Shiksha Saathi trains rural girls and women to become educators, creating opportunities for them to earn while supporting children in their communities. She had once hoped to become a professor, but without the right guidance and resources, that dream remained out of reach. Her own experiences had shown her how much education could change a family's circumstances, and how difficult it could be to pursue one's ambitions without the right support. Years later, she began noticing another problem , this time among children in her own extended family in rural Uttar Pradesh. They were attending school, but when Archana began asking them about their lessons, she found something troubling. 'Children struggled to recall their own lessons' Some of the children were already in Class 7, yet struggled to answer questions about what they had learnt in school. "That's when I realised that the quality of their education was not up to the mark," she says. As she looked more closely at the challenges children faced, she noticed another problem in the same villages. Girls in villages often had few opportunities to earn, even after studying. Coaching centres were limited, and travelling to cities was not an option for many families. "I realised that the girls were also struggling to find ways to earn because there was no tuition or coaching in the villages," Archana says. "So, we thought we should do something for them." In 2022, she started what was initially called Your Coaching. The organisation was formally registered as Shiksha Saathi in 2023. The idea was simple: if children could not travel to cities for better academic support, why not bring that support into their villages? 'Teachers, too, need training' Shiksha Saathi began offering affordable after-school coaching for children from Classes 1 to 12. The fees are kept low, starting at around Rs 100 for younger children and going up to Rs 600 for Class 12 students. Children who cannot afford the fees can still study with the others. But as the centres grew, Archana encountered another problem. By keeping coaching affordable and welcoming children who cannot pay, Shiksha Saathi aims to make academic support accessible to more rural families. A classroom could have a teacher and students, but that did not automatically mean good teaching was happening. At one centre, the team received a complaint about a teacher who was teaching English. When they tested him, they found that his own fundamentals were weak. For Archana, it was an important lesson. "We realised that simply teaching wasn't enough. We needed to train the teachers too," she says. That became the foundation of Shiksha Saathi's Educator Training Programme. Every six months, new batches of rural girls and women are trained to teach children according to their age and learning levels. More than 740 rural girls and women have now gone through the programme. The model began addressing two gaps at once: children received local academic support, while women got a chance to earn within their communities. For young women like Neetu, that opportunity also meant being able to continue their own education. 'I now pay for my own studies' At 19, Neetu became a teacher with Shiksha Saathi, a role she had never planned for. "I did it for myself and for the children in the village," she says. Coming from a Hindi-medium school, she was nervous at first. Shiksha Saathi provided classroom resources and six to seven months of training, gradually helping her gain confidence. Today, Neetu earns around Rs 6,000–7,000 a month, enough to pay for her own education and coaching. For Archana, every child who feels comfortable asking a question represents a chance to make learning more accessible. "I started paying for my own studies and coaching, so I no longer needed to take money from home," she says. For Neetu, the income means independence. She now hopes other girls can find the same confidence. "I want all girls to stand on their own feet and do something for themselves and help the younger children around them," she says. Her experience reflects why Archana wants more rural girls to become educators. "We give priority to girls because they should have the opportunity to learn, work and become financially independent," she says. And while women like Neetu are finding new opportunities through teaching, children in these centres are beginning to experience learning differently. From fearing Maths to enjoying it Among the children attending the centres is 10-year-old Riya, who has studied at Shiksha Saathi for three years. Maths, once her most difficult subject, is now her favourite. "When I used to study Maths before, I used to feel scared. Now, things have changed," she says. She credits her teachers, who take the time to explain concepts and let her ask about things she does not understand at school. Her parents, too, encourage her to keep studying. With support from her teachers at Shiksha Saathi, 10-year-old Riya has grown more confident in Maths, once her most difficult subject. And when asked what she wants to become, Riya has a clear answer: a teacher. For Archana, moments like these are why the work matters. She wants rural education to go beyond marks and school completion, helping children build the confidence to imagine possibilities beyond what they see around them. But making such opportunities available within villages also meant earning the trust of the communities themselves. 'The villagers support us now' In the beginning, getting communities to accept the centres was not always easy. People questioned girls travelling out, whether education was worth the cost, and whether women could work outside the home. But attitudes have slowly begun to change. In one village, that growing support came from a businessman living in Mumbai. After hearing about Shiksha Saathi's work, he offered his house as a space for children to attend classes and arranged water and other basic facilities for them. "The villagers support us a lot now," Archana says. "They tell us that their children are doing well." For Archana, such support matters because it shows that education is gradually becoming a community concern rather than an individual family's responsibility. Today, Shiksha Saathi has expanded across Bhadohi, Varanasi, Mirzapur, Prayagraj, Mau and Ghazipur. Giving more kids the chance to learn Shiksha Saathi now works across six districts, but Archana's vision goes beyond opening more coaching centres. Its youth competitions have reached over 9,000 children, while its 2025 initiative, Yuva Pratibha Parishad, encourages students to think about their ambitions, Plan A and Plan B, and how they want to contribute to society. "In villages, students have the talent, but they don't always have the opportunity," Archana says. "We want to give them the opportunities they are looking for." Community support has helped Shiksha Saathi expand its learning centres across six districts of Uttar Pradesh, bringing classes closer to children's homes. She hopes to reach more districts across Uttar Pradesh and make quality education affordable for families, a goal closely connected to her father's experience. Her father once pulled a rickshaw to support his family while continuing his studies. A stranger's advice eventually helped him secure a railway job, move to the city and give his children a different future. Archana hopes to help other children find opportunities that can shape their futures, just as education shaped her family's. And when children call out, "Archana ma'am!", she listens to their questions. For her, each question carries something her father worked hard to secure for his own children: the chance to learn. And she wants more children to have it. All images courtesy of Archana Jaisal

items.descriptionOriginal: You are driving home at night when a car approaches from the opposite direction. Its headlights are so bright that, for a few seconds, all you can see is a wall of white light. You cannot make out the divider, the edge of the road, or the cyclist who might be riding just ahead. You slow down, wait for the car to pass, and hope there is nothing in your path. Or perhaps you have been stuck in traffic when a vehicle suddenly appears behind you, flashing red and blue lights and honking as though everyone must move aside. If either of these situations sounds familiar, you know how frightening those few seconds can be. In August 2025, a Bengaluru commuter raised concerns on social media about an SUV fitted with flashing red and blue LED lights. The post caught the attention of the police. According to Bangalore Mirror, Jigani Police traced the vehicle and its occupant, removed the illegal lights and initiated legal action. The vehicle owner was also penalised. It was one example of a problem familiar to motorists across India. But what many drivers may not know is that there are already laws governing the lights vehicles can use. And in October 2025, the Supreme Court issued fresh directions to ensure those rules are taken seriously. The case behind that order began with a doctor's concern about the lives being lost on India's roads. Why a doctor took India's road safety problem to court Dr S. Rajaseekaran, an orthopaedic surgeon, had spent years seeing the consequences of road crashes. Injuries, lives lost, and families left dealing with the aftermath of accidents made him deeply concerned about road safety in India. In 2012, he approached the Supreme Court with a petition titled S. Rajaseekaran versus Union of India. His concern went far beyond headlights. He wanted the agencies responsible for safer roads, driver licensing, enforcement, emergency treatment and compensation to work together instead of functioning separately. For him, road accidents had become a national emergency that demanded coordinated action. The petition continued through years of hearings. Then, on 7 October 2025, a bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan issued a series of directions addressing everyday dangers on Indian roads. These included unsafe pedestrian crossings, motorists riding without helmets, wrong-lane driving and dangerous overtaking. And among the problems the court addressed was something millions of drivers encounter after sunset: blinding headlights. Orthopaedic surgeon Dr S. Rajaseekaran approached the Supreme Court in 2012, seeking stronger coordination and accountability to make India's roads safer. Photograph: ( The Hindu ) What the Supreme Court said about blinding headlights Think about what happens when an unusually bright headlight shines directly into your eyes. Even if you are looking straight at the road, the glare can make it difficult to judge what is ahead. For a pedestrian, it may become harder to see an approaching vehicle or navigate the road safely. The Supreme Court recognised this danger. In its 7 October 2025 order , the court noted that high-intensity headlights, including those fitted on two-wheelers, can temporarily disorient oncoming drivers and pedestrians. It directed the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, state transport departments and traffic police to establish and enforce permissible limits for headlight brightness and beam angles. In simpler terms, authorities must ensure that headlights are bright enough to help drivers see the road, without directing excessive light into someone else's eyes. The court also called for these checks to be included in Pollution Under Control (PUC) testing and vehicle fitness certification, alongside targeted enforcement drives against non-compliant or modified headlights. But headlights were only part of the concern. The bench also directed strict enforcement of the ban on unauthorised red-blue flashing lights and illegal siren-like hooters. This includes action against vehicles using such equipment, as well as enforcement against its unauthorised sale. The court directed nationwide awareness campaigns so that motorists understand why these lights are dangerous. But why did the Supreme Court need to intervene when rules about vehicle lighting already existed? India already had headlight rules. So why is this still happening? The rules may sound complicated, but the idea behind them is fairly simple. Every vehicle needs lights that help its driver see clearly without putting other people in danger. Under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, Rule 105 deals with vehicle lamps, while Rule 106 requires headlight beams to meet prescribed safety standards. Section 52 of the Motor Vehicles Act also places restrictions on alterations that change a vehicle from the specifications approved by its manufacturer. Then there are the coloured lights that some vehicles use to demand attention on the road. Rule 108 restricts the use of multicoloured red, blue and white warning lights to vehicles specifically designated for emergency and disaster-management duties. Even authorised emergency vehicles cannot use their flashing lights and sirens whenever they wish. Under the Motor Vehicles (Driving) Regulations, 2017, these warning devices are meant to be used when responding to an emergency call or alarm. So a private vehicle cannot simply install flashing emergency-style lights and expect other drivers to clear the road. And a driver cannot assume that any brighter bulb will be suitable for their vehicle. To understand why, it helps to look at how headlights actually work. How replacing one bulb can make the road dangerous for someone else Imagine buying a powerful LED bulb to replace the original halogen bulb in your car. The idea seems reasonable. You want to see more clearly when driving at night. But headlights are designed to work as a complete system. The bulb, reflector or projector, and the angle at which the light falls are all important. A headlight housing designed for a particular halogen bulb may not direct light properly when a different type of LED or HID bulb is fitted inside it. Instead of concentrating light on the road, an unsuitable replacement can send some of it upwards, towards the eyes of approaching motorists. Even a properly designed headlight can cause glare if it is aimed incorrectly. Research by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) has found that effective headlights need to balance visibility for the driver with glare control for oncoming traffic. That is why brighter does not automatically mean safer. And it is also why the law does not treat every LED headlight as illegal. A factory-fitted LED system that complies with the applicable standards is permitted. An aftermarket replacement is not automatically an offence either, but it must meet the relevant safety requirements and vehicle alteration rules. The important question is whether the lighting system is compliant and safe for everyone sharing the road. In October 2025, the Supreme Court directed authorities to regulate headlight brightness and beam angles to reduce glare on Indian roads. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) Can you be fined for bright headlights or flashing lights? For drivers, this is where the Supreme Court's directions become particularly relevant. Authorities have been asked to conduct targeted checks and take action against headlights that do not comply with the prescribed standards. But that does not mean every bright-looking headlight automatically attracts the same fine. Under Section 177 of the Motor Vehicles Act, when a violation has no separately prescribed penalty, the fine can extend to Rs 500 for a first offence and Rs 1,500 for a subsequent offence. Other violations may attract different penalties depending on the applicable legal provision. Unauthorised emergency-style flashing lights and illegal hooters can also invite enforcement action, including seizures and penalties. The court scheduled the case for a compliance review seven months after its October 2025 order. That was a date for reviewing progress, rather than a blanket seven-month deadline for states to introduce new headlight rules. Whether these directions make a difference on the road depends on how effectively authorities implement them. For vehicle owners, however, there is already a useful takeaway. Before changing your headlights, check that the replacement is compatible with your vehicle and meets the applicable standards. If the light seems unusually high or scattered, have its alignment checked. And if you encounter a private vehicle using unauthorised red-blue flashing lights or illegal hooters, the law provides grounds for enforcement action. Unauthorised red-blue flashing lights and siren-mimicking hooters are banned, with the court directing authorities to crack down on their use. Photograph: ( TNIE ) A few seconds of glare should never put someone's life at risk India recorded 1,72,890 road crash deaths in 2023, according to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. That included 35,221 pedestrians, people who were simply trying to walk or cross a road. There are many reasons why road accidents happen, and the available national data does not establish how many of these deaths were caused by headlight glare. But preventing unnecessary glare is one part of making roads safer. For the driver approaching an unfamiliar bend, the person cycling home after work, or the pedestrian trying to cross a poorly lit road, being able to see clearly matters. Thirteen years after Dr Rajaseekaran first approached the Supreme Court, there are now explicit judicial directions addressing dazzling headlights and unauthorised flashing lights. The next challenge is ensuring those directions are followed. Because when you are driving home at night, you should be able to trust that the headlights coming towards you will help another driver see the road, without taking away your ability to see it too. Αυτόν τον Οκτώβριο αποφάσισε να σταματήσει την αναζήτηση και να αρχίσει να χτίζει. Στις 10 Οκτωβρίου 2026, το βράδυ πριν από το Navr…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every Navratri, Rajesh Hadiya, a 30-year-old software engineer in Pune, found himself asking the same question: where are the garbas near me? The Gujarati garba lover never found the answer easily, and the search frustrated him year after year. This October, he decided to stop searching and start building. On 10 October, 2026, the night before Navratri began, he put a free website online that places garba and dandiya nights across India on a single map. From a yearly frustration to a two-day build Hadiya has more than eight years of experience with Android and mobile apps and runs a developer community called DroidTribe. He reasoned that a problem this familiar could not belong to him alone. "If I have this problem, many others must have it too," he told DeshGujarat. He built the first version of Nearby Navratri in two days with Claude, an AI tool, and has added garbas and features every day since. The project runs on free tools and Cloudflare's free hosting, which leaves the domain name as his main expense. He told Mumbai Mirror that it has cost him only a few hundred rupees. Why a festival of nine nights needs a map Gujarat Tourism calls Navratri in the state a nine-night dance festival, perhaps the longest in the world. Garba, the circle dance at its heart, joined UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in December 2023 as the 15th element from India. UNESCO describes garba as a devotional dance for Shakti, the feminine energy worshipped during Navratri. Dandiya adds colourful sticks, and Nearby Navratri lists both kinds of night. Nearby Navratri brings garba and dandiya events across 35 Indian cities onto a single free map, helping people find venues, timings, entry fees and booking links. Photograph: ( Nearbynavratri ) With so many nights on offer, finding the right one takes effort. Some nights sell passes on third party platforms, while free society temple garbas often sell nothing online, according to the site. How the map works The site opens in a phone browser, with no app to download and no login, and its map runs on OpenStreetMap data. A visitor can tap "Show garbas near me" to see the closest nights first, with distances and directions, and the site says it never stores their location. Each listing gives the venue, dates, timings, starting pass price, and a link to the organiser's page for booking. Passes start at Rs 49, and filters narrow the map to free entry or to passes under Rs 500 or Rs 1,000. Many listings name the nearest metro station, and another filter hides nights whose listings say no stag entry. Readers can explore the map at nearbynavratri.in . The map spans 35 cities, from Ahmedabad, Surat and Vadodara to Mumbai, Pune, Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Chennai, and it reaches smaller centres such as Bhuj, Navsari and Vapi. Room for the smaller garbas Hadiya said smaller events are a priority as he keeps expanding the map. Free neighbourhood and society nights, such as the Vokla Faliya Garbi in Old Bhuj and the Busa Society Sheri Garba in Bharuch, sit beside ticketed AC dome nights in Ahmedabad. From ticketed dance nights to free neighbourhood celebrations, Nearby Navratri lists events of different sizes, making it easier for people to discover garbas beyond the big venues. In the Mumbai region alone, Mumbai Mirror counted 43 events, including the free GM Navratri Mahotsav in Mira Road and a free garba night at VIBGYOR High in Belapur. Organisers and visitors can add an event for free, including society nights that sell no tickets online, by sharing a ticket or Instagram link and the venue's map pin. The site says it usually reviews each submission within a few hours. One person behind the listings Hadiya runs the site alone . He checks each submission against organisers' published prices and timings, accepts society garbas only if they admit the public and updates changes himself, according to Mumbai Mirror. The site collects listings from public event pages and organiser submissions. It says it has no affiliation with any organiser or ticketing platform and asks visitors to confirm details before they travel, because dates and prices can change. It also says it refreshes listings through the festival and removes events that end or are cancelled. What the response shows By 14 October, four days after launch, the site had 9,114 users, Mumbai Mirror reported. Hadiya said almost half of the Google searches that bring people to it ask for nearby dandiya nights, and about a third of visitors click through to a booking page. Navratri closes on Monday, 19 October, with Dussehra on 20 October. Mumbai Mirror reports that, if things go as planned, the map will return every year, so a festival built on knowing where to go may soon have a guide for every season. Sources ' App maps garba nights around you ': by AA Correspondent for Mumbai Mirror, Published on 14 October, 2026 ' Weekend Navratri Plans? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Soil Carbon Sponge Opens a New Path to Cooling the Planet Reading Time: 3 minutes A new report argues that restoring the soil carbon sponge could help cool the planet by rebuilding a hydrological system that has regulated heat for billions of years. The soil carbon sponge, Earth’s living water-management layer, may be one of the most overlooked tools in the fight against climate change. A new report argues that restoring healthy soil could help cool the planet directly. The idea centers on how living soil manages water, not just carbon. Researchers behind the report work with the Conscious Planet Save Soil initiative. Their analysis builds on decades of earlier work by Australian soil scientist Walter Jehne. The report frames water, not carbon alone, as the planet’s primary heat regulator. Water has shaped Earth’s temperature for roughly four billion years. Evaporation and condensation move enormous amounts of heat through the atmosphere. Healthy soil acts like a sponge that keeps this cooling cycle running. Underground fungal networks help build this sponge-like structure over time. Fungi bind soil particles together, creating tiny air pockets that trap water. That structure lets soil absorb heavy rainfall instead of letting it run off the surface. Right now, that sponge is badly damaged across much of the world. About 52 percent of global agricultural land is now considered degraded in some way. In parts of the United States, soil erosion runs up to ten times faster than natural formation. In Europe, an estimated 60-70% of soils are now considered unhealthy. Degraded soil holds less water and supports less plant growth. That shift pushes more solar energy into heating the air instead of evaporating water. Scientists describe this shift using two related terms: latent heat and sensible heat. Latent heat describes energy used to evaporate water, which cools the surrounding air. Sensible heat instead raises air temperature directly, as happens over dry, degraded land. Rebuilding soil organic matter could reverse much of this damage over time. The report estimates that each 1% increase lets a hectare hold 250,000 more liters of water. That stored water supports the plant growth needed for continued evapotranspiration. The report’s authors calculate that healthy evapotranspiration moves about 80 watts of energy per square meter. They compare this to the roughly 0.9 watts per square meter driving current global warming. Restoring the soil carbon sponge, they argue, could offset that imbalance several times over. This calculation reflects a newer and less mainstream approach within climate science. Most researchers still treat cutting greenhouse gas emissions as the primary lever for limiting warming. Even so, many scientists agree that healthy soil provides real, measurable local cooling benefits. Restoring the soil carbon sponge and cutting emissions are not competing strategies but complementary ones, with the report’s authors arguing that land regeneration and decarbonization pursued together can reinforce each other’s benefits across the same climate system. Photo by Sven Hornburg on Unsplash. The report’s authors frame soil restoration as a complement to emissions cuts, not a replacement. Both strategies address different parts of the same climate system. Pursued together, they argue, land regeneration and decarbonization could reinforce each other’s benefits. The report recommends several practical steps for restoring the soil carbon sponge. Cover cropping and mulching can keep bare soil from radiating heat back into the sky. Protecting forests also helps sustain the smaller, regional water cycles that keep landscapes moist. Researchers call these regional patterns small water cycles, distinct from the planet’s larger water cycle. Forests recycle much of their own rainfall internally, moistening the air around them. Losing forest cover can dry out a whole region even without any change in total rainfall. Some cities are already testing these ideas at a smaller scale. A trial in Canberra, Australia, is rewetting soil beneath open grassland to cool nearby streets. Early results suggest that even modest soil restoration can measurably lower local air temperatures. These recommendations echo growing interest in regenerative farming worldwide. Similar cover-cropping and mulching methods are already common practice for many small-scale farmers. Wider adoption could extend these local benefits across much larger areas. None of these steps require waiting on new technology to scale up. Farmers, land managers, and city planners around the world already have the tools to start today. Restoring the soil carbon sponge , one field at a time, could offer valuable climate protection. The post The Soil Carbon Sponge Opens a New Path to Cooling the Planet appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: I n August, videos of bulldozers ripping up the mouth of the iconic Santa Elena Canyon in Texas’ Big Bend went viral, propelling one of the country’s most remote national parks into the national spotlight. Construction crews were hard at work in the early stages of cutting a brand-new “patrol road” for law enforcement just feet away from an existing road to the canyon, whose 1,500-foot limestone cliffs, locals argue, form a natural border wall constructed millions of years ahead of schedule. Locals sprang into action, taking shifts monitoring construction and volunteering to rescue endangered plants — including the Chisos Mountain hedgehog cactus and all the spiny plants that provide protective nests for species like the yellow-billed cuckoo — ahead of the bulldozers. A rally was held on the beach in the shadow of the canyon, where people from all walks of life joined hands in the mud. “People think the Rio Grande divides us, but what the river actually does is unite us,” Hillary Pierce, an organizer with No Big Bend Wall, said into the bullhorn while holding a sign that said DON’T BULLDOZE MY CHURCH . The post A Wall Meant to Divide Is Uniting Left and Right in Texas appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Klamath River Salmon Comeback Surprises Scientists After Record Dam Removal Reading Time: 3 minutes Tribal advocacy and coordinated science monitoring made the Klamath River salmon comeback possible after a century of blocked rivers. The Klamath River salmon comeback is happening faster than scientists predicted. Chinook salmon have already reclaimed 88% of their historic territory in the upper Klamath River Basin. This progress comes just two years after crews finished removing four hydroelectric dams. A peer-reviewed assessment published in Scientific Reports offers the first quantitative look at how quickly migratory fish can recolonize a river system once barriers come down, and it treats the Klamath as a benchmark for restoration projects worldwide. The dam removal project wrapped up in October 2024. It stands as the largest dam removal effort completed anywhere in the world. Four dams, some over a century old, once blocked salmon from swimming upstream along the Oregon-California border. Researchers tracked the Klamath River salmon comeback using underwater sonar cameras positioned near the former dam sites. In 2024, about 7,700 Chinook salmon swam past the old dam locations. By 2025, that number grew to more than 13,000 fish, and together these salmon made up close to one-fifth of all Chinook returning to the entire Klamath Basin. Think of it like reopening a highway that had been closed for 100 years. Drivers did not just trickle back in. They found the route almost immediately and started using it in growing numbers. The salmon pushed through difficult terrain to get there. They swam through rocky whitewater stretches, climbed fish ladders taller than a two-story building, and crossed a 25,000-acre lake. One fish reached an elevation of 1,250 meters, more than 580 kilometers from the ocean, marking the farthest inland any Klamath salmon has been recorded and underscoring just how far this recovery has traveled. Scientists compared this recovery to other major dam removal projects. The Elwha River in Washington State saw a similar rebound after its dams came down. But the Klamath River salmon comeback reclaimed a larger share of old habitat in less time than any other large-scale project studied so far. Researchers believe geography helped speed things along. The upper Klamath Basin has broad, lake-filled headwaters instead of steep, narrow streams. This creates gentler terrain that suits salmon better than the sharp mountain drops found in many other river systems. The Klamath River salmon comeback is being aided by the basin’s own geography, with broad, lake-filled headwaters creating gentler terrain that suits returning salmon far better than the steep, narrow streams found in most other restored river systems. Photo by Gary Halvorson, Oregon State Archives on Wikimedia Commons . Cold, spring-fed rivers in the newly opened areas also help. These waters stay at steady, cool temperatures year-round. That gives salmon reliable conditions no matter the season or how much rain or snow falls that year. For over a century, four dams cut off salmon from these waters. Combined with overfishing and water withdrawals, the population had dropped by more than 90%. In 2002, roughly a quarter of that year’s entire salmon run died from disease tied to poor water conditions below the dams, a disaster that helped galvanize the movement behind today’s Klamath River salmon comeback. Removing the barriers has already reversed some of that damage. Beyond Chinook, researchers spotted coho salmon, steelhead, and Pacific lamprey exploring the reopened sections of the river. Their numbers remain smaller, but their presence shows the recovery reaches beyond a single species. Tribal nations played a central role in making this possible. The Yurok, Karuk, Klamath, and Shasta Indian Nation communities have relied on Klamath salmon for food, ceremonies, and cultural traditions for generations. Their decades of advocacy helped drive the push to remove the dams and set the Klamath River salmon comeback in motion. Scientists caution that early success does not guarantee lasting recovery. Most Klamath Chinook salmon live two to four years, so researchers need several more seasons before they fully understand how this generation will fare. They also want to see whether salmon start reproducing successfully in the newly reopened streams. One especially hopeful sign involves spring-run Chinook salmon, a variety that vanished from the upper basin decades ago. The newly reconnected cold-water streams could offer the right conditions for this ecotype to return, either naturally or through reintroduction efforts. Researchers plan to keep watching closely during the spring and summer months when these fish would typically appear. The momentum extends well beyond fish counts. River advocates have also pointed to broader gains, from clearer water to the return of native plants along the banks once buried under reservoirs, a shift that occurred as the dam removal project reached completion. What happens in the Klamath now offers guidance for river restoration projects worldwide. As more aging dams reach the end of their working lives, communities elsewhere face similar decisions. This basin shows that when rivers reopen, nature can respond with remarkable speed, and the Klamath River salmon comeback may just be the opening chapter of a much longer recovery story. The fish did not wait for permission. They found their way home. The post Klamath River Salmon Comeback Surprises Scientists After Record Dam Removal appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM An Australian device that splits rooftop solar power across an entire apartment building just won the country’s top design honor. Melbourne-based Allume Energy took the 2026 Australian Good Design Award of the Year for its SolShare system , which its creators describe as a “traffic controller for solar.” The device also won the sustainability award at the same ceremony, held Friday at ICC Sydney, where more than 1,000 entries competed across 13 disciplines. Why apartment solar access matters Homeowners with their own rooftops have driven most of the residential solar boom , but apartment dwellers have largely been on the sidelines. Individual rooftop installations don’t work well in shared buildings: the costs multiply, the wiring gets messy, and you need a separate inverter for each unit. SolShare cuts through that. One rooftop system, one installation, and the device handles distribution to each apartment automatically. Dr. Brandon Gien, chair of Good Design Australia, called it “an amazing piece of technology” and a beautifully designed solution to a complex problem. “Millions of people live in apartments, and many have had limited access to the benefits of rooftop solar ,” he said. “SolShare is a clever Australian design innovation that addresses that problem in a practical way, and it is already delivering benefits at significant scale.” One of the world’s oldest design competitions The Australian Good Design Awards go back to 1958. Past recipients of the top prize include the Cochlear hearing implant (2000), Marc Newson’s economy class seats for the Qantas A380 (2009), the Flow Hive beehive design (2016), and filmmaker James Cameron’s Deepsea Challenger submersible (2012). SolShare now sits in that lineup. Other sustainability winners at the 2026 awards The night’s other awards pointed the same way. Finnish company FabPatch won the fashion and textiles discipline for a rub-on fabric repair system. No Wrap , an Australian-designed reusable pallet securing system, and Holy Carp , a plastic-free compostable alternative to the soy-sauce fish packets in sushi packaging, both won gold in their categories. A ceremonial gathering space at Melbourne’s City Square, designed in collaboration with Wurundjeri elders to make Woi-wurrung language visible and welcome visitors to Country, won for the built environment. Sydney Children’s Hospital’s wayfinding project replaced standard clinical signage with native animals and plants grouped into three local environments: wetlands, sand dunes, and sea cliffs. Gien said the awards are meant to recognize design that can “bring joy to our lives, but not at the expense of the environment.” A small white box on an apartment wall that gets whole buildings into the solar conversation, without requiring anyone to overhaul the roof, is a reasonable candidate for that. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Hungary’s parliament voted last Tuesday to repeal the 2021 Child Protection Law that banned the portrayal or promotion of homosexuality and transgender identities in schools and media. Within minutes, the EU announced it was releasing €4.2 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in funds frozen over rule-of-law violations, a connection Budapest had been counting on. From political weapon to political liability Orbán’s government pushed the 2021 law as a child protection measure, framing gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, and for years it worked. Then his government pardoned the deputy head of a children’s home convicted of covering up his boss’s child sexual abuse crimes, and what had been a political asset became the defining scandal of his final term. Magyar ran his campaign on protecting children in state care and largely sidestepped the LGBTQ rights issue; his party needed conservative votes, and he was not going to risk alienating them. Five years of legislation, unwound in one vote Tuesday’s package went beyond the 2021 law, touching Fidesz-era changes to education policy and assembly rights. Civil rights group Háttér Society , which had been fighting the child protection law for five years, said most of the problems it had flagged in the draft had been fixed. “We are very happy that this got adopted,” said Tamás Dombos of Háttér Society. “We’ve been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years.” The repeal also cleared Hungary’s path to rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe , two major EU programs suspended during the Orbán years over rule-of-law violations. Tisza holds the same two-thirds parliamentary majority Orbán’s party once had, which meant the package passed without needing to negotiate. Beyond the repeal Háttér Society welcomed the vote, though the group was clear about how much remains unaddressed. It still wants full recognition of same-sex marriage , adoption rights for same-sex couples, and the right of transgender people to change their names on official documents, none of which are in the new legislation. Magyar has been careful in how he frames the issue. “I’m very cautious,” he told Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat. “As prime minister, it’s my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities.” “We are still knocking on a closed door,” Dombos said, “but at least they are listening on the other side.” For a community that spent years being actively targeted, that is a real shift, even if full equality is still a long way off. items.descriptionOriginal: Hear ye, hear ye! You may not be aware, but town criers still exist — and the best of the bunch recently came together to show off their skills in an international competition. Held in Chester, England, the World Town Crier Tournament took place late last month with 25 competitors from eight nations. While town criers date as far back as ancient Greece and Rome, their prevalence in England beginning in the Middle Ages resulted in the image many associate with the role today. Literacy rates were much lower then, so criers were responsible for communicating news, beginning announcements with an exclamation of “oyez,” which is pronounced “oh yay” and derives from a French word meaning “to listen.” Decked out in period attire, the 2026 tournament participants performed three cries: one on their home towns, one on a retail store that sponsored the event, and another on their hotel accommodations. They were judged on vocal power, clarity, showmanship, and audience engagement. Kevin Howarth from Queensland, Australia, was named the overall winner, while Joris Goens of West Flanders, Belgium, took second place. Representing the host country, Christian Ashdown from Surrey, England, came in third. Ashdown spoke to SWNS after the event, describing his win as “a very pleasant surprise.” The 57-year-old noted that “there were some top criers” at the competition — and he would know. He’s been crier of Haslemere, a historic market town in Surrey, for 16 years and has won prior championships. A projects and amenities officer for the Haslemere Town Council, Ashdown said he never intended to be a town crier, but when his predecessor decided to retire in the middle of the busy Christmas period, the mayor called asking if he’d fill in. He hesitantly accepted and eventually fell in love with the role. He’s now the chair of the Ancient and Honourable Guild of Town Criers , which is the largest and oldest body of town criers in the world. Ashdown says there are 117 members and that town crying is becoming more popular as the guild has begun posting on social media. The job mostly consists of greeting people on special occasions and market days, as well as representing the town during contests. Criers must wear a costume, which is usually Georgian-inspired as that was the peak of town crying in England. Because they generally work on a volunteer basis, many hold down other jobs as well. “It had never crossed my mind to become a town crier. I knew what they were, but I didn’t know they still existed,” said Ashdown. “I knew nothing about it, but I have very much embraced it.” He added: “People love it and they thank me. It is all positive which surprised me actually.” Despite the perception of town criers being artifacts of the past, he noted that the position “has never really died off funnily enough. It is something that has never gone away.” He said that common mistakes are saying “oyez” while talking, rather than at the start of a cry with a pause, and focusing too much on volume. He also advises fellow or aspiring criers not to use their voice too much the day before an event, as they’ll need lots of water and throat lozenges. “Try not to scream and shout too much. You have to pace yourself,” Ashdown explained. “Just be nice and clear. It is not necessarily always about the volume; it is enunciation.” This article was originally written by Isobel Williams for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets. items.descriptionOriginal: Ten years after a childhood bike crash, Rika Matsuda unfolded an origami crane a stranger who witnessed the crash had given her and found a message written inside -- a Japanese expression meaning "cherish the moment," or more fully, that we should treasure each encounter because it may never come again. The man had slipped the words in quietly, without drawing attention to them, letting them wait until she was ready. What the story reveals is something almost too simple to name: that a caring stranger's gentleness, offered in a few unhurried minutes at a water fountain, can fold itself into a life and stay there. "He didn't say anything," Matsuda recalled. "He just smiled and handed me the origami crane."

items.descriptionOriginal: You’ve finished your morning Nice News read but are still craving some uplifting, thought-provoking media — might we suggest turning to a podcast next? We’re big fans of the medium (so much so that we released a season of our own podcast last year!) and love how these audio shows can inform, inspire, and entertain during mundane moments of the day. We rounded up nine engaging shows that we think are worth a spot on your playlist, whether you’re doing the dishes, walking the dog, or just looking to unwind on the couch. No Such Thing As a Fish Prepare to laugh and be amazed. The recipient of the Heinz Oberhummer Award for Science Communication in 2019, No Such Thing As a Fish features researchers from the BBC’s comedy game show QI who spotlight a trove of hilarious and mind-boggling facts they’ve dug up over the previous week. The episodes are sure to leave you smiling after each listen. “It explains what the Second World War and carrots have to do with each other or how long you have to cook a space egg,” per a statement from the Oberhummer Awards. “And while you listen, laugh, and marvel for 40 minutes, you often don’t notice how much you’ve learned.” On Humans A favorite of Nice News Assistant Editor Rebekah Brandes, On Humans seeks to answer three questions: “Where do we come from? How did we get here? And what kinds of creatures are we?” In each episode, host Ilari Mäkelä interviews scholars primarily about our origins as humans, delving into specific topics like shamans , why we laugh , and the early days of farming . The show “always leaves me feeling smarter and more curious,” Rebekah said. Good Hang With Amy Poehler Amy Poehler isn’t trying to dole out advice or “make you better” — she’s simply looking for a good time. In Good Hang , which won the first-ever Golden Globe for best podcast earlier this year, Poehler interviews celebs and other “fun people” to provide a cozy, relaxed alternative to the plethora of self-improvement-focused media out there. Start with standout episodes featuring Jennifer Lawrence, Seth Meyers, and Tina Fey. Home Cooking Pals Samin Nosrat, author of Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat , and Hrishikesh Hirway, creator and host of the podcast Song Exploder , dished up cooking advice for amateurs with a side of friendly banter in Home Cooking , which ran from 2020-2025. A self-described perfectionist, Nosrat explained to Vogue in 2020 that the show centers a different mindset around cooking: “It’s about putting something out there to make people feel comforted and like they have technical support in the kitchen and some way to pass the time by hanging out with these funny, very dorky friends.” Unconditional With Maggie Lawson Animal lovers know there’s something special about the bonds they share with their pets — and this podcast celebrates exactly that. Hosted by Psych actor Maggie Lawson, the series explores the special connection celebrities like Henry Winkler and Janel Parrish have with their pets, and features interviews with animal experts about the “healing effects” of our furry friends. “Anyone who is obsessed with their pets will feel so seen by this podcast,” said Nice News Writer Marika Spitulski, adding, “I already want to be [Lawson’s] friend and hang out with her dog Linus.” Weirdly Helpful How can we take control of our “news diet”? And what’s considered proper handshaking etiquette in our modern age? These questions and more are answered in Weirdly Helpful , a series of bite-size episodes (each around 20 minutes or less) that spotlight guests who cover unexpected but intriguing ways to make life better. “Thanks for making me feel inspired while giving me concrete steps to evolve,” one reviewer wrote. Happier With Gretchen Rubin In 2024, we picked Gretchen Rubin’s brain about practical ways to lead a happier life — and in her award-winning podcast, the author and happiness researcher shares more strategies, ideas, and personal anecdotes to inspire you to live joyfully. Try one of her “A Little Happier” episodes for a quick fix; each lays out a lesson in five minutes or less. You can also check out her “Move Happier” series, intended to be paired with 26 minutes of movement as part of her Move 26 in ’26 challenge . The Allusionist If you’re a fan of NPR’s “Word of the Week” series, we bet you’ll love The Allusionist , which won smartest podcast at the 2018 British Podcast Awards. In each episode, host Helen Zaltzman dives into the intricacies of language, including the etymology and cultural significance of some of our most used words (and profanities), with a hefty dose of humor. Start with her April 13 episode “Hues” to learn why some of Merriam-Webster’s lexicographers took decades to define certain color names. Get Birding On HBO Max, you can catch Sean Bean ruling his corner of Westeros as the Stark family patriarch in Game of Thrones . On your podcast feed, though, he’s a soothing presence pointing out birds as they fly over his garden. The English actor took over as host for Season 4 of Get Birding , inviting ornithologists into his backyard and beyond to talk all things avian. The biweekly episodes, which you can also watch on YouTube, cover everything from why birdsong makes us feel good to why birds sing at daybreak . RELATED: How to Build a Personalized Mental Health Tool Kit for Days When You’re Feeling Down When you buy books through our links, Nice News may earn a commission, which helps keep our content free.

items.descriptionOriginal: What if retirement offered an opportunity to give something back to the natural world? In Virginia's Shenandoah Valley, two retired neighbors, John Rice and John Sessler, are doing just that, transforming their farmland into thriving habitats for wildlife. Working alongside Smithsonian conservation scientists, they've helped protect nearly 2,500 acres of private land, creating corridors where animals can move, find food, and flourish. Their days are spent removing invasive plants, restoring native wildflowers, and watching the landscape slowly come back to life. What began as a personal love of nature has become something much larger: a living legacy of conservation, nurtured through patience, dedication, and the simple joy of caring for the land.

items.descriptionOriginal: A 13-year-old has earned the distinction of being “America’s top young scientist” for 2026, taking first place in 3M’s prestigious Young Scientist Challenge. Raji Doshi, an eighth grader from Farmington, Connecticut, won the contest with an algae-based invention that could help save marine ecosystems. She and nine other finalists aged 11-14 created their prototypes over the summer, each of them working with a mentor to develop their ideas. Raji won the $25,000 grand prize after the challenge’s final events on Oct. 12 and 13, presenting a natural system that addresses ocean acidification by increasing alkalinity and removing carbon dioxide. Ocean acidification, which began during the industrial revolution, is primarily caused by the seawater absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The change in PH reduces the abundance of carbonate ions: essential structures that many marine lifeforms, like corals and crustaceans, need to build their shells and skeletons. “Raji’s project reminds us that when you’re passionate about something, you can use that interest to change the world,” her mentor, 3M product engineering specialist Deborah Isabelle, said in a press release . “She loves collecting seashells and was distressed that ocean acidification is starting to damage the seashells and the creatures that live inside them.” The contest also recognizes two runners-up, who each received a $1,000 cash prize. The three honorees, all girls, point to promising changes in the STEM arena, where women have historically been underrepresented. Seventh grader Aaisha Asif came in second place for her eco-friendly adhesive made from natural proteins; and ninth grader Sharvi Mahajan took third for her EEG-based device that tracks fatigue and predicts microsleep, alerting drivers and others in high-risk fields. Looking at the full lineup of finalists , it’s clear the future of science is bright. “The 3M Young Scientist Challenge highlights the incredible potential of young people to tackle real-world challenges through science,” said William Brown, 3M Chairman and CEO. “The talent and creativity displayed by this year’s finalists was exceptional, and we congratulate Raji on earning the title of America’s Top Young Scientist.”
