items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Reading Time: 5 minutes 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Spending all day in a truly comfortable bra is already a challenge. Tracking down one made from 100% organic cotton – with legitimate certification to prove it – is even harder. The market for comfortable 100% organic cotton bras has expanded, but quality is all over the place, and plenty of labels that claim “natural” can’t back that up with documentation. Why Organic Cotton Matters for Everyday Comfort Most people don’t realize how chemically loaded a conventional bra can be. Standard synthetics and treated cotton often carry azo dyes, formaldehyde finishes, and PFAS, substances pressing directly against skin for hours every day. The Center for Environmental Health detected BPA in sports bras from major mainstream brands at levels up to 40 times the established safe limit. Certified organic cotton changes that picture. GOTS certification (Global Organic Textile Standard) controls the entire supply chain from farm to finished garment, banning the synthetic pesticides and chemical finishes that standard cotton processing allows. For people with sensitive skin, eczema, or simply a preference for fewer synthetics, a GOTS-certified bra isn’t a luxury; it’s a practical choice. And comfort follows naturally. Organic cotton breathes well, wicks moisture without relying on synthetic coatings, and softens with wear rather than pilling or stiffening. The absence of harsh dyes also means less skin irritation over time. 1. Q for Quinn Q for Quinn is a small, family-owned Canadian brand founded in 2018 by Melita Cyril, who originally designed organic cotton socks for her son’s eczema before expanding into a full line of natural-fiber essentials for adults and children. The brand’s bra and bralette lineup covers several styles: a criss-cross bralette, a pointelle bra, a racerback sports bra, a full bust sports bra, and a shelf tank. Fabrics come in either 95% organic cotton with 5% elastane or 100% organic cotton. The fully cotton styles are biodegradable end-to-end, using natural rubber-cotton elastics and 100% organic cotton thread throughout; pricing starts between $52 and $64, and sizing runs XS through 3XL. Every applicable product carries GOTS certification through Ecocert Greenlife under license 256894. Product pages spell out each component – body fabric, elastic, thread, and closures – so nothing in the construction is hidden. Undergarments are made in certified facilities in Tirupur, India, and the brand excludes chlorine bleach, azo dyes, and formaldehyde finishes from its entire supply chain. Where it fits: Women with sensitive skin, those avoiding chemical exposure during workouts, and shoppers who want full material transparency in a bra, particularly for low-to-medium impact activities like yoga, Pilates, and walking. 2. Roaman’s Roaman’s is a plus-size fashion retailer with roots stretching back decades, now operating as part of FullBeauty Brands and headquartered in Indianapolis. The brand focuses exclusively on sizes 12W through 44W, it doesn’t start from a smaller size and grade up, which makes it genuinely purpose-built for plus-size shoppers rather than an afterthought extension of a standard range. The catalog spans a wide range of women’s clothing, intimates, swimwear, sleepwear, tops, bottoms, and shoes. With over 100 years in women’s fashion, the brand positions itself as an industry leader and pushes fashion-forward designs at prices that don’t require a big budget. Shopping options include the website, a printed catalog, and a store credit card. Roaman’s clothing was used to dress cast members on TLC’s 1,000 lb Sisters , a placement that put the brand in front of its core audience. Customer support runs through phone and email, and the website offers account management, order tracking, and a rewards program. Where it fits: Plus-size shoppers looking for a wide selection of intimates and clothing in one place, with consistent sizing across categories. Worth checking: Roaman’s is a general plus-size fashion retailer. Shoppers seeking certified organic cotton bras should confirm material details before purchasing, as the brand doesn’t position itself around organic certification. 3. Siella Siella is a Canadian lingerie brand launched in 2020 out of Montreal, backed by Chateau Bodywear, a family business with over 75 years of experience manufacturing underwear and lingerie, founded in 1945. That manufacturing depth gives Siella a level of vertical control that newer brands rarely have. The line focuses on wireless bras, underwear, and loungewear, with a stated emphasis on comfort, support, and a second-skin fit. Siella describes its approach as designed by women, blending modern femininity with everyday comfort. Prices range from approximately $25 to $105 USD, with bundle discounts of up to 20% available. Free shipping kicks in on orders over $95. U.S. customer service operates on EST timezone at +1 800-665-0589. The brand emphasizes organic cotton options and benefits from its parent company’s manufacturing infrastructure, which supports tighter control than outsourced production typically allows. Siella has been featured in Diary of a Toronto Girl’s roundup of top lingerie brands. Where it fits: Shoppers who want wireless bras that prioritize everyday comfort and are open to a Canadian brand with a long manufacturing history behind it. Worth checking: Organic cotton certification details aren’t publicly disclosed the same way as some competitors, so shoppers should confirm certification before purchase if that’s a deciding factor. 4. Bestform Bestforms, Inc. is a company founded in 1985 and headquartered in Camarillo, California, with 51 to 200 employees. The company operates as a B2B manufacturer in the business forms and print industry, producing patented membership card products, integrated labels, variable barcoding, unit set forms, continuous forms, and custom labels. Bestforms describes its model as “trade only,” meaning it works through intermediaries rather than direct-to-consumer channels. The company’s tagline is “BestCards, Labels and Digital Solutions, Forms,” and its track record centers on responsive development for commercial printing needs. Bestforms does not appear to operate as a lingerie or apparel retailer. No bra products, organic cotton garments, or related consumer goods appear in the company’s product lineup. Where it fits: Business clients in need of commercial printing, label manufacturing, or custom card production, not a category match for consumers shopping for organic cotton bras. Worth checking: Shoppers searching for lingerie under this name should confirm they’ve reached the correct brand, as the bestform.com domain belongs to a commercial printing manufacturer, not an apparel company. 5. AmpleBosom AmpleBosom is a UK-based online and mail-order retailer founded in 1999 by Sally Robinson, operating from a family-run farm in Old Byland, North Yorkshire. The company specializes in bras, lingerie, swimwear, nightwear, and clothing, with a size range that runs from 28 to 58 in AA through N cups, one of the widest ranges available anywhere in the market. AmpleBosom doesn’t manufacture its own products; instead, it stocks bras and lingerie from established names including Empreinte, Elomi, and Fantasie. The team is estimated at 25 to 100 employees, and the business has stayed independent since it launched. It earned early recognition when the BBC series Inside Dot Coms featured it in 2000, notable for an e-commerce model that was well ahead of the mainstream at the time. Expert bra fitting advice is offered both in-person and virtually. Payment is accepted online, by mail, or by phone; in-store payment isn’t an option. Pricing varies by brand and item, with promotions available throughout the year. Where it fits: Shoppers who need larger or harder-to-find cup sizes and want access to multiple specialty lingerie brands in one place, with expert fitting support available. Worth checking: AmpleBosom is a UK retailer; U.S. shoppers should factor in international shipping costs and delivery times, and should verify whether specific organic cotton options are available among its current brand selection. Bottom Line Brands in the comfortable 100% organic cotton bra space span a surprisingly wide range – certified organic specialists, plus-size fashion retailers, and, in at least one case, a commercial printer that has no business appearing on this list. For shoppers who prioritize verified certification, full material transparency, and construction that’s genuinely gentle on sensitive skin, the real options thin out fast. Roaman’s and Siella both serve comfort-focused buyers but from different angles: Roaman’s through extended plus sizing, Siella through wireless everyday styles. AmpleBosom suits anyone needing an unusually wide cup range paired with professional fitting guidance. Know what matters most to you – certification, sizing, support level, or country of origin, and the right choice gets a lot clearer. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable Reading Time: 3 minutes How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable The lights flicker during a storm, and you suddenly notice the grid you rarely think about. More of your power now comes from the sun and wind, which don’t follow a schedule. Clean energy can remain steady as the weather shifts because modern grid upgrades help balance supply and demand and ensure reliability behind the scenes. What Is a Smart Grid? A smart grid is an electrical network that uses digital technology to monitor and manage power from the source to the home. It sits at the heart of grid modernization, which involves upgrading the physical equipment and digital tools that generate, move and manage electricity. Older grids relied on one-way communication, but a smart grid lets utilities and customers share information in both directions. The most visible piece is the smart meter. In 2022, utilities in the United States had about 119 million smart meter installations , or roughly 72% of all electric meters. Advanced versions have built-in two-way communication, so they can record and send data instantly. A smart grid relies on several connected parts working together: Smart meters: These devices track your energy use and share it with your utility. Sensors: Devices along power lines and equipment can flag problems before they spread. Automated switches: These switches can reroute power around a fault without waiting for a crew. Energy storage: Batteries save extra power , such as midday solar, for use when demand rises. Two-way communication: This link lets utilities and customers share data and respond to each other quickly. Why Does the Traditional Grid Struggle With Clean Energy? The grid that powers your home took shape in a very different energy world. Large, steady power plants sent electricity to homes long before rooftop solar panels or wind farms existed, and the equipment reflects that history. Today, over 70% of the power grid is over 25 years old. Variable solar and wind, plus growing demand, strain equipment with limited ability to see or adjust to changes in real time. Engineering and utility consulting firms help power companies plan upgrades to infrastructure, sensors and smart meters. Each improvement can give operators a clearer view of the system, enabling them to respond to changing conditions sooner and keep clean power flowing. That approach can turn an older network into a smart grid built for clean energy. How Can Upgraded Grids Balance Wind and Solar Power? Wind and utility-scale solar generated 17% of U.S. electricity in 2025, up from under 1% in 2005. However, wind and solar only produce power when the wind blows or the sun shines, unlike power plants that can ramp up on demand. Modern grids tackle the gap between when clean power is available and when you need it. Batteries can store surplus solar power for evening use, and smart controls can automatically adjust the grid as supply rises and falls. Forecasting can help operators predict wind and solar output in advance and prepare accordingly. Demand response programs can also encourage you to shift energy use to times when clean power is plentiful, easing pressure on the grid during peak hours. These tools may help wind and solar become a steadier part of your power supply. Why Does Extreme Weather Raise the Stakes for Reliability? Severe storms, heat and winter weather can all disrupt steady power. From 2000 to 2023, 80% of major U.S. outages were weather-related, with the latest decade seeing about twice as many as the first. A modernized grid can help keep your community’s power on when conditions turn rough. Sensors can quickly detect damage, and automated switches may isolate the damaged section so the outage affects fewer neighborhoods. Self-healing systems, which detect faults and automatically reroute electricity, can keep more homes connected. Microgrids, which are small, local networks that can operate independently, may also help restore power faster. Together, these tools can shorten the time you spend in the dark and make clean energy feel dependable even during difficult weather. What Could a Smart Grid Change in Your Daily Life? Smart grid upgrades can make clean energy more useful in daily life by changing how power moves to and from your home: Rooftop solar: A two-way grid can make it easier to send extra power from your panels back to your community. Time-of-use pricing: Some utilities offer lower rates during off-peak hours, which rewards flexible habits. Electric vehicle charging: Smart charging can schedule your car to charge during off-peak hours. Quicker repairs: Better monitoring may help crews find and fix problems faster. What Can You Do to Support Steady Clean Power? Clean energy is only as reliable as the grid that carries it. Grid modernization works quietly in the background to keep clean power steady in your home, from the smart meter on your house to the upgrades down the street. A good next step is checking what your own utility offers, such as smart meter data, time-of-use plans or solar programs. Small choices like these can help a more dependable, cleaner grid take shape, and you can find the options are closer than you think. The post How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems Reading Time: 4 minutes How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems Readers of this site tend to think in systems. A beaver dam that restores a creek, a wildlife crossing that saves panthers, a court that grants fish legal standing, these stories share a common thread: small, deliberate interventions ripple outward into healthier ecosystems. Pest control rarely gets discussed in that same frame, but it belongs there. Every spray, bait, or barrier a homeowner chooses either supports or undermines the insects, birds, and soil organisms that keep a neighborhood’s ecology functioning. That matters more than most people realize, because household pest management sits at the intersection of two things this audience cares about deeply: protecting pollinators and other wildlife, and making smart use of limited resources. The choices homeowners make about ants, termites, or rodents do not stay contained to a single yard. Chemicals drift, water carries residue, and beneficial insects do not distinguish between a target pest and a pollinator caught in the same treatment zone. In fast-growing communities around San Antonio, this tension shows up constantly as new development pushes into former ranchland and native habitat. Homeowners in that region increasingly ask pest professionals to treat infestations without collateral damage to the monarchs, native bees, and birds that still move through these corridors. Companies like EcoForce Pest Management , which serves the Cibolo, Texas area, reflect a broader shift in the industry toward targeted, lower-impact treatment methods that still get rid of pests without broadcasting pesticide across an entire property. Why Pest Control Choices Ripple Through Local Ecosystems Pollinators are not a side issue in this conversation, they are central to it. Insect pollinators add more than fifteen billion dollars in crop value annually in the United States, which means any pest control practice that harms bees, butterflies, or other pollinating insects carries a real economic cost well beyond the yard where it happens. Routine, calendar-based spraying, the kind that treats a property on a fixed schedule regardless of actual pest pressure, increases the odds of harming these beneficial insects compared to treatment that responds to an actual, identified problem. This is why the distinction between reactive, blanket pesticide use and targeted treatment matters so much ecologically. A homeowner who sprays broadly “just in case” is making a bet that trades short-term convenience for long-term harm to the insects and soil life that keep local food webs intact. A homeowner who waits for evidence of an actual infestation, then treats only the affected area, protects far more of the surrounding ecosystem while still solving the immediate problem. What Actually Drives the Cost of Pest Management Cost in pest control is rarely about the price of a single treatment, it is about how often treatment has to happen and how much damage accumulates before anyone intervenes. A termite colony left undetected for a year can cost thousands of dollars in structural repair, while the inspection that would have caught it early costs a fraction of that. Rodents chewing through wiring create fire risk and expensive repairs that dwarf the cost of sealing an entry point before they ever got inside. According to EPA , integrated pest management relies on monitoring, pest-identification thresholds, and preventive habitat changes, reserving chemical treatment as a targeted last resort rather than a routine first response. That framework is not just ecologically sound, it is financially sound too, because prevention and early detection cost less than remediation almost every time. The expensive scenarios are always the ones where a problem went unnoticed long enough to cause structural or health damage, not the ones where someone paid for a seasonal inspection. Where Eco-Friendly Methods Pay Off Over Time Eco-friendly pest control is sometimes assumed to be the pricier, more delicate option, but the opposite is often true over a multi-year horizon. Sealing cracks, managing moisture, and removing food sources reduces the pest pressure that would otherwise require repeat chemical treatments. Fewer treatments mean lower cumulative cost, and they mean less pesticide entering soil and groundwater where it can affect everything from earthworms to the birds that eat them. The table below lays out some of the real tradeoffs between reactive, chemical-heavy pest control and a more preventive, ecologically minded approach, using figures drawn from EPA guidance on integrated pest management. Factor Reactive, broadcast treatment Preventive, IPM-based approach Pollinator risk Higher, due to non-targeted exposure Lower, treatment is targeted to confirmed pests Core strategy Calendar-based spraying regardless of need Monitoring and thresholds before any chemical use Economic value protected Not factored into treatment decisions Helps preserve pollinators tied to $15B+ in annual crop value Lowest-cost prevention step Rarely prioritized Sealing entry points, moisture control, sanitation What this comparison shows is that the cheapest long-term option and the most ecologically responsible option tend to converge. A property that invests in sealing, drainage correction, and regular monitoring spends less over five years than one that relies on repeated broad-spectrum treatments, even though the upfront preventive work can look like an added expense in year one. Smart Places to Economize Without Compromising Protection Homeowners who want to save money without cutting corners ecologically should focus their budget on the structural fixes that prevent infestations in the first place, since these are the cheapest interventions with the longest payoff. Sealing foundation gaps, repairing damaged screens, and fixing leaky pipes that create standing water all cost far less than a single severe infestation treatment, and they address the root conditions that attract pests to begin with. These are also the steps least likely to involve any chemical exposure at all, which makes them a win on both the cost and ecological fronts. Where spending does make sense is in professional inspection and identification, because misdiagnosing a pest problem leads to wasted treatments and wasted money. A targeted response to a correctly identified pest, applied only where needed, almost always costs less over time than a generic, whole-property treatment applied out of uncertainty. For readers who care about the pollinators, soil organisms, and backyard wildlife that this site regularly celebrates, that targeted approach is also the one that does the least collateral damage to the ecosystem right outside the door. The post How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Arielle: And I’m Arielle. Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. Arielle: Yes, welcome back. Karissa and I have had a week off because last week we had a wonderful guest episode with #CreateConnectCare. If you missed it, then definitely go check it out. Karissa: Yeah, it was a great episode. I missed sharing the solutions, though, last week. Mm-hmm. And I’m glad to be back with you today, Arielle. Arielle: Yeah, there’s a lot of seasonal solutions and, uh, just some, some fun discoveries that happened this week. But before that, how are you, Karissa? Karissa: Doing well over here. The weather has been so strange all across the globe. We’re already in the middle of October, but you would not know it, at least in California. Arielle: Yeah, it’s been really weird here in the Netherlands as well. Every time I think autumn has arrived, and it’s, like, rainy and gloomy, and I’m kind of getting into my cozy vibe, the next few days are, like, sunny and warm again. Not that I’m complaining. I would not complain about that, but it’s just, it’s a bit hard to get into the seasonal rhythm… I don’t know if our listeners and fellow Optimists are feeling similarly, but I know that I’m just feeling a bit weird. Other than that, nothing to report on my end. Karissa: Yeah. I feel similarly. I guess I’m enjoying a little bit of stillness between the busy summer months and the festive season. We’re gonna go full force into the holidays here, and then this year will be over, so um- Arielle: Yeah. It definitely went by quickly, but there’s still a lot of positive news out there to share before the end of the year. And if you want all of those positive solutions straight to your inbox, then you should consider signing up for our daily or weekly newsletter. You can do that on our website, or the link is in the show notes. Karissa: And if you want these solutions and more on your social media feeds, we’re @optimistdaily on everything except X, where we’re @OdeToOptimism. Arielle: You can also reach me and Karissa directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We would love to get any suggestions, comments, questions, feedback, so feel free to shoot us an email. Karissa: Before we go any further, we’d love to thank our Optimist Daily Emissaries who financially support us. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is in the show notes. If financially supporting us isn’t in your budget right now, we thank our Optimists who share these solutions and follow us on socials. Arielle: Yeah, there are a lot of free ways to support us, and we appreciate everyone who does that. Karissa: And without further ado, Arielle, I think we should dive into this week’s new solutions. Australia’s renewable energy record Karissa: The first one that we had to share this week is “Australia sets a new renewable energy record, with rooftop solar leading the way”. So Australia just hit a new record. Solar- and wind-powered 80% of the entire national grid on a single Saturday. And the wild part about that is that more than half of that came not from massive solar farms, but from panels on people’s rooftops. For about 30 minutes, 4.3 million rooftop solar installations collectively carried more than half of the country’s total power load. The researcher who tracks this called it record season. Conditions were so good, he expects these records to get broken again within weeks. These individual homeowners, and not, like, utility companies, drove a national record, and that’s exciting all in itself. Arielle: Yeah, it really drives home the point that the energy transition doesn’t have to center around big infrastructure. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: It’s a reminder that, yeah, if there’s small-scale adoption, then that can really add up quickly. Karissa: Absolutely. And with Australia having an 82% renewable target for 2030, this kind of milestone is expected to become routine. So that is optimistic indeed. Performance anxiety & sport psychology Karissa: The next solution is titled “”How to quiet performance anxiety, according to sport psychology””. A sport psychologist who works with NFL teams and Olympic athletes has a pretty counterintuitive take on confidence. You don’t wait until you feel it, you act your way into it first, fake it till you make it, and the feeling follows. So she has a whole toolkit for doing this in the middle of a high-pressure moment, and the technique that an NFL receiver used after a playoff fumble is one of them. I didn’t know about this technique, but it’s called the learn, burn, return method, which is a three-step process for recovering mid-performance from a mistake. Learn one thing from it, use a physical gesture to signal moving on. For example, the Vikings receiver Adam Thielen made the toilet flush gesture famous in a 2020 playoff game, where he’s just kind of pretending to flush the toilet and get rid of that mistake, which is a fun thing. And then reset it all with a certain phrase. The performance anxiety conversation used to live almost entirely in sports, but I mean, now it’s everywhere, whether it’s in job interviews, presentations, creative work, even dating. So I think it’s important to expand upon this concept. But yeah, there’s a lot of great tips in this article from Cindra Kamphoff, who is a PhD in sport and performance psychology, and she gives a lot of great tips here, including writing powerful phrases before a high-stakes moment, which I really liked that one. So go check it out if you want some more pointers. Coral shade experiment Karissa: The next solution is “”How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave””. Scientists in Florida just published results from an experiment where they literally put little floating umbrellas over coral to protect them from the heat, and it worked. But the lead researcher was pretty blunt. This is triage, not a total solution for coral bleaching. So I loved the images here in this solution, because it really had like… The um- umbrella is kind of a… It, it’s not… I at first pictured an umbrella, like our pop-up umbrella, and I thought that was kind of a cute image, but it’s kind of just a floating, like Arielle: Like a shade, Karissa: basically Shade, yeah. Like a, just a little piece of, um- Arielle: Yeah, like a tarp … Karissa: yeah, a tarp. That’s a great way to explain it. The shaded brain coral started recovering color after these umbrellas were put in, and the unprotected ones kept bleaching through the hottest part of the season. Coral bleaching events used to happen about once a decade, but now they’re happening every five to six years, and reefs don’t have enough time to recover between them. By March 2025, 84% of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures high enough to cause bleaching. The researcher’s quote in this was so honest, that shading is not a cure-all. This is a solution that is kind of just buying time for the bigger problem. Arielle: Yeah. It’s important to address the root problems, but yeah, if we need more time, which we definitely do, then why not? Karissa: Absolutely. Did you know that coral reefs cover less than 0.2% of the ocean floor, but shelter a quarter of all marine species? So that’s a pretty wild ratio, and we gotta protect them, just like we need to protect the rest of our beautiful planet as well. Skincare mistakes Karissa: The next solution is “”The common skin care mistakes dermatologists say are working against your routine””. Five dermatologists were asked what bad skin habits they most want patients to break, and the answer keeps coming back to the same thing. Most of us are overdoing it when it comes to our skin care routine. And there’s also a pimple popping rule in here that I think a lot of people will appreciate, and I’ll start with that one. It’s the one good squeeze rule for pimples. It’s okay to pop a pimple, but if it doesn’t come out on the first try, stop, because continuing just pushes bacteria deeper and can cause those dark spots that stick around for months. I admit if it has a white head, then I have to pop it. But usually, of course, that comes out with the one good squeeze, and it… I do think it’s, it’s very, um, satisfying, so. Arielle: Yeah. No, I’m so guilty of this. I love popping pimples. Karissa: Me too. Arielle: Um, and I will keep going at it, and I have had that, like, hyperpigmentation thing happen. Mm-hmm. And it’s just not cute. Yeah. And I, I have to abide by this. You know what’s really helped me, though? Those pimple patches. So- Karissa: Yeah, I was gonna say the same thing … Arielle: first of all, they’re fun, so you can have, like, a little purple star or whatever on your face instead of a- Yeah … a bright red glaring pimple. Um, but I do it less for, like, the… Well, of course I, I do it so that the pimple will heal, but it’s more so that my fingers just don’t get on it. Because if I see it- Yeah … then I just wanna squeeze it. Karissa: I resonated with the point that skin care has developed a trend cycle that rivals fast fashion. There’s new ingredients, new products every week, and TikTok routines that keep expanding what we’re, you know, supposed to do. So dermatologists really emphasize that sticking with simple is oftentimes better. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah, and just what works for your skin. Because everyone’s skin is different, and you can’t just be chasing the trends all the time if it doesn’t work for your specific type of skin. So if you have a routine that works for you, then just stick to that. Don’t get, like, you know, uh, distracted by the shiny new serum. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Exactly. Flu shot timing Karissa: Next solution is “”Why October is the best time to get your flu shot this year””. Flu is already showing up in emergency rooms across the West, and the numbers are running about seven times higher than the same week last year. Experts are saying October is the window to get vaccinated, and there’s actually a new mRNA flu vaccine in the mix for the first time, which is a really great breakthrough. So yeah, seven times higher than this time last year is pretty rough. It’s in Western states now, but it’s expected to spread east. And the flu vaccine’s effectiveness data is pretty interesting. 29 to 56% effective against of cases that send people to the doctor, but better against severe illness. The framing here with vaccines in general is to remember it’s keeping you out of the hospital, and keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery, which is a quote from the article. About the mRNA flu vaccine, you might recall this term being used for, uh, the COVID vaccine, and it’s now being applied to the flu vaccine for adults 50 and older this season, and it’s supposed to be more effective. Arielle: There was a, a number in this article that kind of broke my heart. It said that last year there were at least 195 child deaths from flu-related causes, and preventing such high numbers could be as simple as just getting vaccinated against the flu. So yeah, and I don’t mean to fearmonger, but it definitely struck a chord with me when I read it. Karissa: Yeah. Tens of thousands of Americans die of flu each season, and that tends to surprise people. I feel like flu deaths are chronically under-discussed. So of course, yeah, like you mentioned, Arielle, not to fearmonger, but get that flu vaccine, and it’s a good time to get it now. Octopus nursery Arielle: Well, on that note, we’re going to bring it to some lighter topics, let’s say. Uh, the first solution that I’m going to share with everyone is titled “Scientists discovered the world’s largest octopus nursery off the California coast”. Scientists were studying one of the most closely monitored stretches of ocean in the world, and somehow missed 20,000 octopuses just hanging out on the sea floor. Turns out there’s a field of hydrothermal springs down there that’s functioning as the world’s largest known octopus nursery, and researchers only found it in 2018. So these hydrothermal springs keep the water warm enough to cut the octopuses’ egg-brooding time from years down to about 1.8 years, which still sounds like a l- a long time to me. Yeah. But if it’s, if it’s cutting more years off of it, then that’s great. And this is why so many octopuses congregate there specifically. The octopuses build their dens from whatever they find on the sea floor, including human objects that have drifted down to the deep sea. This went undetected until 2018 in well-studied water, which raises the question of how many other gatherings like this exist in unmapped thermal fields elsewhere. There’s been growing public fascination, I think, with octopus intelligence and behavior in recent years, and this story lands right in that conversation. And yeah, I, I think I remember when My Octopus Teacher came out, and I think that was kind of when everybody was like, “Oh my gosh, octopuses are actually so, so smart and so cool.” Um, have you seen it, Karissa? Karissa: No, I haven’t, but now I wanna go watch it because I… this solution really, uh, stood out to me this week and I love it, so I’m really interested in learning some more. Arielle: Yeah, this week we have such cute ocean stories, like picturing little corals under their umbrellas and, like a whole bunch of octopuses chilling out. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Making babies. So… Karissa: Yeah, fun stuff. Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers Arielle: The next solution is titled “Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters”. A Japanese disaster scientist had an idea 20 years ago while studying earthquakes in Indonesia. What if the country’s mosque loudspeakers, already everywhere and already maintained daily, could double as earthquake warning systems? That pilot is now underway, and the drop-and-cover finding buried in the story is just as interesting. And if you don’t know what I mean by that, just wait. I will get to it. So Indonesia might have only five to 10 seconds of warning before an earthquake hits, and yeah, the mosque loudspeakers tested five times a day by local communities are more reliable than phone networks that can fail the moment the ground starts shaking. What I mean when I say that the mosque loudspeakers are tested five times a day is that, um, the call to prayer happens five times a day, so they definitely know that the speakers are working because the call to prayer is happening. And the drop-and-cover thing that I mentioned earlier is the standard international advice for when there’s an earthquake. You’re supposed to drop low and cover, like get under a table or something. But this advice was meant for places with well-constructed buildings, and in Indonesia, where homes are often unreinforced masonry, the people who survived earthquakes in the past actually ran outside. You know, there is growing conversation in disaster preparedness about community-maintained infrastructure versus centralized government systems, and this is a real case study for why local trust really matters. Indonesia and Japan are both on the Pacific Ring of Fire, but they have very different building standards, so the survival advice gap is a real public health issue, and I’m happy that this is being addressed with infrastructure that already exists and doesn’t really need any extra upkeep since they’re being used all the time. Egg carton reuse Arielle: The next solution is titled “Six smart things to do with an empty egg carton before you toss it in the recycling bin”. Before you toss your next empty egg carton, hear me out. Those 12 little cups, or 10 or six, depending on how many eggs you get, they turn out to be surprisingly useful around the house, and the seed-starting one especially. So that’s one of the uses that I’m going to get into. You just fill each cup with soil, you plant your seeds in them, and then when it’s time, just plant the whole thing into the ground, and then the cardboard breaks down, and the roots never get disturbed. So that would be something that I would do if I had a garden. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: Another one that I liked was the jewelry organization thing. So you can create little cups for your jewelry, and right now, all of my jewelry is just, like, willy-nilly all over the place in different rooms in tangles. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: So I don’t need a garden to do that one, so maybe I will try that one out. Karissa: Yeah, I, I love this, and there’s really a big momentum around reducing household waste without buying more eco products, and this is about using what you already have. Japanese sweet potatoes Arielle: The next solution is titled “What sets Japanese sweet potatoes apart, nutritionally speaking?” Japanese sweet potatoes are those, like… They just look like sweet potatoes, but they’re generally kind of longer, I find, and they look purple on the outside, and then when you cut them open, they’re white on the inside. And it turns out that even though they are still sweet potatoes, they are doing completely different things nutritionally than the ones, like the orange ones that so many of us know and love. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: And the comparison is more interesting than you’d expect. Japanese sweet potatoes are higher in vitamin C and E and anthocyanins, the same pigments that make blueberries and red cabbage dark, while orange ones are the beta carotene champions. They’re complementary, not interchangeable. The fiber content is about four grams per serving, which puts them in, like, a genuinely filling territory for a carb. And luckily, there’s no evidence-based recommendation for how many to eat per week, so you don’t necessarily need to limit yourself if you end up really, really loving Japanese sweet potatoes. The only thing is that dieticians say, um, make sure you don’t, like, hyper-fixate on them, just like on any food, and don’t make them your only kind of vegetable. Have you tried Japanese sweet potatoes before, Karissa? Karissa: Honestly, I don’t think I have. And I’m kind of not the biggest fan of just, like, normal sweet potatoes either, so they’re okay, but, like, I… And if they’re out, like, at a restaurant or something, like, and you know, it’s in front of me, I’ll eat it, but I usually, like… I, I never feel like preparing it myself. But maybe I’ll give Japanese sweet potatoes a try, and maybe I’ll fall in love with them. Overwintering bees Arielle: The last solution that we are going to share with everyone today is titled “What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees”. This could be considered a counterintuitive one, but maybe not so counterintuitive for longtime Optimists. The best thing you can do for native bees this fall is put down the rake. All that scraggly stuff you’re about to tidy away, the leaf piles, the hollow stems, the dead-looking cane fruit, that’s where the bees love to be. There are over 3,600 native bee species in the US, and most aren’t honey bees. It’s those solitary wild bees that are in steep decline, and most of them nest in your garden over winter. So don’t compost your cut stems in fall. If bees have already nested inside them, composting kills the larvae still developing in there, and I did not know that. I didn’t realize that there’s, like, little baby bees… inside cut stems. Also, try not to worry yourself about the bare patches of dirt in your lawn if you have them. I know it might look like neglected land, but that’s prime bee nesting habitat, apparently. Ground-nesting bees need bare, un-compacted soil to excavate their nests. Karissa: Wow, I didn’t even realize that there were that many, uh, bee species in the US for one, but, um… native bee decline is an issue that feels kind of, uh, abstract until you realize that the solution is literally just doing less yard work, and I love that because- Mm. Yeah … working in the yard can be such a pain. Arielle: Yeah, I mean, I kinda wish I had one. But it can be, uh, it can be toilsome. And maybe the solution sounds familiar to some people… because we have covered No Mow May before, and I think there have been a few articles about, like, just not raking so much in the fall. Yeah. Um, ’cause that doesn’t just help bees, but it also helps other insects and critters that are important for the ecosystem. Quote & Outro Karissa: Well, Arielle, that was a great roundup of solutions, and before we head off for today, we have a positive quote to leave you off with. Arielle: This one is by Robert Frost, and it is, “The best way out is always through.” Karissa: Simple. Arielle: So yes, that’s, uh, yeah, nice and simple, but hard to do sometimes when you’re faced with a situation that you kinda wanna get out of, but you just have to endure and go through it. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Uh, but yeah. Well, on that note, Karissa and I wish all of you a very happy weekend, and we will be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, stay optimistic. Bye! The post Podcast Transcript October 16th, 2026— Flu is already spreading: why October is the window to get vaccinated, plus nine more solutions first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Έφηβοι σώζουν τη γιαγιά και το 2χρονο παιδί παγιδευμένο κάτω από το νερό σε ένα καρότσι
items.titleOriginal: Teens Save Grandmother and 2-Year-Old Trapped Underwater in a Stroller
items.description: Δύο έφηβοι από την Ιντιάνα μετέτρεψαν μια τρομακτική στιγμή σε απίστευτη διάσωση όταν πήδηξαν στη δράση για να σώσουν μια γιαγιά και τα δύο μικρά εγγόνια της από μια λιμνούλα, συμπεριλαμβανομένου ενός 2χρονου που είχε παγιδευτεί κάτω από το νερό σε ένα καρότσι.
items.descriptionOriginal: Two Indiana teenagers turned a frightening moment into an incredible rescue when they jumped into action to save a grandmother and her two young grandchildren from a retention pond, including a 2-year-old who was trapped underwater in a stroller.

items.title: Τα ηλιακά πάνελ Magenta μπορεί να είναι το πιο έξυπνο κόλπο των αγροβολταϊκών
items.titleOriginal: Magenta solar panels may be agrivoltaics’ cleverest trick yet
items.description: Οι φάρμες λαχανικών και οι ηλιακές φάρμες χρειάζονται πολύ ηλιακό φως και ανοιχτό χώρο. Πώς όμως χωρίζουμε τα περιορισμένα εδάφη μας μεταξύ αυτών των δύο προτεραιοτήτων; Μια κομψή λύση είναι να τοποθετήσετε καλλιέργειες και ηλιακούς συλλέκτες στην ίδια γη—και να μοιραστείτε το ευρύ φάσμα του εισερχόμενου ηλιακού φωτός μεταξύ τους. Μια νέα μελέτη στο Cell Reports Physical Science το κάνει αυτό με φωτοβολταϊκά…
items.descriptionOriginal: Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them. A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels —without sacrificing the harvest. Agrivoltaic schemes— putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California . Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs. But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses. A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , growing corn for energy to solar production. It’s no contest. In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity. Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants. The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower. This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses. Lu et al. “ Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems .” Cell Reports Physical Science , 2026.
